other night. One critic was Mr. Dorchester Hights, of
Boston, the other was Mr. Jack Park, of Chicawo.
They discussed a certain actor. “In his acting,” re-
marked the Boston critic, “I«liscovered with a single,
and, as it were. casual wlance, that there were lacking
most apparently the first requisites necessary for the

not a noble one!—to become a high and exalted lumiu-
ary of the Thespian art. And so, in my critique, it be-
came incumbent upon mé, asa true exponent of my
convictions, to launch upon him my severest and
barsbest disapprobation, the which I did with no co-
Yert attempt to disguise in the most infinitesimal de-
gree my dissatisfaction with his interpretation of the
dramatist’s——”

**Yes,” observed the Chicago dramatic critic, ‘‘I
ripped him up the back myself!"

tion of almost violent insurrection. Gov.
Flower has called out the militia to quell the
railroad rioters at Buffalo, N. Y,; the soldiers
are still doing active service at Homestead, Pa..

and the eastern part of Tennessee fs at the
mercy of a mob of 3,000 armed and desperate
miners. Life and property are imperilled.

As yet there has been no bloodshed in this
State, but much railroad property has been de-
stroyed. The prompt fesponse to the call to
arms undoubtedly prewnted furthor violence.
but the condition is Still so serious that the
Governor believer !t expedient to keep the en-
tire National Ge4rd in readiness to march to
the scene of ction at a moment’s notice.

In Hom-tead there was a brief skirmish be-
tween he strikers and the militia the other
dav Several rounds of shots were exchanged,
vut fortunately no lives were forfeited.

The situation in Tennessee, however. is more
serious. Up to the present time the troops
have been unable to successfully cope with the
striking miners. The soldiers have been routed

from their strongholds and the mob is in undis-
puted possession of the eastern part of the
State. They have captured Tracy City, Inman.
Oliver Springs and Coal Creek, driven the sol-
diers away and burned the stockades. The
governor has ordered out the entire State
militia and a serious conflict is looked forward
to, The miners are reported to have received
reinforcements from Kentucky and are pre-
pared to make a stubborn fight against the
authorities. They are all heavily armed and
are desperate men in an encounter. The out-
come of the struggle is awaited with great
anxiety.

Meanwhile, what are we coming to?

“Donato, an ex-bull-fighter, was the man who may
be said to have originated the skirt dance, now so pop-
ular,” said Capt. Thompson to me the other afternoon.
“He had lost a leg, gored by a bull, in Spain, and when
he came to London, he sang on the stage fora living.
Enveloped in a big cloak, Donato stood on his one leg,
danced and postured, and folded the long flowing coat
about him as he danced and postured, much as Loie
Fuller and Minnie Renwood do to-day.”

Harry Neagle, just back from London. says Vaude-
ville is all the rage over there, and regular theatrical
business dull. He says “Lights of Home” bas one of
the best shipwreck scenes he ever saw.

Armed Miners Attack
Four Towns and Shoot
Down Defenders.

HARD-FOUGHT BATTLES.

Stockades at Tracy City, In-
man and Oliver Springs
Taken and Burned.

BATTLE AT COAL GREEK.

Col. Anderson’s Little Garrison
Makes a Brave Defense.

GEN. CARNES TO THE RESCUE.

[SUBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION.)

Strikes and riots are still rampant. The trouble
which began at Homestead, Pa., has spread. Tennes-
see is in a state of insurrection. The New York State
militia has been called to arms to quell the rioters at
Buffalo. At Homestead, Pa., the soldiers are still do-
ing active service, and there was a conflict between
them and the strikers a few days ago.

It isin Tennessee, however, where the greatest alarm
is felt. Fora week or more 3,000 armed miners were
in possession of the eastern part of the State, and ter-
ror reigned. They captured Tracy City. Inman and
Oliver Springs, and made a desperate attack on Coal
Creek. The battle at the latter place resulted in a
great loss of life. '

The miners met with but little resistance at Tracy
City and Inman, and after capturing the strongholds
and releasing the convicts they immediately burned
the stockades. Then they marched in a body upon
Oliver Springs. This stockade was defended by thirty
or forty soldiers and a few guards. The attacking
party, however, is said to have numbered 1,800. The
defenders saw the folly of resistance and surrendered.
The victorious miners took possession of all the arms,
loaded the convicts and soldiers on a cattle train and
started them off. Then the miners poured oil over the
stockade and burned it.

Great excitement was caused in Knoxville, Memphis,
and other cities by the outbreak, and the Governor
was denounced for not calling out the entire State
militia. :

The miners then marched on Coal Creek with th
same determination to wipe out the little garrison of
150 men commanded by Cul. Anderson,a brave ex-
Confederate soldier. The attack was made on August
18, anda fierce battle was fought. Assault after as-
sault was made, but the little garrison made a brave

AWAITING BULLETINS IN MEMPHIS.

and effective defense. Col. Anderson was asked to
surrender, but he curtly refused to do so. The sol-
diers had a Gatling gun, while the miners were armed
with acannon. The noise of the battle was heard in
the neizhboring villages, and the wildest kind of ex-
citement ensued. Wild rumors were afloat. It was
eaid that the little garrison had surrendered, and that
Col. Anderson had been lynched by the miners.

Later dispatches stated that Col. Anderson had been
captured under a flag of truce and threatened with
hanging unless he ordered bie command to surrender.
He, however, defied his captors, This report proved
true,

Mearwhile Gen. Carnes, with 700 volunteers and
regulars, was on his way to rescue Col. Anderson and
his garrison.

A dispatch, dated August 19, tells the following
story:

Brig.-Gen. Carnes, in command of the soldiers, has
routed the miners at Coal Creek. He thinks he can
maintain his advantage and enforce peace. He has
700 men, armed with regulation army rifies, one Gat-
ling gun and a small field-piece.

Col. Kellar Anderson has been surrendered to Gen.
Carnes by the miners. He is alive and weil.

Gen. Carnes passed through Knoxville yesterday
evening at 7.30 o'clock. This morning he advanced
on Coal Creek, capturing the town and several miners.
He notified the insurgents, who were camped near by,
that unless they surrendered Col. Kellar Anderson he
would put bis prisoners to death.

They promised to make the exchange, but inste:d of
doing so effected a sortie and intrenched themselves
in the town from which Gen. Carnes had temporarily
withdrawn.

Gen. Carnes advanced again and at 4 o’clock had
possession of Coal Creek and 2U0 prisoners.

He again sent forth a demand for Col. Anderson, and
this time the prisoner was produced unburt.

Col. Anderson bad been keptall night in the moun-

CUTCING THE WIRES.

tains aud the miners several times discussed the pro-
priety of hanging him. He was subjected to numer-
ous insults and indignities, but he bore himself coolly
and courageously.

There is intense excitement all over the State, and if
it is necessary there will be 20,000 voluntears massed
at Coal Creek by Monday.

At Memphis, while the fate of Col. Anderson, who is
a popular citizen of that place, was in doubt, the
streets were thronged with citizens anxious to start
for the seat of war.

A number of telegrams were sent to Gen. Carnes ad-
vising him to hang every miner he could lay hands on
if Anderson was harmed.

It is believed that the insurrection is practically
quelled, but the troops will not be withdrawn until or-
der is absolutely assured. °

Fort Anderson has been relieved by thearriva) of th
reinforcements and is no Jonger in a state of siege. On
the contrary the tablesare turned and the miners in-
stead of being hunters of men are the hunted. Gen.
Carnes made a forced march from Offuts Station,
north of Clinton, to the neighborhood of the beleag-
ured camp, reaching there at daybreakin the rear of
the line of rabble which marked the miner's lines.

On his arrival on the ground a wild scene of confu-

| DEPARTURE OF THE

NEW YORK BOYS

sion ensued. Scouts in advance of the line had either
failed to do their duty or been captured, and the posi-
tion of the miners was not known. The forwaré move-
ment was very cautiously made. Gen. Carnes and bis
heterogeneous army of citizens and about three hun-
dred militia left the train at Offutts Station, fearing a
trap somewhere on the railroad, and pushed forward
across the country.

GEN. CARNES’ DIVISION SURPRISED.

As they cautiously felt their way amid the rocks and
rushing streams of the mountains a sudden explosion
from a bomb of dynamite startled the men as they
shook the clogging mud from their overburdened
shoes or wrung the acc: mulated rain-water from their
sodden clothing. From Offutts to Coal Creek, by the
route taken by the co!umn of Gen. Carnes, was a la-
boriogs climb, and as laborious a descent of a moun-
tain pase as the foothilis of the Cumberland range
affords any where, and is good eight miles, as you go
but “one thousand as you slip.”

As the head of the column cautiously pushed out
from the cloud of fog and darkness which had envel-
oped itas it came down the side of the mountain, a
shot rang out. A young soldier named Walthall had
gotten upon a rock to try and get a view, when he was
struck by a ball and fell headlong among his comrades
a corpse.

A body of miners had chosen a sheltered rock which
formed a natural defense, and from its shelter fired
a volley which caused the only casaalty. Curiously
enoysh, the miners had taken no other provision to
prevent the rear attack, their outposts being the vol-
unteer service of a few men who felt the dangers of
an exchange of clothing which capture would mean.
A mad rush was made for the cover of the rocks and
trees of the mountains.

Not all were so craven, fora desultory firing began
and was kept up for a while. Oué or two of the militia-
men were struck by their oullets. Eighteen of the
miners were captured, the balance having escaped in-
to the*woods.

Gen. Carnes’s advance guard at once formed intoa
charging line, and after receiving a scattering volley
from a few who failed to take the first opportunity of
escaping from the rapidly approaching arm and hand
of the law, two of the Sheriff's posse, John Walthall,
» clerk in the offices of the East Tennessee, Virginia &
Georgia road, of Kuoxville, and Bosh Givens, also of
Knoxville, were shot and killed.

This detachment had a most arduous task to per-
forta in crossing the mountain at night in the midst of
a heavy rain and lowering clouds of mist, which wade
itimpossible to distinguish objects more than a few
feet away, with an unknown and supposedly alert
enemy surrounding them. Every rock, bush and tree
mtght be the hiding-place of an enemy, and there was
an almost certain fight in front of them when they
should arrive in the locality of Camp Anderson. It
was under cover of night that they were enabled to
reach their destination almost without disaster.

At Clinton, before leaving for the immediate front,
they were subjected to innuendoes and threats, with
numérous bits of information that the way was lined
with dynamite and strong bodies of well-armed and
disciplined miners swarming on every side.

Two bodies of dead miners were found after the
skirmish, and several wounde’ were taken in and
cared for. With these exceptions, the casualties among
the miners are unknown.

The Riots at Buffalo, N. Y.

The strike of the switchmen in the Cheektowaga
freight yards at Buffalo, N. Y., resulted in Gov. Flower
calling out the State militia. The strikers are said to
number from 300 to 400 men, but their sympathizers
are reported to number thousands. On Aug. 15 riot-
ing began. Trains.were blockaded and freight cars
burned. Sheriff Beck called on the Sixty-fifth Regi-

FOR BUFFALO,

ment of Buffilo. and the soldiers took possession of
the yards on Aug. 16. The situation became serious.
Trains were stalled, and a conflict between the author:
ities and the rioters was imminent. The present force
was inadequate to guard the railroad property, and
finally the Snerift and Mayor appealed to t! e Gover-
por. The latter orderad the entire State militia under
arms, and 8,000 armed soldiers were at once dis
patched to the scene of the riot. Among the regiments
who left for Buffalo on Aug. 18 were the Twelfth,
Seventy-first, Troop A and Twenty-second of this city
and the Thirteenth and Twenty-third of Brooklyn. All
the other regiments were held in readiness.

The presence of the militia at Buffalo broke the
blockade and trains began to run with more regu-
larity. The people of Buffalo aleo rested more com-
fortably. The yards and the miles of tracks were
placed ander military guard. There was no conflict
between the-strikers and soldiers, but the latter were
compeed to submit to insults and taunts. On one or
two occasions the militia charged the mob with fixed
bayonets in order to disperse them. No shots were
fired, and with the exception of two soldiers killed by
accident, no casualties were reported. One soldier was
shot by the accidental discharge of a rifle in the hands
of a comrade, and another was crushed to death by a
freight car.

Since the militia took possession of the city there
has been no outbreak, but the situation is still very
wrave,and the authorities deem it expedient to keep
8,000 suldiers on the spot. and bold the remainder of
the Nat onal Guard in readiness for an emergency.

The Trouble at Homestead, Pa.

The trouble at Homestead, Pa., has not been settled.
The militia are still on guard,and on the night of

IN AMBUSH.

Angust 17 there was a sharp but brief conflict between
the soldiers and the strikers. Ou the evening in ques-
tion, aga freight train was crossing over the ‘‘Pem-
icky” bridge at Humestead, going south, some one on
the train opened fire on.the steamboat Little Bill,
which was moored this side of the bridge. Several
shots were fired in rapid succession. Those persons
who were in the pilot house narrowly escape: death.

The soldiers guarding the boat opened fire on the
train. shine provisional guard on the other side of the
river ned in the fire,and so did the other pickets
posted inside the mill. A volley of lead poured into
the train, but as far as could be learned no serious
damage resulted.

Provost Marshal Major Crawford heard the firing
and started with a squad of men for the mill. They
went on a double quick and soon were at the scene.

CAPTURE OF ANDERSON.

When the squad arr ved fully 1,000 of the men in the
mill were crowded along the shore.

They were greatly excited. The light from the coke
ovens across the river lit up the scene. Aboard the
Little Bill and the Tide soldiers were hurrying to and
fro, each with bis gun at half cock.

Across the river orders could be heard, clear and
plain, as they were given to the provisional guard, and
occasionally a shot was fired. After a search along the
tracks the Marshal recalled his men and they returned
to camp.

DOG, “DONE” AND DAISY.”
(Supsxct or ILLvseTRaTion.|

One afternoon recently a pretty girl hired a donkey
at Cone’ Island for the purpose of taking a ride a:eng
the beach. Everything went lovely until a naughty

wrobpgs.

“I met Burns,” she said, ‘in this city, about a year
and a half ago, and was introduced to him by a mut-
ual friend, who resid:s in Covington. He invited me
to accompany him to Eichler's for supper, and I ac-

much he loved me,and asked me to marry him. I

also have to get the consent of my parents. I prom-

WOUNDED HIS WIFE’S ABDUCTOR.

Some months ago Lewis Dean of Petersburg, Ind.,
persuaded the wife of John James of Montgomery to
elope with him. The couple weut to Petersburg, and
there lived as man and wife for some time, but James
finally induced hie wife to return to him with a prom-
ine to forgive her.

The other afternoon in company with a man named
Moore, Dean drove up to the home of James in a
buggy. Leaving the horse with Moore, Dean ap-
proached the house, and when he reached the door he
said: “James, by —— I've come to get your wife, and
you had better not interfere with me.” He then seized
Mrs. James and carried her to the buggy, whereupon
James procured a rifle and fired it point blank at the
would-be kidnapper. Dean then drew bis revolver
and fired at James. The men then ceased firing and
Dean retreated.

A number of loggers, who were near by. rushed to
the James home and surrounded Dean. James, who
was shot through the left arm, burried to the city and
gave himself up. He then-caused a warrant to be is-
sued for Dean and Moore.

Officers who burried to the scene of the shooting
found that Dean had been taken by Moore to Peters-
burg, where he was found in charge of three physi-
cians. Dean was fatally wounded.

ALREADY FORTH RY

Jack McAuliffe in Trim for His
Coming Battle.

HE SAYS HE WILL WIN.

Not a Believer in Severe Train-
ing Methods.

DOWN TO FIGHTING WEIGHT.

Jack McAuliffe.the holder of the “Police Gazette”
championship belt, is now busily engayed in training
for his battle with Billy Myer, for $5,000 a side and a
purse of $10,000 offered by the Oly mpic Club and the
lightweight championship of America, at Bay St.
Louis. He is attended by Matty Crowe and Jack Nel-
son, of New London. The latter accompanies Jack
upon all his walks, and spars with him regularly, but
upon Crowe falls the real work of the training, which’
has not, however, yet become irksome.

There is leas severity in the daily routine than is ob-
served by most men in training. The cool and invig-
orating air is conducive to sleepiness, and the three
men do not arise very early yet. They commence their
day witha plungein the cold waters of the stream,
followed by « bard rub down and vigorous exercise.

Then breakfast is on the programme, and the re-

JACK M’AULIFFE.

sources of the poultry popniation of the vicinity are
taxed severely to supply the cottage larder, while the
destruction of chops and the numerous accompani-
ments is marvelous. McAuliffe is not yet ona strict
diet, but is satisfied, he says, with the ordinary coun

try menn.

McAuliffe says that he hears that Myer is working
hard and will make the effort of his life at New Or-
leans, but he is perfectly confident of an easy victory
over the Westerner. It will depend wholly upon Myer,
he says, whether the fight is short or comparatively
long. x

“I am in the business,” said McAuliffe, “wholly for
money. The reputation is good for nothing beyond
the revenue which it brings. If there were only repu-
tation in it I should go into the shop and work for a
living. For that reason I have always refused to fight
for small purses. :

“To win this battle with Myer means not only a
great purse for me, but an entire season’s engagement
in England at $500 per week, for which I shall sail im-
mediately after the New Orleans battles. I know of

MAULIFFE PUNCHING THE BAG.

no other fights in the future, unless the trip to Eng-
land should be the means of arranging one.
“Tam well pleased atthe idea of meeting Myer in

Mew Orleans, although it weuld, of course, have been

easier and better had the match been arranged for
Coney Island, as some of my friends tried to have it.

“But Presideut Noel is a first-class man, and his
club the pluckiest in the country. If you don’t think
80, look at the $60,000 which they are to risk upon
those September battles. It is great luck that our
match is arrauged for the first evening, as it gives me
a chance to see the other two.”

“But you may get your eyes closed so that youcan’t,
Jack,” suggested one of the listeners.

“My boy, if you want to grow wealthy, just stake all
your money, Do matter at what odds, that your uncle
will get into no such condition,” retorted McAuliffe,
with a smile of confidence.

His forenoons are quiet, representing very little
work, altbough he has been threatening to labor from
early morning in some neighboring hay field and
make Crowe and Nelson accompany him, the mere an-

e AT A LIVELY GAIT.

nouncement creating consternation on the part of the
two trainers on several occasions when they have be-
lieved he really meant it, for aftera careful examina-
tion of requirements and results they are not am-
bitious, they say. to become farmers.

“Really, about all I do here mornings,” said Mc-
Auliffe when first asked the question, ‘‘is to chase
ducks.”’

“Be careful and have it explained,”” broke in Crowe,
“that this farm and stream abound in ducks, for the
boys might think that it was a kind of ‘chasing the
duck’ known to fame, but outside the limits of this
State.”

{tis rather a light luncheon that they have at the
McAuliffe training table, for not very much later, and
before the heat of the day is over, the lightweight
champion and bis attendants don heavy sweaters, and.
with shor€ walking sticks, start on a five-mile tramp.

He frequently loses three pounds in one of these
tramps, which.is considered remarkable. His heavy
russet walking shoes are always soaked with water.

Here he remains for a couple of hours working most
of the time. His favorite exercise is throwing the
great “medicine balls,” although he rows a little,
works at the chest weights, spars a few rounds with
Nelson, and, as he expresses ii, saya “‘how-de-do” to
the dumbbells, In addition he has had the gloves on
with every member of the club, much rivalry existing
for the opportunity of having a “zo” with the clever
visitor, while the resulting set-tos furnish increasing
amusement.

Since working off the most of b's ‘at, McAuliffe has
been following another of his ow» uotions and putting
his legs and arma in a strong pickle, which he keeps
all brewed in the club rooms, notwithstanding the
delicate olfactory nerves of some of the members.
He says that it toughens the fiesh without bardening
it and he knows of nothing that would work to as
good advantage with him.

He does not retire very early, and will not do so
during his training, he says.

McAuliffe writes from Bay St. Louis that he is down
to his fighting weight, and appears confident of win-
ming. He says that Jimmy Colville, of Boston, will
be his timekeeper.

Ever since the introduction of the new-fangled, all-

was continually talking abeut the freedom of action
the adoption of the new underwear and the abandon-
ment of underskirts gave to one, but she isn’t saying
aword about itnow. Cause why? Oh. only a little
accident, just one of those little things Mabie to occur
anywhere and toany one. She was riding down Penn-
sylvania avenue the other night accompanied by her
best young man, who rides a bicycle; the electric light
made the avenue almost as light as day. except in the
shadow of an occasional tree,and just as the young
couple started to show the pedestriaus what speed was
in them something snapped, there was an ominous,
tearing sound, and the young lady found her serge
skirt pulled clean off the waist and tangled around the

the machine, and made a bee-line for an open side-
door, which was fortunately near-by. With only her
blushing face peeping from behind the door she di-
rected the young man to untangle her skirt and bring
itto her. The young lady hasa big brother who now
makes her life miserable by asking her how she en-
joyed her first public appearance in tights.

Ted Pritchard’s March to the

NOCKER-OUT.
The Man Whom Jim Hall Con-

quered in Four Rounds.

A NOTABLE PRIZE RING HERO.

Probably one of the greatest pugilists that has stood
in the arenain the middle-weight class, with the ex-
ception of Jack Dempsey, since Tom Sayers, the chaw-
pion of England, is Ted Pritchard, of Lambeth, Lon-
don, Eng. Pritchard, from his boyhood days, has
been a pugilist, and, like Jack McAuliffe, the light-
wéight champion of America, and John L. Sullivan, is
a born fighter.

Pritchard is by trade what people politely call a
Knight of St. Crispin, like Joe Goss. His father welts
the soles and now Pritchard welts the bodies. He was
born in Lambeth, London, England.

Pritchard drifted into the profession of the noble
art at fourteen years of age by winning two competi-
tions promoted by Mickey Welch, and followed it up
with another brace, organized by Johnny Welch, ere
he reached his fifteenth year. Pudney Sullivan was
the first to check his career of success, and Bill
Whately followed suit. ‘‘A bit of a boy,” but very
cute Ted was now offered bis first start in life. A man
who traveled with a penny show gave bim an offer to
form one of the troupe of boxers, and Pritchard glad-
ly accepted the proffered engagement. :

He went on a tour, and if bis clients did not appre-
ciate his knocking out propensities, the same cannot
be said of hisemployer. He proved a regular little
Tartar, and made his mark upon the dial of many a
would-be clever youth whose vaulting ambition over-

TED PRITCHARD.

leaped itself. After a little while he separated from
the fold and returned to London, and soon joined an-
other company of strolling players.

Finally he resolved to abandon the life of a show-
man,andtry his luck in “the smoke.” There hap-
pened to be a competition at Plumstead, England, and
Pritchard entered. When it became known the en-
trants declined to compete, as some of them had met
Pritchard on the road. Yorkey, of Leeds, however,
would not be stalled off, and the promoter determined
to give the prizes for a six rounds contest; but Pritch-
ard outed the Yorkshireman early in the competition.

Pritchard then entered the all-comers competition,
promoted by Frank Hinde, at the Imperial Theatre of

PRITCHARD IN FIGHTING ARRAY.

the Royal Westminster Aquarium, London, Engiand.
For the final he bad to meet Dave Burke. It was a
most exciting encounter, Dave being severely pun-
ished and in dire distress, but he stood to his guna
most manfully, and Pritesard having to put forward

all the ability of which he was possessed, finally won.
Later he was matched with Jem Hayes, for £100
aside, under Queensberry rules, the contest tak-
ing place at the Lambeth School of Arms on Feb. 19,
1889, when, after boxing 4 rounds, the friends of
Hayes broke into the ring and the stakes were subse-
quently awarded to Pritchard. Ou June 6 in the same
year, and at the same place he met Alec Burns, who
was matched as an Unknown, under similar condi-
tions. This also proved to be of very short duration,
as Pritchard, getting home a heavy blow on the jaw in
the opening round, gave hie wan no rest afterward,
and won in the second round.

Pritchard’s next battle was with Alf Mitebeji for
$2,000. The encounter was decided at London, Eng..
Dec. 15, 1890, and Pritchard won in four rounds,

The Pritchard aud Burke fight was decided on March
12,1891. The battle waa for £1.000 and the middle
weight championship of Euglaud. Burke was knocked
out in the third round.

Pritchard was subsequently matched to fight Jem
Smith for £1,000 and the championship of England,

PRITCHARD KNOOKS OUT JEM SMITH.

The battle was decided on July 27, 1891, at London,
England. In the first round Smith took a decided
lead. He gave Pritchard a heavy blow on the body,
drove him all over the ring, and floored him twice be-
fore time was culled, Pritchard then seeméd to be
dazed. In the second round, however, a sufprising
change occurred. Pritchard was sprightly, while
Smith appeared to be weak. Pritchard forbed the
fizhbting with such effect that Smith soon showed signs
of baving enoug!. ‘Twice the men went dowg, but at
the close of the round Smith was hardly able to stand.

The third round was a one-sided affair. Pritchard
had quite his own way, and placed bis opponent prone
and helpless on bis back, The display was far from
scieutific. Both men tried to settle the affair as quick-
ly as possible. Both Smith's eyes were blackened, and
his cheeks were puffed and cut considerably.

One night recently Mrs. C. E. Noble, of Poughkeep-

cigarettes were the cause of his down fall.

By Jim Hall, the Shifty Austra-
lian Pugilist.

TED WAS BADLY PUNISHED.

[Scasect or ILLvsTRaTtion,]
[SPRCIAL CABLE TO THK POLICK GAZETTE. ]
LONDON, August 90, 1897.

The glove fiuht between Jim Hall, of New York (formerly of
Austraiia), and Ted Pritchard, of Lambeth, the champion prize
fighter of Engian«d, wageecided a Brighton to-day. Pritchar:,
owing to the fact that he had defeated Alf Mitehell. Burke and
Jom Smith, the latter for the championship of England, was
the faverite at 6 to 4 = The felt ended in a victory for Hall,
who knocked out the English champion itn the fourth round,
Hall displayed great form and surprised Pritchard's backers

The men fonght with smal! gloves, according Ww Queensberry

Warren Lewis, of New York. the well-known American sport-
ing man, and Chariey Mitchell backed Hall, while George
Baird, better known as Squire Abington, backed Pritchard.
Warren Lewis backed his protege heavily and surprised the
natives by the way he bet his ‘‘menkeys” on the Australian.

The fight took piace at Perthsiade, in the presence of forty
spectators. Charley Mitchell won the toss for Hall, and placed
him with his back to the sun, which beat down fiercely on the
men.

Pritchard was seconded by Sam Blakelock and Jack Baldock,
" while Charley Mitchell and Charley Rowell, who trained Hall,
seconded him. Warren Lewis was Hall's timekeeper.

Bets were made at 7 to 4.0n Pritchard. One wager of £100 that
Hall would not stay three rounds caused Hall to smile. The
Australian was taller by three inches and had a much longer
reach than his adversary. It required only a glance to see that
both boxers were aplendidly trained. At the weighing-in
neither put the scales above 160 pounds.

Hali’s immense advantage in reach and height was noticeable
as they squared off. Pritchard spent littie time in looking over
bis adversary. but sailed in wickedly, probably with the idea of
xetting through the Job as quickly as possible. His leads, how-
ever, fell shert in nearly every instance, and the Australian's
remarkable cleverness astonished not only the Engilsh cham-
plom, but everybody about the ring. Spry as he was, Pritchard
was no match for Hall, who met him at each rush with well-
directed left-hand biows on the face and neck. Seeing how little
chance he had to break through Hall's guard, Pritchard tried to
close in, At this style of fighting he had no chance whatever,
for Hall dreve him off handily. From the end of the first min-
ute until time was called they were constantly at it, with the
Australian showing admirable generaiship and tremendous
punching powers.

Afver a few exchanges In the second round, Hall, whose
timing of blows had previously been excellent, made a mi>scal-
culation in a jead and Pritchard crossed him, landing with ter-
rible force on the Australian's jaw. Down he went ina heap.
Pritchard ginred at his fallen opponent and a confident smilo
played on his lips. Walking toward his corner he held out his
gloves #9 that Baldock could lousen the strings. His seconds
yelled enthusiastically and hailed Ted as champion.

“'Ow's yer Australian now?” cried Biakelock, eying Mitchell
contemptuously across the ring.

“A fight's never won till it’s over,” retorted England's great.
eat fichter.

And before the timekeeper reached ‘‘nine”’ In his count Hall
was on his feet. This angered Pritchard, who pitched in ham-
mer and tongs. But Hall, dazed as he was, soon recovered and
was really doing most of the fighting when the round closed.

It was a keen disappointment to Baldock’s man, this unex-
pected turn in the affair, and he showed signs of distress in the
third round. The fall seemed to have brightened the Australian
up, for he made a sorry spectacie of Pritchard before taking his
seat for thethird time. A succession of short-arm punches on
the faceand jaw disfigured the English boxer's dial, and he
seemed to collapse. There was notascraich on Hall, and he
was breathing naturally when reund 4 was called. Pritchard
was very much disCreseed, and the jarring he received rather
muddled him.

Alter feinting once or twice, Hall let drive his left to the point
Of the jaw, and Pritchard tumbied over. He arose with creat
difficulty and Hal) waited until he had reached his feet squarely
before sending in his right hand. The blow landed on Pritch-
ard’scheekbone. Once more he toppled and fell. After a few
seconds he rolied over and lay on his face untli he was counted
out. It was fully a minute before the ammonia which his sec-
onde held under bis nostrils brought him back to consclousness.
Mitchell and Rewel: lifted Hall above their heads and a great
demonstration followed. °

The fourth round lasted only 1 minute 60 seconds.

Not a little interest was manifested in the ontcome of this
fight in America, for the reason that Hall, though an Australian,
has renonnced his allegiance to the British throne, and declared
his intention of becoming au American citizen. He went abroad
under the management of Parson Davies, whose fame as an tn-
citer of interest In pugtilistic affairs is world wide, and besides it
was American money that enabled him to meet the English
champion.

Hall tried to get a pugilistic footing in America by taking on
Fitzsimmons, but the conqueror of Jack Dempsey would have
none ef him. and in his eagerness for a fight the Australian had
to zo abroad for a title that would command Fitzsimmone’s at-
tention, and elther make him fight or relinquish his claim to the
championship. Hall made himeelf extremely popular during
his brief sqjourn in America, and althongh he engaged in no
finish fights he took the fancy of the leading sports. He proved
to be a clever man in the nse of his hands, and hie name was
placed among the tip-toppers despite the fact that he only gave
exhibition set-tos.

After the battle Richard K. Fox wired from Liandudno,
Wales, congratulations to Hall. The following cable was re-
ceived from Warren Lewis:

Hall is a wonder. He beat Pritchard easily, and surprised
sporting men here. Hal) will go back on City of Rome with me.
Americans backed Hall heavily, and received odds of 7 to 4.
Richard K. Fox says Halil is a wonder. On my return will de-
posit $6,000 with PoLice Gazette, match Mall to fight Bob Fits-
simmons for $10,000 a side and largest purse. About $20,000
changed hands on result. Warren Lewis.

GETTING READY FOR THE FIGHTS.

No time Is being lost by the O'ympic Athletic Club in New Or-
leans in making ita preparations for the big fights which will
take place in its arena next month.

The work on the arena is being pushed rapidly, and the ad-
ditions to the amphitheatre are nearly completed.

The big electric clock which was ordered bas not arrived, but
the officials are looking for it every day.

It is an absolute certainty that the crowd which will attend
their fights will exceed that which has attended any of their
noted seasons of carnival civen in New Orleans yearly, and ap-
plications for seats have been coming in with a rush.

The club management is sure of a successful nan ‘ial termin-
ation of the milis, and will do everything tu the power to
make their guests comfortadie.

The central office has not been opened, but it will be in a day
or two, and all applicatiens for information will meet with ready
service at the hands of Capt. Wiliiams, whose work as advance
representative of the club In the arrangements of the fights
have made him well known to every sperting man in the coun-
try.

At the Academy of Music, New York, on August 15,
George Godfrey and C. C. Smith, both colored, boxed four
rounds. &porting men who looked for a knockout were disap-
pointed. Still Smith was pretty badly punished in the wind and
his nose will be sere for many a day. Godfrey was much the
smaller man, and when he discovered that Smith was far from
being what sports term a “stuff,” he tried to get his adversary
to lead. Smith lost confidence when he tried several times and
missed. Godfrey would feint and ,then let drive at his oppon-
ent’s wind with his right. Twice he landed with tremendous
force. After that he coutented himself with prodding the big
man inthe nose. Smith was outclassed, and at the end of the
fourth round Jack Alder, the referee, declared Godfrey the
winner.

JAMES F. GILLESPIE,
(With Porrrairt.)

James F. Gillespie was born in Wheeling, W. Wa., on Sept.
21, 1867. Ring weicht, 140 pounds; height, 6 feet 73g inches,
Without training or competent instruction, he early entered the
ring and developed extraordinary ability to endure punish ment.
He is a long-win.Jed, patient fighter, growing more vicious as
the contest proceeds, is never discouraged by a reverse in the
ring, and often wins what seems a losing battie. First battle,
boat Prof. Atthur Mitchell London. Eng., 6 rounds. Dec. 18,
1891. Beat James Conners, of Pennsylvania, in 4-round fight,
thouch referee declared a draw. Conners declined to renew the
battle. Won seven local contests, and on March 19, 189%, met
and defeated Joe Jones, ot London, Eng., in a desperate battle
of 67 rounds Gillespie Is the acknowledged local champion of
West Virginia, and will meet any man of his class who can post
the requisite forfeit. He is modest, unassuming and courageons,
and will yet be heard from among the game and gallant fighters
who have made his class the boast and glory of the sporting
world, We predict for the broad-shouldered, genial young pu-
gi'ist a career that will neither disgrace himself nor disappoint
his friends.

“NORA MACHREE.”

In “N ra Muchree” Miss Sadie Scanian, who appears at the
People’s Theatre this week, has a play exactly suited to her
protean genius. She appears in the title rele, and it affords her
ample scope for the display of her versatility as an actress as
well as to introduce a number of beautiful songs of her own
composition. The character of Nora Machree \s a reproduction
ot Irish life, and no one can give the proper coloring, the true
touches of light and shade, unless thoroughly conversant with
every detail the character demands and able to reproduce them.

EACH THINKS HE WILL WIN.

The question that is agitating sporting men is how
the great contest between John L Sullivan, the champion of
the world, and Jim Corbett, the California Wonder, is going to
end, Shrewd betting men are, strange to say, backing Corbet,
when one would suppose their money would go on Sullivan,
Among these men are Phii Dwyer, John McCormick, Dave
Gideon, Alf Lakeland, Al Smith, Jack McDonald and Matty
Corbett, ali well known turfmen and bookmakers. There are
two reasons why these sporting men back Corbett. The first is
they believe John L. Sullivan is not the gladiator he was sev-
eral years agu: that he has been fighting tor over a decade and
has not the vitality left he should have owing to his following
the motte: “As we Journey through life let us live by the way.”
Second: the fact that Corbett defeated Kilrain in six rounds,
while it towk Sallivan seventy-five rounds to accomplish the
same feat, and then Corbett fought Poter Jackson to a stand-
still, and then Jackson defeats Slavin in short order—aiter the
latter had deteated Kilrain in nine rounds.

The assertion that Sullivan is not the great pugilist
he was six years ago may be true, and the battle on Sept. 7
wi that question, but trying to make Kilrain the trial
horse whereby to Judge Corbett’s Oghting abilities amounts to
nothing. At the time Sullivan fought Kilrain the latter was not
fit to fight; neither was Sullivan in condition to defeat a first-
class man. This fact was clearly demonstrated by the battie, if
it might be styled such. Sullivan was tired, and the excessive
heat heavily handicapped his chances.

Not long after Kilrain fought Sullivan he met Cor. “
bett In a six-round contest. He was not by any means well, and
trusted so much in his supposed ability that he did not prepare
for the battle believing he had to meet a selling plater instead
of a first-class. clever, active boxer. At the end of the six
rounds Oorbett was declared the winner. Thecontest was not
& Gnished battice. Neither was conquered, and Klirain was will-
ing w renew the contest in eight weeks for $5,000. Slavin later
defeated Kilrain fairly. Slavin's victory over Kilrain was more
decisive than Corbett’s because in the latter case Kilrain did not
stop, neither was he knocked out, while Siavin did put him to
sleep. _Corbett’s battle with Jackson was a creditable perform-
ance an: the only line to gauge his fighting ability and stami-
na, and yet Peter Jackson was suffering from an injury, and still
the honors were equally divided. The Jackson and Corbett con-
test proved that the latter was thoroughly game and possessed
wonderful stamina, and it is upon his endurance that he ex-
pects to defeat Sullivan by tiring him out In the ring,

Prior to Sullivan fighting Charley Mitchell in
France on March 10. 1888, it was claimed that if Sullivan did not
defeat Mitchell in ten rounds Mitchell would win, because Sulli-
van could not stay. Snuilivan did not win owing to the fact that
he spent more time in pleasure than in working while training.
He did not lose but he exploded the theory that he could net
fight for hours. Sullivan again, when he fought Kllrain, proved
he was not only @ great fighter but ho prssessed the staying
powers now so necessary in fisticencounters. If Corbett ex-
pects to outlast Sullivan in the ring the fight will necessarily be
along one, Sullivan will make the pace het, hit hard and often,
and if Corbett stands up and mixes it with the champion, the
battle will not be a protracted one.

oe a

The reason the Jackson and Corbett battle lasted
80 long, Jackson said, was owing to the tact that his sprained
leg gave out, and he could not follow up advantages. By the
way Jackson followed Slavin, who was supposed to be the best
man in the world when he challenged Sullivan, Jackson's claim
looks plausible. Corbeit, on the other hand, claims he would
have finished Jackson only that his hands gave way from con-
tinual blows which he landed on Jackson's head, and thus the

matter stands.
Ae Bw

Sullivan’s admirers, Pat Sheedy, Charley Johnston,
George H, Engeman, Capt. Ordway, of Buswn, claim that if
Sullivan only enters the ring in condition he will win. They ad-
mit Corbett is a clever boxer, but they do not believe he will be
able to stand the heavy blows Sullivan will land, while they
know that the Californian’s hands are not tough snough to do
Touch injury to Sullivan. Corbett has the advantage in height
and len.th of reach, and probably he is more active in the rig,
but the wonderful hitting powers of Sulliven, if he is strong,
has plenty of wind and io condition, should win.

Sullivan has been battling in the prise ring since
1879, and during his wonderful fistic career he has never met
with defeat, and has only been knocked down twice. He has
met champions from all parts of the world, and in every battie
he engaged In if he did not win he did not lose, He says that
his coming contest with Corbett, if he wins, will be his last, and
he ls going to do his best to win. All reports about bis not
training faithfully are absurd. He is aware that if he wins he
will receive a purse of $25,000 the largest purse ever offered, and
the largest amount of money two pugilists from Jack Brough-
ton’s time to date ever fought for, besides $20 000 in stakes.
Bhould Sullivan win, at the lowest calculation he will receive
$80,000—$5,000 from the stakes and the purse. Shouid Corbett
defeat Sullivan he will receive the purse and $10,000 of the
stakes, making $85,000, his backers will only retain the $10,000
they posted, but Corbett will have to defray his own training
expenses.

a ee

The fight is now beginning to be the topic of con-
versation, and before many moons it will be settied whether
John L. Sullivan still holds the “Police Gazette” champion belt
and the champlenship of the world, or James Corbett. Should
the latter win he will be kept busy in defending his title, for
Peter Jackson, Joe Goddard and Frank P. Slavin are still in the
race for the championship.

No matter what any one may think of Sullivan
personally, no one who has seen him, as I have, fur the past
two weeks, could help admiring his fortitude and grim deter-
mination to reduce his bulk and increase his strength and ac-
tivity, in spite of all obstacies. One of his heels was badly
* chafed and a mosquito bit him on the toe when he was asleep
He picked it with his finger nail and it became very sore; so
much so that he limped perceptibly when he walked; and yet [
have seen him, swathed in heavy woolens and dressed in heavy
clothes, go nine miles, twice a day, and come back #0 wet
with perspiration that it fairly dripped fromm the ends of iis
fingers, while his shoes looked as though he had waded throagh
the canal which connects the Peconie an! Shinnecock Bays.
After these pedestrian trips he would be rubbed down with
coarse towels until his skin glowed like a pale cherry. Oniy
thoxe who have heard him say, after one of these rubbings,
“Oh, how good a cold bottie would co now,” can have any iden
of the ordeal training is to a man of Sullivan's nature and
tastes. To my mind, there is something neroic in his self-denial
and his labor, for he recognizes fully that at his age, and with
the thdatrical prospects betore him. his whole future hinges
upon his defeating Corbett He feels confident that he will win
in a few rounds, and he is fitting himself to make them the most
terrific ever seen inaring. Since he shaved off his mustache
his face looks thinner and more drawn than it did. The fat has
been removed from his stomach, and he isa far more shapely
man now than he was when he faced Jake Kiirain at Richburg.

GOOD WORK AT THE OARS.

The annual regatta of the Middle States Regatta Association,
at Passaic, N. J.,0on August 18, attracted nearly 16,000 specta-~
tors. Great interest was manifested in the affair, owing to the
fact that Edwin Hedley, probably the fastest amateur stuller
since Charies Courtney’s t me, was to meet Fred Hawkins, an-
other amateur wonder with the oar. Hedley belongs to the
Vesper Boat Club, of Philadelphia, while Hawkins is the cham-
plon of the Manhattan Athletic Club, and is credited! with being
able to row three miles fast enough to defeat Wim. O'Connor,
John Teemer, Edward Hanlon or Jake Gaudaur. Be this true or
untrue Hedley proved himself a superior oareman and speedier
than Hawkins. Just befure the start Hawkins was informed
that he would have to r-w under protest if he started. Haw-
kins was protested at the National régatta held at Saratoga, and
his case is pending decision. The protest was male to protect
the association in case the Saratoga protest is sustained.

Hedley got away well, and txking the lead won handily from
Hawkins, who evidently did not relish the protest. It appeared
as if the Manhattan crack did not put In his best licks to win.
This is the first time Hawkins ever lost a race on the Passaic
course. R

ENGLISH SPORTING NEWS.

The following letter was received from Warren Lewis anent
the Hall and Pritchard fight for $10,000,

Eprtor Pouce Gazetre—I promised when I left New York I
would keep you posted. I hav# seen London and Paris by day
and night and will be glad when I reach New York. Before two
woeks elapse the great match between Jim Hall and Ted Prit-
chard will be deciied and either Hal! will be £1,000 (that ls $5 000
in American money) richer or Pritchard will still pose as un-
beaten. All the stakes are posted, both men are in fret-cinss
condition, and I expect there will be a stubborn battle no matter
who wins.

Pritchard is the favorite, and English turfmen and members
of the clubs I have been Introduced to claim he is the best man
England has produced since Tom Sayers'’s time.

This is hardly fair on Jom Mace, who is still living here, tor I
think, notwithstanding Sayers fought fifteen batties, that Mace
in his day was Sayers'’s equal, and | doubt if Pritchard is as
areata pugilist us Jem Mace. But what is the difference? We
have the greatest pugilists In the world in America In Suilivan,
Fitesimmons, McAuliffe and Dixon, altheugh my money will
back Jim Hall to fight Bob Fitssimmons if Hall defeats Pritch-
ard, but ‘Police Gagette” rules must govern, for when pugil-
lets fight by those rules draws don't come tn.

The Sullivan and Corbett fight is creating considerable talk
bere. Charivy Davies, Joe Choyneki, Peter Jackson and myself
will leave for New York by the first steamer afer Hall and
Pritchard fight, for we want to nee the Sullivan and Corbett
contest,

I met Richard K. Fox. He Is just as busy here as he is in New
York, writing, securing portralts and offering prizes for compe-
tition. He gave an elegant cup for a 800-yard race to be com-
peted fur recently, and he thinks of arranging an international
regatta

George Strong, of Denver, made a poor showing when fight-
ing Tom Euston. Such fighters should stop in Ameries before
they come to England to learn to fight. Euston knocked him
outin the fourth round. There was one satisfaction, Strong
was net @ Trepresoutative American champion, and he did nut
hall from New York.

Peter Jackson, under Charley Davies’ management, has been
coining money. He had a big show at Leeds. Frank P. Siavin
has opened a sporting house in London. He wants to ight
Peter Jackson or the winner of the Sullivan and Corbett fight.
I learn that Billy Madden has secured Joe Goddard. The latter
is lucky and so ls Madden, for with the latter to do the hustling
and Goddard the fighting, there will be plenty of money and
glory for both. Best wishes to all my friends in New York.
No more until I see you. WARREN Lewis.

“The career of George Dickinson, a notorious burg-
lar who was sentenced three years ago to fifteen years’
imprisonment for burglary and attempted murder,
furnishes another remarkable example of criminal
audacity and daring. Dickinson had previously earned
several terms of imprisonment in diflerent States, and
two years ago settled in Philadelphia, where, keeping

his criminal Career @ Secret, he became a member of a |

prosperous firm of shirt manufacturers,

“During the day be was a respectable merchant, with
a reputation for generosity and goodheartedness, while
at midnight he plied his vocation as a burglar. He al-
ways wore evening dress while engaged in tbis nefari-
ous work, and conducted bis operations in the most
stylish and gentlemanly manner. Dickinson was, in
fact, a veritable Jekyll and Hyde of real life, occupying
fashionable appartments and indulging in all the
pleasures of the modern aristocrat. During a few
months previous to bis arrest more than one hundred
mysterious burglaries occurred in Philadelphia, for
many of which Dickinson was believed to be re-
sponsible.

WHEN SULLIVAN AND
MITCHELL WERE IN JAIL.

My coming battle with Charley Mitchell will be with-
out hard feelings, said John L. Sullivan, the other day,
because we have been pretty good friends since the
time we occupied cells in jail in France, After our hard
and bloody tight at Chantilly, the French cops arrested

|} weight lifter of America, challenges any

us. It was a long way from Boston common, I hadn't |

and when I growled at the turnkeys, they pelted me |

with parley voos [ couldn’t understand,

Mitchell could talk a sort of hamstrung French

80 that before we got our release we were pretty good

| British appetite along.

“There'll be no sparring across the table,’’ was the

“Not any,” sald I, “I won’t even throw a plate at
you,”

HIS HARD EARNED COIN PROVED A MASCOT

A Woman Angel Who Had Pluck to Stick to a Money Loser Until it Brought Her
Back Some of the Money She Sunk in it.

The crowd was talking about theatrical angels—thonse
men who put up for and the man-
ager who knew it all remarked:

“Every time I hear about an angel, I think of Big

money shows,

Jack Cooley. the gamest angel any company ever had,
and he was only a property at that. Any fool
millionaire with money can be an angel and never mind
the loss. It requires no nerve to pay out money when
you bave millions still remaining in the bank. The
real test of an anvel comes when heis risking his last
dollar to keep the show going and is interested in the
venture from other motives than simply liking the
pretty face of a chorus girl.

“EKightor nine years ago Cooley was the property
man of a company I was managing on the Pacific
Coast circuit. We were trying to get tothe rich pick-
ings on the far slope of the Sierra Nevada, but after we
had been out six had reached
Denver we struck a period of bad business,

Than

or seven weeks and

“T was talking long chances on winning with small
backing, tor I only had three or four thousand when T
took the company on tour, and this was nearly ex-
hausted by advances on salaries and railroad fares be-

fore the curtain rose the first night in an Oh town,

We Just managed to pay expenses and a little besides |

until we struck Colorado, and there trouble began

“Salaries figured up about @900 a week and railroud
fares about $250 a week more, notto mention printing
bills. When we begun to play to $75 a night I saw the
end was in sight and the usual two weeks’
notice. Those last two weeks wiped out my bank
balance, and I was ready to pawn my watch for the
price of a ticket to New York when the leading man
made me a proposition.

“*I know you cannot pay our fares back to New
York,’ he said. ‘And even if you could we would all
of us be dead broke and out of work when we got there.
I bave been talking things over with Camille Hilde-
gard, the leading lady, and she is willing to Join me in

to spare,

“ T have seen several wealthy show angels in my

The nearest approach to his nerve was that of a Weat-
ern man—a Californian—who came to New York to
enjoy life, and naturally drifted into theatrical society,
where, as a g00d spender, he was speedily put next to
a new comic opera which couldn't fail, if 1t had saffici-
ent backing to give it a good start.

“This Westerner wasn’t stuck on any girl in the com-
pany, and the manager was merely an acquaintance,
though his standing in the profession was first rate.
This Westerner dropped $40,000 on a musical produc-
tion that failed, without turning a hair, and when it
came to settling accounts, he simply handed the man-
ager @ blank check and told him to fill inthe amount
himself, but to keep the show going three weekg
longer because he had some friends from San Francisco
coming East and he wanted them to see the show, even
if it was a failure,

“Philadelphia may be a slow town, but it has fur-
nished a pretty swift proposition in the way of angels,
No less than five or six big musical productions of the
past six years bave been financed by this Philadelphia
angel, and not one of them has ever made a dollar.

“Still this angel retains his interest in theatricals, and
he will tell you that he expects to get back all his losses
by the next venture. A conservative estimate of the
total losses of this angel in the past six years would
place the sum at approximately $150,000,

“Rubber shoes supplied the sinews of war for the ad-
vent of a very charming actress, who made her stellar
debut season before last on Broadway. A wealthy
manufacturer of overshoes, having accumulated about
$7,000,000 in bis humane vuccupation, died and left this
tidy little fortane to his wife, sister of the actress.

**Now, the widow loved her sister dearly, and when
the sister expressed a desire to star, the rubber millions
were placed at her disposal. Three plays in all were
produced for this young woman, and the first two
were failures in which approximately $50,000 was lost.

** About $75,000 more was invested ina third produc-
tion, and though the papers praised it, business was so
bad thatthe actress-star had to rent the theatre out-
right in order to continue her engagement. Every
Saturday morning the widow of the rubber magnate
called upon her sister and left a blank check to cover
the umount of the losses on the week. In the six or
seven weeks run the losses amounted to about $10,000,
andI should imagine that the lady’s three starring
ventures consumed about $65,000 of the profits of the
rubber shoe industry.”

M’PARTLAND WAS EASY.

Recently, Ed De Groote, the French middleweight,
knocked out Jim McPartland,a heavyweight, from
Chattanooga. Tenn., in the fifth round of a scheduled
ten-round fight. The Southerner did all the rushing,
but for the most part his blows did no damage, as De
Groote would continually sidestep them. In point of
science McPartland knew nothing about boxing, and
went out in the fifth round from a left swing to the
jaw. The bout was held at the Hardwicke Opera
House, Dalton, Ga,

PHILA. JACK BESTED SULLIVAN,

Philadelphia Jack O’Brien and Twin Sullivan fought
a twenty-round draw in far-off Dawson City, Yukon,
recently, in the presence of a great crowd.

Sullivan would not go into the ring unless O’Brien
would agree toa draw if both men were on their feet
atthe end of the twenty rounds. O'Brien did not re-
ceive a mark, and his cleverness greatly surprised the
blg crowd of miners present. The men were guaran-
teed a purse of $5,000, with the privilege of percentage.
The gross receipts were about $20,000, and the men
received 36,000 each. The men will probably fight again

at Skaguay, Alaska.

According to James J, Corbett, the aathor of ‘‘Scien-
tific Boxing,’ which is No. 9 of Fox’s Athletic Library,
George Dixon and Champion Jeffries were the two
coolest fighters that ever stepped into a ring.

The former would sit in his dressing room, read the |

papers and discuss fighters of promise before a battle.

The famous ex-cham pion further says:

I remember on one occasion the little negro asked
for pen and ink. He quietly wrote a letter to a friend
in the Middle West. Notthe least bit of nervousness
was displayed and the letter is to-day preserved by
Dixon’s friend as a souvenir of the great little man’s
nerve,

On another occasion Dixon sent for a bootblack to
come and shine a pair of shoes, as he wanted them
after the fight to wear to a dinner to be given in his
honor by some friends, if he won.

Jeffries’ actions are somewhat different, but display
even greater coolness than those of Dixon.

When a match is made, Jeff shows great interest
and talks to his friends almost continually of the
coming struggle. Asthe date of the battle ap-
proaches, Jeff grows indiflerent. This is due
chiefly to the fact that he realizes his condition
is gradually nearing perfection and that he will
be capable of doing his best when he steps into

Peter Jackson and myself were probably the
most nervous of all the big fighters. Jackson,
at Jeast an hour before a fight, would begin drink-
ing brandy in small bits.

At the bell Jackson would be keyed to a high
pitch and his nervousness would be plain to
every spectator for at least two rounds, when he
would settle down and work like a whirlwind,

Before I won the title I never appeared on the
stage. I was at home in the ring, as much 80 as
at the dinner table. But when I made my first
trip around the country as an actor, I lost a lot
of coolness. The long strain I was under éach
told me, Consequently, when I met
Fitzsim mons I was a diflerent man than when I[
faced Sullivan; I was extremely nervous,

Bob Fitzsimmons, by the way, always lets
some one else do the worrying. His wife, he
claims, used up enough nervous energy for both,
He always held that many a good fighter dropped
a battle becuuse he did too much thinking.

One of the great troubles with

day on

young fighters
nowadays is that they enter the ring too young.

I mean that they tackle big gume too soon
after they have had success among the small fry.
Iiad the
’Frisco boy gone slower lhe would to-day be in
the same position, if not higher, than Jimmy
Britt. Eddie was anxious to reach the top and
outran himself before he landed.

Take Eddie Hanlon as an example.

Look at several others. Terry McGovern was
champion at 20 and a back number at 22. Young
Corbett won the title at 21 and should now be at
his best. He has gone back so far tat he will
never recover the lost ground. Battling Nelson
took a longer time to rise, but overdid things at
the top.

With heavyweights it generally takes longer
to come; Lut the stay is usually of greater length.

There 18 one place in the world where fighting
is flourishing at the present time and little is
heard of the battles. Tn faroff Alaska the knight
of the padded mitt is enjoving prosperity.

I received a letter from a friend the other day mak-
ing me an offer to come to the region of ice and snow
to meet 4 local inan on Dominion day. I sent word to
him that I was no longer in the ring and informed him
of two or three others who would fill the bill,

My friend informs me that he cleaned up nearly $20,-

000 In the past three years at the fighting game. This

would be # good place to pull off the Mitchell-Sullivan | posted on up to-date drinks,

JEFFRIES AS A REFEREE

—SLUGGING THE OFFICIAL HAD BECOME A POPULAR PASTIME—

FILLS A LONG FELT WANT

Marvin Hart May be a Champion but He is the Poorest
Representative the Title Ever Had.

THE RUSSIAN LION’S PECULIAR METHOD OF TRAINING |

Corbett Retires from the Controversy with Fitzsimmons---Ruhlin will again
Demonstrate His Ability to Fight---Small Talk.

Jim Jeffries has demonstrated his ability
to fill a long felt want with glittering success, and as a |
referee he can go along making money, and easy
money at that, After the Hart-Root fight at Reno
there was no kicking, no cussing the referee, and if the
loser attempted to take it out of the man who gave
the fight to the other fellow no mention of the fact
was made inthe dispatches from the ringside. It is
not recorded either that there was any questioning of
the orders or decisions of the referee.

Referee Jeffries is barred from the fighting game
proper because nobody will fight him. By officiating
at figits between aspirants for the honor he has been
compelled to pass up he will be doing the public a favor,
especially if he sticks to the platform laid down of lick-
ing the man who fakes a fight over which he presides,

At $1,000 per fight, the figure he received forthe Reno
affair, it ought to be worth the big fellow’s while.

Although he does so reluctantly, George
Siler, the distinguished expert on fistic matters, is in-
clined to sidestep Bob Fitzsimmons and recognize
Marvin Hartas the present champion of the world.
In doing #0, however, he lays no bouquets at the feet
of the indomitable Marvin, for he says: “He is the
poo:*st champion since the days of John L, Sullivan.
I do not wish to insinuate,’’ he continues,” that Hart is
not « good man, but his climb to the top rung of the
pugilistic ladder came at a time when the man who
occupied that position for six years concluded to step
down and out for lack of worthy opponents, and at a
time when no really good men, such as Fitzsimmons
and Corbett, were around to block his way.

“In looking the heavyweight puzgilistic fleld over I
can see no white man capable of trouncing Hart, so be
is indeed fortunate that the crop of good, big fighters is
scarce. Undoubtedly the best big man in the business
at present is Jack Johnson, the colored heavyweight
champion, and Hart shows excellent Judgment in
drawing the color line. It is the opinion of all fair-
minded witnesses thot Johnson beat Hart in their re-
cent fight at San Francisco, and undoubtedly can re-
peat the trick, so it probably is better for the game that
Hart drew the color line.”

I am more skeptical about Hart’s ability than Siler
is, and base much of my opinion that he is not of
cham ptonship calibre upon the alleged fake fight with
Black Johnson, to which Siler refers; if Hart could not
lick Johnson “on the level’”’ and draws the color line
to evade another meeting, I think his championship
claims have no virtue in fact, and that his chances will
be a poor betting proposition if it ever comes to a hook
up with Fitz, I’m willing to be convinced that Hart Is
a champion, but “I’m from Missouri.”

Speaking about Marvin Hart, Frank Gotch,
the wrestler, is quoted as saying:

“T have seen Marvin in action and am forced to ad-
mit I was not seriously impressed*with his work. He

George Hackenschmidt, the Russian Lion,
has demonstrated tne fact that contrary to general
opinion, the same training regime which puts fighters
into condition should be followed by wrestlers. In
pursuing this course himself, the great wrestler revo-
lutionized the training methods of wrestlers while he
was in this country. His ideas of getting into condi-
tion were so unique that the majority of grapplers have
imitated him, with the result that the majority of the
knights of the mat have been considerably benefited
in the way of condition. Inthe past, wrestlers used to
get into shape by merely working exclusively on the
mat, They never thought of giving any attention to
road work, or boxing or fencing or any other exercise
that would aid them in making their muscles supple.
The result was that while they were on the floor, either
acting as the aggressor or on the defensive, they were
allright. But as soon as they were in a standing posi-
tion their legs begun to tire and they were compelled
to get down on all fours once more or suffer a chance
of being thrown.

Hacxenschmidt surprised alot of wrestlers who were
anxious to lend their services in his training camp
wlen the Russian suggested a spin on the road. He
was told that the custom was an uncommon one in
this country, and that if he indulged in too much of
this kind of exercise he would certainly feel the effects
of it. The Russian simply smiled and went ahead
with the methods that had aided him so much in the
past. He ran five miles every day, boxed, fenced, and
only gave abouta half hour to wrestling.
quence, when he faced Jenkins at
Garden he was in the best of

AS a conse-
Madison Square
trim. His wind was per-
fect and his legs never gave him any trouble,

Jenkins’ methods of training are similar to those of
the foreigner, except that Tom does not believe in tou
much road exercise. He boxes and does a number of
flipflaps in the gym and develops his wind by a num-

ber of stunts. Most of his labor, however, is contined
to wrestling. He says thet a wrestler should do a lot of
this exercise, because in this way he trains the musvles
that he uses on the matinan important bout. Frank

Gotch trains a good deal itke the boxers. There is noth-
ing that he likes better than road work, Speaking
about his methods, Gotch recently said: ‘A number of
wrestlers put in their time working on the mat, but I
find that I am always in better shape and that I can
last longer when I train on the road. I also do con-
siderable boxing.”

Big Jim McCormick for a twenty-five-round go at

The California sports who have been hankering to see

statement made at Reno after Hart had won from
Roor.

McCormick is said to look like a fair specimen of
heavyweight timber. He is 6 feet 1 inch in height,
with a tremendous reach, but is not as heavy as
Ruhlin by something like fifteen or twenty pounds.
He expects to fight at about 190 pounds, while Rublin
will probably tip the scales at 210 or over.

Patrons of Harry Hill’s will recall Jerry

Hill, Steve Taylor, Daisy Daly, George Rooke and even

fighter of his time, once fought Jack McAuliffe a draw,

sparring sketch, and Murphy made money, but lost it
all later. Several weeks ago he went to the Metro-
politan Hospital, where he began to show signs of
mental decay. He was sent to Bellevue for observation,
and transferred to Ward’s Island whe-e he is confined
as a hopeless paretic. He is about 40 years old.

completely. For instance there is nothing that wil)
take the heart out of a fighter who bas long enjoyed a
vogue as champion more than a defeat. It causes him
to worry and fret until his nerves and health begin to
suffer,and in the he will become a wreck and
sometimes die. But for being whipped by Bob Fitz-
simmons Jack Dempsey might bave heen alive to-day,
Dempsey never forgot his defeat at the hands of the
Cornishman, and the late Nonpareil’s friends have
never forgiven him for causing it. After Dempsey
lost to Fitz he began to show signs of failing health.
lie wus depressed in spirits and seemed to be brooding
over something, and it was apparent to all his friends
that there was something amiss with him.

It was several years after that fight that Dempsey’s
admirers learned that the once invincible pugilist was
dying of a broken heart. Jack conveyed this impres-
sion in every word aud gesture. In order to forget the
reverse, Dempsey began to drink, and his health began
to sufler. Every possible thing was done to cheer
Dempsey up, but to no purpose.

“Don’t let that beating by Fitz bother you, Jack,”
Dem psey’sfriends said to him. ‘He isa bigger man
than you are and you were not disgraced. The public
will never forget you, and you are just as popular as
ever.”’

“That’s all right,’”’’” Dempsey would say, ‘but I’ve
been licked and the championship of America is gone.
I would not mind it, but a bloody Englishman took it
from me and that hurts me the worst.”

All the same Dempsevw’s cronies succeeded in ca-
joling him into the belief that he still could fight. They
induced him to come North and got him a match with
Tommy Ryan, at Coney Island. Poor Dempsey was
but a shadow of his former self and Ryan madea
punching bagof him. The mill was stopped before
Dempsey could suffer the humiliation of another
knockout. Dempsey never recovered after that. He
became very ill and died in the West from consump-
tion.

Jobnny Griffin, the Braintree Lad, felt bis defeat by
Solly Smith, at Roby, Ind., very keenly, and from
that time on his decline set in. Before Smith took bis
measure, Griffin never knew the taste of liquor. He
was a model young man for a pugilist, admired and
popular, Smith’s victory stung Griffin to the quick.
He lost all pride in his ambition, began to dissipate,
and what might have been a laudable career came to
an untimely end.

Jim Hall, the once noted Australian middleweight,
was never himself again after Bob Fitzsimmons laid
him low at New Orleans more than ten yearsago, It
was reported many times that Hall was dying of an
incurable malady, but he managed to regain bis health.
He still speaks of the defeat, but is more or less recon-
ciled to it. Kid Lavigne went down hill at a rapid
gait after Frank Erne wrested the championship from
him, Lavigne tried several times to show that he still
possessed the qualities of an excellent fighter, but it
was no use. The defeat rankled in his breast and he
never was himself again.

Billy Plimmer was rarely heard of after Pedlar
Palmer dropped him for the count for the second time.
For two years afterward Plimmer was ill and it was
oiten reported that his mind was affected. Plimmer
brooded a good deal over his lost laurels. He kept
aloof from his friends and went into a sort of
retirement.

Govern at Tuckahoe, N. Y., that Plimmer mustered

JACK DROPPED ONE.

The event of the evening at the Broadway A. C.,
Philadelphia, on July 13, was Jack Johnson facing two
men, Morris Harris and Black Bill Harris was the
first to face the big fellow, Johnson, and the latter was
not slow in finishing his first opponent. Harris put
several to the body inthe first round, while Johnson
sent his rightto the face. Again Harris lel for the
body and Jack uppercut him with his right, dropping
Morris, Jack repeated the blow a moment later and
Harris went down and out. After a minute’s rest
Black Bill took the centre of the stazge and he did very
well, Bill stayed the three rounds with Johnson, and
in the first two he stood up and fought Jack, with the
result that some hard exchanges were witnessed. Both
reached the face bard and often in the first round.

In the second they came to a clinch and each used
his right tothe body and ribs. Jack missed a vicious
right he aimed at Bill’s jaw and the latter sent his left
They swapped hard ones to the face before
the bellrang. Again some good exchanges were seen
in the last round, but Johnson got the upper hand with
a right and left to the Jaw, and he was entitled to the
verdict. But Bill made a good showing.

The opening number was between Teddy Moloney
and Jimmy Livingston, which was stopped in the

MARTIN BESTED CONNELLY.

Tommy Connelly, the Reading, Pa., boxer, met Terry
Martin, cf Philadelphia, in his home town on July 13,
in a ten-round argument,

It was a furious bout from the start to the finish.
Considering bis weakness from six weeks of illness
with typhoid fever, the Reading boy's showing was all
that could be expected. Martin was the aggressor in
every round, and several times it looked as if he would
knock the Reading man out. Martin is fighting ata
fust pace these days. He has a terrific wallop. The
Philadelphia boy had the advantage in height and
weight.

THE MORAL VALUE OF PUGILISM.

To the*many cranks and fanatics who de-
nounce pugilism and boxing as brutal and de-
moralizing practices, amounting in principle to
positive crimes, we beg to commend the follow-
ing highly significant circumstances;

Last week two Virginian editors fell foul of
each other in the usual Virginian editorial way.
Aftér exchanging all manner of characteristic
sarcasms and epithets, the fatal word “ cow-
ard’’ passed between them.

Now in the good old days when pugilism and
boxing were heartily abused, and had no such
defender and champion as the POLICE GAZETTE,
these two Virginian editors would have met
upon “the field of honor’ armed with pistols,
and fired at each other ina strictly chivalrous
and murderous manner, until one or the other
dropped dead

Rut the teachings of the POLICE GAZETTE are
all-powerful evenin Virginia. The elder editor
wrote to the younger to say ‘that he could not
conscientiously fight a duel with pistols be-
cause he had a wife and children: dependent
upon him, whose claims upon him he would
not disregard orimperil by putting himself up
to be shot at like a Christmas turkey. But, feel-
ing that he owed some satisfaction to his foe,
and entertaining a natural desire to do battle
in some form, he would be pleased to assert his
manhood with bare knuckles, according to the
rules of the Marquis of Queensbury.

Case No. 2 is that of a couple of colored suit-
ors for the hand ofa quadroon belle, who were
so fierce in their rivalry that murder was con-
fidently looked for ‘until Frank White, a well-
known sporting man, persuaded the men to
fivht it out with bure fists, onthe understand-
ing that the winner should take the girl and a
purse of $10.

Surely an institution so restraining and so
ameliorating that it can transform the homi-
cidal instinct into a manly and healthy effort
to win a fair and well-contested victory is one
which not only the community at large but
every crank included in it ought to applaud
and seek to establish,

A VERY JUST DECISION.

Judge Brown, of the U, S: Circuit Court sitting
at Leavenworth, has decided that if the State
ot Kansas enforces its prohibitory law, it must
buy the breweries, distilleries and vineyards
which are rendered useless and virtually con-
fiscatead by the law. It is diffieult to see why
saloons, the value of whose fixvures and bar
appurtenances is also destroyed, do not come
within the purview of the decision. The im-
mense properties involved in this new view of
the case will go far to stagger the cranks and
fanatics. The prohibitory States will hardly be
prepared to invest in the beerand whisky busi-
ness to the extent required by this version of
their responsibilities,and the result will bea
general backing down of the Pharisees. For
when it comes to hard cash the best of them
lets go of his “reform” principles.

DRUMMERS TO 0 THE FRONT.

c.imination of this kind reacts on the people
enacting it. Wherever the drummer abounds,

wanted to take the body down before daylight, but
some of the townspeople demanded that it should re-
main banging for the gaze of honest citizens and as a
warning to all transgressors of the law. A photogra-
pher arrived on the scene ai daybreak and photo-
graphed the kody. Hundreds of persons during the
early ndurs of the morning viewed the body. Men,
women and children looKed on the horrible spectacle
without evincing the slightest emotion or expressing
a feeling of regret.

A Chinaman’s Courtship.

“Clara Belle,” the Cincinnati Lnquirer’s New York
correspondent, seems to be 4 confidant for all the
young women ot her“set.”. She makes public this
private letter to her, written, as she says, by a stout
blond with yellow hair and a sunny disposition:

“My story is simply this: I undertook to lead a
Chinese laundrymaa to salvation. J called at his shop
and did what I could to teach him English and Chris-
tianity. At first nothing would do but I must get him
the fawily washing—they are so mercenary. I got him
that and continued my visits. At the next to the last
visit be frightened me terribly. He showed me one ot
my garments folded away in a sandal-wood box, which
be took up and pressed tu his heart. I demanded the
garment, but could not get it. I went next time deter-
mined to get it or have the wretch arrested. It w.is
toobad. Hewas getting along so well; could read a
primer and bad renounced tbe worship ot idols. But
I would have my garment, and I told himso. .We
were In the back of the shop, and suddenly tt was 1n-
vaded by at least two dozen Chinamen. half the num-
ber with musical instruments and the rest with gro-
tesque food.

“*A Chinese feast was opened, and much wusic of a
diab lical kind was indulged in. [ could see I was
somehow the heroine of the occasion. Alas! I was
soon to understand it. An alderman was sbown in
and introduced tome. Glad to find a civilized being
present, [ asked him what was the matter. ‘Il am sent
for to marry you tothe keeper of the shop,’ said he;
‘aln’t you taking a bold step? Well. I guess he tound
out what I was taking. I just openeda few flocd-ga'ies
of wrath at bim, walked over and bexed young Ling

' Qu’s ears (that was the heathen I bad been teaching) |

till he crawled under the table, and then [I walked out

like a tragedy queen. The idea! Just to think of it—
' the silly fool thought I was courting him all the while

i was teaching him be had a soul to save.

Ugh?!”
