John Ashton, of Providence, R.I., Billy
Madden’s champion and the “coming man,” met
John Carroll, of Brooklyn, in a hard glove fight, 6
rounds, “Police Gazette’* rules, at Keystone Rink,
Wilkesbarre, Pa., Saturday evening, Jan. 23. Over
1,000 paid admission to the contest. C. H. Smitb acted
as referee, and Mike Meehan, member of the City
Council, was timekeeper. Ashton was seconded by
Billy Madden, and Carroll by Mike Mooney, of Wil-
hamsburgh. The first round opened with cautious
sparring, Carroll on the get away and dodging tactics.
Ashton, leading with the left, landed onthe cbest,
which brought about half-arm exchanges, Carroll
gettingaway. Ashton furcing tbe tighting, several good
blows were exchanged. The second and third rounds
were a repetition of the first. In the fourth and
fifth rounds there was some territic _ hitting,
Ashton landing with his left in the stomach
three or four times, nearly doubling Carroll up.
Ashton forcing the tighting. and it he foilowed up his
advantage, would have Knocked Carroll out. He
landed one terrific cross counter on Carroll's left side
of head that Knocked him very shaky on his pins
The sixth and last round was fierce. Ashton landed
his left on Carroll’s mouth, drawing blood. Carroll
used both hands with good effect in this round and
fought for all he was worth ana got some good hits on
Ashton, who took no. notice, but rushed Carroll and
fought him on the ropes, and would have undoubtedly
finished him only time was called to preventgolice
interference, and the fight awarded Ashton, The re-
spective weights were Ashton 180, Carroll 165.

THE BASEBALL WAR,

A Threatening Danger to the Business--Necessity
for Future Peace.

Tt is rather a singular fact that all the row and cun-
fusion in the American Association sbould have heen
caused by the wen who control the Brooklyn Club,
Thev began it during last season,and made covert
offers to David Orr and James Roseman, two of the
best playersin the Metropolitan team, and by these
offers endeavorec. to induce them to join the Brook:
lyn nine. This step failed, because the men were un-
willing to face tbe risk of the black list. Then the
plot to oust the Metropolitan Club from tke assogia-
tion was conceived, and taking advantage of the
transter of ownership, the Brooklyn leaders induced
tbe otber clubs toconsent to and assist 1n puttibg out
the Mets. But Mr. Wiman, the new owner of the
club, knew his rights,and by the recent decision in
the Philadelphia courts, readily and effectually ob-
tained them.

The result was that the Mets are again in the organ-
ization, and will play in the American series of cham-
pionsbip games during 1886. One would suppose that
this settled the whole difficulty, but it now appears
that the men who brought such humiliation and ex-
pense upon the association are not content, and are
stirring up moretrouble. Hoping that Mr. Wiman
would do anything for peace, they demanded Orr and
Roseman as the price of their consent to
take back the Mets into full fellowship, anu
for a time induced the other clubs to join them in that
stipulation. But Mr. Wiman refused to yield the
truits of his victory and the quéstion was dropped.

The Brooklyn Club, however, is disposed to fight
Mr. Wiman tor ibe possession of Orr and Roseman
and there is every probability ot & struggle in the
Courts. Now, it is to be boped that the men who have
invested large sums of money for the maintenance ot
baseball clubs in the American Association will rallv
round Mr. Wiman and prevent any more law busi-
ness. It is a well-known fact that profes;ional base-
ball plavers are becoming restive and that most of
them are desirous of asserting their independence. If
the Brooklyn Club andthe Mets go to law over Orr
and Roseman it may result in destroying all past
agreements and make players so.independent that the
question of salaries will be a tremendous one. It was
long ago seen that some sort of arrangement should be
made whereby the running expenses of a protessional
team might be kept within certain limitsin order that
the business of managing them would ‘have a reason-
able certainty of securing a profiton the investment,
the trouble and risk. What is the most siugular part of
the whole business 1s that two or three men in a single
and not very important club should be able to make
so much mischief. There is probably over a million
of dollars invested in baseball, yet all this capital is
placed in peril because a few men choose to dety all
existing regulations, and break every line of baseball
law for their own selfish ends.

Under the national agreement the Mets are entitled
to Orr and Roseman, because they announced them in
their reserve list last October, and the fact that the
disputed men signed contracts with Brooklyn on the
right of the illegal expulsion of the Mets, gives the
Brooklyn Club no legal bold upon them. The courts
put the Mets back in the association by deciaring that
they had not been lawfully ejected ; consequently,
any contracts signed on the ground they had been ex-
pelled are rendered null and void. That is common
Jaw and itis also common sense. But baseball men
should learn one thing, and that is that law proceed-
ings sometimes makes more wounds than they cure,
and as the professionai clubs have been legislating
among themselves in avery ignorant and heedless
way, it behooves them to be very careful how they
poke their fingers into the legal furnace.

and possesses a plump and compact form. She can
strike a blow which an ordinary man would find it
difficult to parry,and few of her female rivals feel
confidence enough in their powers to stand up in the
ring against her.

Miss Peckham’s most formidable opponent fs Miss
Nellie Edwards, who also spars at Harry Hill's tre-
quently. She is a blonde, somewhat taller than Miss
Peckham and possessed of what the pugilistic fratern-
ity term ‘a Jong reach.” Miss Edwards is exceeding-
ly quick on her feet, and the manner in which she
hops around and defivers blows, like the pattering of
hail, is apt to contuse an opponent.

At a leading Bowery saloon the star boxer is Emma
White, a rather pretty girl of twenty-one, who has
very small hands, which seem, however, to be as large
as bams to the stariled visions of the green young men
who sometimes go upon the stage and take a round
with Miss White. Toa reporter Miss White said last
evening.

“We receive from $15 to $25 per week at this busi-
ness. It takes six months’ practice to be a good
sparrer. Jimmy Kelly, of Kelly & Murphy, the
boxers, who are now in Europe, was my teacher. I
used to be nervous when I first began tbe business,
but I’m not afraid to face even Jobn L. Sullivan now.’
and Miss Emma put up herhands and sparred away
at an imaginary Bostonian.

Billy Edwards, the champion light-weight, was
asked by the reporter bow he trained women for the
prize ring.

“Well, [ haven’t done much of that sort of work

lately” was the reply; “but the system pursued is |

almost identical with that by wbhicb men are brought
jnto cordition, ‘The girls are made to practice for two

or three hours daily with dumb-bells not over one
pound in weight, and with ligbt Indian clubs. The
lessons usually last for an hour at a time and a smart
girl will soon be able to spar with most anybody.”

“Are they as hardy as men ?”

“Ob, nO; they get ‘winded’ too easily, and haven't
the endurance of men. Then they become discour-
aged more quickly and suon give upa fightin which
they are getting the worst of it. About 130 pounds is
the best weight fora woman boxer. They are put on

‘a diet while training, but it is rather to strengthen

them (hao to reduce their weight, as weight is not
considered ina match between women. Rare roast
beet and almost raw potatoes, a glass of beer occasion-
ally, and abstaining from pastry is the best dieting
for them.’’

There tsa wealthy merchant residing on FiJth avenue
whose three daughters take lessons almost daily.
They have a gymnaéium: fitted up in the house, and
ifa mashing slim should insult one of those girls bis
head would subsequently feel as if a mule had
kicked it.

STOLE HS FATHER’S BRIDE.

A Wealthy Chicago.Merchant Robbed of a Young
Wife.

The details of a recent romantic marriage in high
life transpired in Chicago last week, but the efforts of
the reporters have s> far failed to disclose the names
of the principals. The case is one in which the young
son married the youthful affianced of his father on the
eve of the latter’s intended wedding. The father is
& prominent merchant, forty-four years old, the lady
eighteen: and beautiful, and the son twenty-one and
only recently fromcollege. Dr. Clinten. Locke, pastor
of Grace Episcopal Church. performed the ceremony,
innocent of the tact that he was sealing tbe theft ot a
bride from one of the leading members of bis congre-
gation. :

It appears that the father in the story advised Dr.
Locke to be prepared to marry him at 7 o'clock on
Saturday night in the church. Dr. Locke was ac-
quainted with neither the affianced nor the son ot his
communicant,

At 6 o’clock on the Saturday evening in question a
young couple presented themselves at the pastor's
studio to be married. He doubted their legal respon-
sibility, but upon presentation of a murriage license he
waived his objections and made them man and wife.
His suspicions were not even excited by any stmilarity
of names. Mrs. Locke was an interested witness,
In relating the affair she said :

“They were the handsomest couple I ever saw.”

Promptly at 7 o’ciock Dr. Locke repaired to his
church, and there found the father, attended only by
two male friends. ;

“Iam sorry,” said the intended husband, “but Miss
is il, and the wedding will have to be post-
poned.”

The possible deception flashed upon the minister,
He told of the quiet ceremony i the parsonage.

A scene ensued in which the father, enraged, swore
he would take the lives of both offenders, and at last,
prostrated, was led out to the back in waiting. The
young couple have disappeared. The old gentleman
is very wealthy, as are the parents of the young lady.
It is scarcely probable that the remaining facts in the
aftair can remain long concealed.

BURIED TREASURE.

Searching for Coin in the Helderbergs, Near
. Albany, N. Y.

Peter Hart, a shoemaker of Guilderland, Albany
county, N. Y., says a dispatch to a morning paper, bas
put the whole cogptry side in commotion. While
drawing wood on the Indian Ladder mountain a tort-
night ago he founda badly spelled letter, written on a
sheet of foolscap and -held down on a log by a Dit of
hemlock bark. It was dated September, 1885, and pre-
tended to be the confession of crime by John Robert
Swift, who claims to be the son ofa rich Englishman.
The writer says he came to this country in September,
1875, and continues : ;

“Coming over the ocean [ became acquainted with
a@ noted thief and burglac and he coaxed me to go with
him to Calitornia,and there we became acquainted
with two othér men of bad repute. The one was an
Irishman named John Hailey. at least that was the
name he went by. There we robbed a bank and stole

He then says he and Hailey came to New York and
then went to Canada, as it became hot for them. Then
they went to the Helderberg mountains, Albany coun-
ty, where they lived inacave. A quarrel on July 4
led to Hailey’s death, and Swift says that he left $15,-
000 in the cave in asatchel. Now the people are busy
searching for the treastre,

McARTHUR’S LUCK.

He Put In His Thumb and Drew Out a Plum.

Col. William M. McArthur, of Limington, investsin
the Louisiana State Lottery and draws the second cap-
ital prize of $50,000.

For a week or more, rumors have been afloat about
the city, that somebody living in one of the Saco
river valley towns 1n this county; had drawn a large
prize in the Louisiana State Lottery, and a Journal
reporter was set to work to materialize the rumors if
possible. Afteratime the man was located in Lim-
ington, and Thursday afternoon, the reporter went to
that town to ferret out the lucky tndividual, whose
reticence had tbus far kept his-name from the public.
By what means he succeeded it is unnecessary to
here state. Suffice it to say. that he found his man in
the person of Col. William M. McArthur, @ prominent
and bighly respected citizen of Limington village.

Col, McArthur, more from curivsity than from any
expectation of drawing a prize, bought ticket No.
14,928 ot The Louisiana State Lottery Co., which in the
company’s drawing of the 15th of last month, proved
to be one of the lucky numbers as it drew the whole
of the second capital prize ot $50,000. Last Saturdav,
the Louisiana National Bank ot New Orleans, for-
warded to the First National Bank of Portland, the
money, and Col. McArthur is now In possession of the
profits of the best paying investment he ever made.

With the income of bis 850,000 and a pension of $30a
month, which he draws from the government on ac-
count of injuries to his left side and ankle, received in
battie, the Colonel will be able to keep the wolf from
his door for wapy years to come.—Siddeford (Me.)
Journal. Jan, 9

To the Sporting Editor :

In arceent issue of vour paper my name was used, with others,
as being afraid wo meet Sam Collyer for the light-weight champion-
ship of America. Will you allow me space to correct that state-
ment, as I will meet any 133 or 135 pound man living, any time,

Very truly yours, Bruty Frazier.

There is now a prospect of an international prize
ring encounter for the championship of the world, for $5,000, be-
tween the champions of the old and new worlds. Tne English
Sporting press have pronounced Jem Smith, of London, who recent-
ly defeated Jem Davis, Jem Mace’s protege, in a contest fought by
the London prize ring rules, for $2,000 and the championship, and
several English sporting men are so carried away with Smith's
great ability and tremendous hitting powers that they offer tomatch
him, win or lose with Alfred Greenfield (whom he fights for £300,
$1,500 a side), against John L. Sullivan, the champion of America,
for £100, ($2,000) a side and the ‘‘Police Gazette” champion belt of
the world.

The pending negotiations for an international prize
ring encounter between th: recoguized champions of the Old and
New World brings one back twenty-five years, to the time when the
Great Heenan and Sayers battle was fought. Siuce Jem Mace,
Ne1 O'Baldwin and Joe Wormald left England, and Harry Allen
died, England has been Without a recognized champion, although
many claime! that distinction by being successful in glove contests
by new rules introduced by a man who liked to see boxing accord-
ing to his ideas. and who, after framing a set of rules for the guid-
ance of amateurs, had the editor of the Sporting Life, London, ar-
range a set to govern professional boxing. Now that the prize ring
has been revive Lin Englaad, and its supporters are ma ry of the
same class who patronized and upheld the prize ring during 1850
to 1860, and taking into consideration England has turned out what
may be termed a genuine champion who is ready to meet
all comers in the roped arena, it is more than proba-
ble that another great international battle will be arranged.
The English champion has thrown down the gauntlet and courage-
ously offers to mecs any man for the heavy-weight championship
belt of the world and $1,000 a side. Sullivan holds the champion-
ship, and there is not the least doubt but that he will boldly eater
the arena and defend the trophy against the English champion.

No matter whether the proposed battle is fought in the United
Stated, England or France, it will create a widespread interest,
and if the proposed encounter is satisfactorily arranged and decid-
ed only by the best man winning, the P. R. will receive another
boom. The champion of England's defi has been replied to by the
donor of the belt, who states that he will pot only permit Jem
Smith to contend for the trophy if Sullivan is willing, but it is
proposed «iso to give a purse of $2,500 toward the $2,000 a
side, the proposed amount of the contest. As far as
Sullivan is concerned the match is made. Sullivan only desires
that gloves must be worn instead of bare knuckles, and all the
other conditions propesed by Smith suit. Of course the battle must
take place on American soil. The stakes, $4,000, with the $2,500
offered, and the champiou belt, which with the diamonds cost
$2,500, will amount to $9,000, within $1,000 of the largest stake ever
contested for in England or in this country. So that there can be
no hitch in the matter as far as stakes are concerned, Richard K.
Fox would back Sullivan against any man in the world
for $10,000 if it was necessary, and should Greenfield de-
feat Smith, which is very doubtful, and the latter's
backers, who belong to a well-known ¢lub in London, refuse to
back him. Smith is said by Bill Richardson, of Shoreditch, Jem
Mace, and all the prize ring critics to be a wonder. George W.
Atkinson, of the Sporting Life, Dan Thomas, of the Sporting
Chronicle, speak of him with the highest praise. He fights in con-
dition at 1X5 pounds which is within 8 pounds of Sullivan's weight,
while he is only twenty-three years of age, just four years younger
than the champion, but in height Sullivan has 2 inches the advan-
tage. It makes no difference about his, Smith's, height, age or
weight, as he has proved he possesses all the most essential points
necessary to make a first-class boxer—courage, science and stamina
—and he has plenty of money behind him, yes, a small for-
tune if he ouly i in 1 ing Greenficld. We
have not the faintest idea that he can conquer Sullivan
but judging from all reports, Smith will be the most dangerous op-
ponent Sullivan ever met, and no matter how many advantages
Sullivan possesses over the heavy weight division, for the sake of
his reputation and the national reputation, of the Stars and
Stripes and Erin-go-Bragh, he will have to make great preparations
for the battle in order to be on equal terms with the foe. Since
negotiations fur the proposed great international match has opened
there is great excitement on both sides of the Atlantic, and every
one is patiently waiting to see the result of the Smith and Green:

All heartily welcome—every one! The sporting rooms of this
paper are always open to all classes of sporting men, no matter
whether they desire information or want to arrange matches.
Every sporting man should bring his friends to see the elegantly
Surnished ofices, to witness the galary of champion emblems,
trophies, pictures and the other many objects of interest, The
largest and anly life-size picture of John L. Sullivan, the renowned
pugilist, known as the Drohan picture, The picture stands five
feet in height, represents the champion in full ring costume, and
is the most artistic portrait of a pugilist ever seen, and is well
worth a visit.

On Jan. 17 Officer Conner caught Stony Cameron, the
boxer, of Greenpoint, and a confederate stripping copper from a
ferryboat at Astoria, and arsested them. On the way to the station
house Cameron turned and dealt the policeman a blow in the face.
The blow staggered the policeman, and before he could recover him-
self Cameron had broken from his grasp and was making off. Con-
ner called on him to stop, but as no heed was paid to the demand
he fired athim. The bullet took effect in Cameron's left leg. He
fell headlong to the ground, aud wascaptured. The wound isin the
fleshy part of the leg. The builet was not extracted.

Jack Burgess, the well-known Brooklyn pugilist who
succeeded in winning the $250 purse offered by the Crib Club of
Boston, from George La Blanche, the Marine, called at this office
Jan. 12. Burgess stated that when La Blanche could not conquer
him by hard thumps with his fists, he tried to win Japanese style
—buttiug—and when he found that he could not make him stop, he
tried other unfair practices. Burgess thinks Dempsey will beat La
Blanche any time they meet, with a fair referee, who will see that
the rules are not: infringed upon. Burgess displayed a deep cut
over his left eye, done by I.a Blanche’s ram-like propensities.

The athletic interests of Yale College at New Haven
begin to be largely quoted, afd much is anticipated by those who
hope to see better luck for Yale in 1886 than in 1885. So far as the
course on the Thames at New London next summer is concerned,
‘*Bob" Winston, the trainer of the crew, said recently that Yale's
athletic interests: are far brighter now than at any time since he
had been connected with the co'lege. There is more‘interest shown
this year than last. The gymnasium is filled all day acd up to the
time ofclosing at night. The athletic team is training carefully, so
that when spring opens much time need not be spent in getting the
men into condition.

Jim Glynn, of Williamsburgh, with several friends,
called at this office, deposited $10 forfeit and issued a challenge to
Jack Clark. of Long Island City, to fight for $100 a side in a room,
with not more than half a dozen aside. Glynn fought on Long
Island last spring for a purse made up from the sale of tickets.
Although over three hundred witnessed the fight, but $74 was shown
up as the net proceeds of the sale, and all that was staked on the
battle. Glynn was defeated. as he says unfairly.gwing to the
interference of Clark with a gang of heelers, who yumped into the
ring, assaulted him and frightened the referee to decide against
him. Glynn deposited? a forfeit. and calls on Mr. Clark to cover
the same and arrange a match, when he claims that he will prove
to Clark that he (Clark) cannot whip one side of him.

The Onota Lake boat house, near Pittsburg, has been
the scene of many a lively cock fight during the past few years
among birds belonging to North Adams and Pittsfield sporticg men.
On Jan. 19 about forty men were gathered about the pit watching
some lively fights among some of the best cocks in that part of the
country. Two mains had beea fought when a man on the lookout
came iv and shouted ‘‘Police!“’ Six Pittsficld sheriffs were driving
up at arapid pace. The party scattered and took to the woods.
Several men were identified, however, and among them were some
of the most prominent citizens of both towns. They will be ar.
rested and brought into court. @ix game cocks were captured by the
officers and locked up in the jail for safe-keeping.

The great Inter-State curling match between New
York and New Jersey was playedon Haledon Lake, Paterson, N,
J.,on Jan. 14. Ninety-six curlers participated, and it was the
largest INAS tate match ever played, and thcre were twelve rinks
a side. - The match was rendered all the more interesting from the
fact that each, State had won four victories in the previous eight
matches. Mr. David Foulis, secretary of the Gra d National Curl-
ing Club. wag appointed umpire, and the game gommenced at one
o’vlock and finished at five P. M., wheu it was found New York had
won,by 48 shots, Mr. Robert Kellock, of Yonkers. won the Hamilton
medal by having the longest score on the winning side. New York
was represented: by rinks from the following clubs: Caledonian,
New York; Caledonian, Brooklyn; Manhattan, Yonkers; New
York, Empire City, Thistle, New York, and Thistle, Brooklyn. The
total score was 268. For New Jersey there were rinks from the
Jersey City, Newark, Paterson, Ivanhoe and Little Falls clubs.
The aggregate score was 220.

Every turfman is well aware that Ed. Corrigan is
the owner of several great race horses. and one of inis best is Free-
land. One would suppose from the weekly budget of challenges
Corrigan issucs, thathe is just as proud of notoriety as his race
horses. i

Three and four times a month he makes the an-
nouncement that he will match Freeland to run Miss Woodford,
the Queen of the turf.owned by the Dwyer Brothers.

Corrigan is very careful about stipulating in his chal-
lenge that the race must be run in the West, when he is well
aware that the Dwyers are not going to run their great flyers in
the West.

If Corrigin’s semi-monthly challenge was worded
to run oa any track in the East, I would have an idea that the
great western turfman was in earnest, and until he makes that
specification in his defi, I shall look upon the long interviews and
challenges as merely buncombe.

If the Lorillard of the West, as Corrigan is styled,
ani I don't know why, is eager to arrange a race to run at Sheeps
head Bay, the Dwyers will arrange a race for as much money ag
Corrigan wants to gamble if he will allow the Dwyers to name the
distance.

Freeland is, or was during 1885, a great race horse,
but he had slightly the best of every race he arranged, and one, I
am certain, was won before it was run.

Freeland may go through another racing campaign
but I think it is very doubtful, tor expect to see him break down
the first race he runs, because I think he has had too much
running.

This is business, let Corrigan put up or shut np.

vet came across.

I learned that he intended to attempt to kill 35
pigeons out of 5) with one hand, ee at 27 yards’ rise, from

I think that the sporting public must grow weary
of so much gasconade about John L. Sullivan and Paddy Ryan
going to meet in the orthodox 24-foot ring.

a*-an

Every one knows Sullivan has plenty of funds and a
champion‘belt (preseuted by Richard K. Fox) to contend for any
time he is ready to meet any challenger, no matter whether he is a
Trojan or hails from Merrie England.

Again everybody is aware that Sullivan is ready at
all times to meet any ambitious aspirant for fistic fame with gloves
in the magic circle, so that if a match is proposed or he is chal-
lenged and a match not ratified no one can lay the blame to his
door.

On the other hand, Ryan lacks men behind him who
will put up their money.

He has backers, it is said, but they are not the right
kind, because they refuse to furnish the ex-champion, who may be
willing to meet Sullivan, with the sinews of war, and Ryan is thus
made acatspaw to boom up the business of some speculating sa-
loon-keeper.

By the way, I read in the Chicago papers that Chas.
E. Davies, better known as the Parson. announces that he has a

donor) ready to put up any time Ryan and Sullivan agree to ar-

I think if these gladiators want the opportunity to

again settle the question of supremacy this is their opportunity.

Every one knows that Charles E. Davies will bring

1 understand the Executive Coinmittee of the Na-
tiona! Association of Amateur oarsmen wet at New York on Jan. 9
and resolved to disqualify as an amateur oarsman Frank J. Mum
ford, of the Perseverence Boat Club, of New Orleans, La.

There were numerous charges brought against Mum-
ford, the principal oues being that at a race in Philadelphia on
July 9, 1880, he made a dcal for a money consideration with one’
competitor to withdraw, and with another tu make intentional
fouls, thus winning the race easily. Again, at the annual regatta
at Washington on Aug. 1, 1884, he lost a race under suspicious
circumstances, having pretended to break the slide in his boat.

I understand it was alleged, through a friend, he bet
large sums of money against himself in ths race. Mumford had
several times been summoned to present himself before the com-
mittee, but had always failed to appear. On Saturday, however,
Johu Fitzpatrick, President of the Perseverence Club, appeared in
his favor. and, after hearing him, the committee at once decided
to di-qualify Mr. Mumford. Rule 15 was altered so as to give the
referee power to order a race rowed over when any contestant
suffers from outside interference

Jacob Snell is the largest weight that shakes
the nimble drummer by the hand on the road.
He drops the scale to no less than 450 pounds. He has
a heert almost as large as his body and every travel-
ing man smiles with the prospects of good living
when he stops at the Snell House, at Fonda, N. Y..
and looks upon thé genial, rounJest face that pre-
sides over the comfortable hostelry. Brother Snell's
weight has also been telt among his fellow townsmen,
who have made him sberiff of tbe county in which he
lives,

A box car on the J., M. and I. Road, Co-
luipbus, Tnd.. Jan. 19, which had some loose grain
scatiered on the floor, was invaded by a flock of goats
(between twenty-five and thirty), and some of the
boys closed the door, and the box was tiken out to In-
dianapolis “empty,” as was supposed. When arriving
at Indianapolis one of the vrakemen inp the yard
opened the car door, when the billygoats jumped out
one after another, scattering in every direction. The
crew engaged in a chase of four hours, catching fif-
teen of them, supposing they had been shipped as
freight. ‘They then went to hunt the agent to see the
waybill, and see how many goats had been shipped,
when they discovered the joke,

George Brown, an attorney of Decatur,
TIL, isthe plaintiff? in a curious damage suit now on
trial in the Circuit Court. The defendants are the
Chicago, St. Louis and Pittsburg Railway and the Pall-
man CarCumpany and the action is to recover $50,000,
growing outcf theiralleged negligence. Brown's wife
died in May last and the body was sent to Zanesville,
Ohio, by way of Indianapolis, accompanied by Mr.
Brown and other relatives. I[n’some manner the corpse
was put off at Indianapolis, the relatives going on
through to Columbus. The corpse remained twelve
hours and when it finally arrived at its destination
was ina bad state. The time ot tne burial bad to be
changed and friends could not look at the remains,
The defendants claimed that they performed their
duties and sre not gu‘ity of negligence.

An aged farmer from Bullitt county, Ky.,
namecd Henry Logstoue, wiile traveling op the Short
Line Railroad last week, from Louisville to Cinein-
naul, was made the victim of an old swindle, conducted
by a young sharper whose name could not be ascer-
tained. When nearnng Covington, the young man,
whose neat dress and cultivated tanner attracted the
attention of the farmer, suduenly arose in his seat, and
hastily running through his pockets, exclammed that
he had lost his pocketbook. He remarked to Logstone
that the loss of the money would temporarily place
him in # very uncomfortable position, as be was en-
gaged largely in manufacturing wooden wares in St.
Louis and was on a tour of inspection among the dif-
ferent manufactories. He stated that his firm was a
wealthy one, and Known extensively throughout the
country. Proceeding further with his smooth talk,
the young man finally asked the ‘favor of a loan of $0,
at the same time apologizing for his seeming imperu-
nence, but pleading the necessity and urgency of the
case. wogstone wes only too glad to favor a manutae-
turer in high standing. remarking that all business
men who bad ever seen anything of the world must
bave been placed ina like predicament at some time

could be obtaiued earlier.

or other. The sharper passed over his card. gave the
farmer a hearty shake of the band, and said that he
would send the money to his address at bis earliest
convenience. He got off at Covington, and disap-
peared.

The young woman's tights are not a bit too large for

rent. She lost no time ir getting into a new puir of

TALES OF THE
TENDERLOIN.

Story of the Life of Aggie, the Beautiful Woman Who Became
Famous in New York as * The Diamond Queen.”

SHE WENT THE MERRY PACE THAT INVARIABLY KILLS.

Met an Old Admirer One Night, Who Gave Her a Chance to Begin Life All
Over Again, and She Told Him Her Only Romance.

The wind was beating the snow blindJy down on the heads of the hurrying pedestrians, and the hands of
the clock in the Heart of the Tenderloin both pointed at 6, which made it very easy foreven adrunken man
to tell the time. The work-a-day people were hurrying to their homes, and the others—those who fourish after
dark—were just beginning to rouse themselves for the night.

Any one who knows New York will tell you that the Heart of the Tenderloin is that patch of heart-shaped

open ground which lays between Broadway ou one side and Sixth avenue on the other, and Thirty-fifth street on
the top, and the man who knows

THE HUNTER IS IN JAIL NOW.

There is a noted hunter in Detroit, Mich., who has
just got into trouble through tollowig ber particular

and young girls tempting oflers to come to her house

ciever ways lure them into the meshes of immorality

So clever has she been at her business as hunter that

Ot late, however, she has been making a specialty o1

DUFFY'S WILD WOOING.
[SUBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION.)

Acting on the principal that faint heart never won
fair lady,a roan named Duffy, who is a Paterson
machinist, has made such violent love to the fair object
of his affections that she had to have him arrested.
She isa lovely widow and he fell in love quick. He
went to her home, saw her in the parlor, and falling on
his knees, asked her to marry him. She refused and
then he seized her about the waist, carried her bodily
to the front piazza and threatened to throw her over
the rails to the pavement below unless she consented
to become his wife. The widow screamed and her
mother came to her assistance. The result was a flerce
battle in which Dufty got the worst of it.

Later he was arrested and held to await the action of
the grand jury.

For the first time in a year Dixon fought like his old-
time self. His recent experiences with Tommy White
and Frank Erne taught him a salutary lesson, and he
conscientiously worked for this battle, with the result
that when he stepped into the ring he was trained to a
condition of physical perfection. It was evident that
he was determined to convince the sporting public that
with careful preparation he could fight as well as ever,
and there were many of the spectators who regretted that
his opponent of the night was not Frank Erne, instead
of Murphy. Dixon had worked off all superfluous
flesh, and at 3 o'clock in the afternoon he tipped the
scales a trifle under the required weight, 120 pounds.
Murphy was also under the stipulated weight. The
latter has always been considered a bad man to beat.

BLUE-EYED DAISY

“FLEW THE COOP.”

oun == so

She Told Her Rather That She Was Working But All of Her
Work Was Confined to the Festive ‘‘ Growler.”

HAD LOTS OF FUN WITH THE BOYS EVERY DAY.

Now She Has Skipped for Good and the Memphis, Tenn., Police Are Looking
for a Blue-Eyed Girl With Blonde Hair and a Perfect Figure.

There is an empty chair in a Memphis, Tenn., house-
hold to-day, and the pretty blonde girl who occupied it
bas gone away with one or more of her boy compan-
fons. She was the eldest daughter and the pride of the
household, but now her reputation is gone, and if her
father ever lays bands on her she will have a hard time
of it. Her name is Daisy Winter, and although she is
only fifteen years old, yet she is bright,
pretty and clever, and she attracted
more attention from the young men
of the neighborhood than she ought,

She was fond enough of the boys, too, °
and she used to spend a good deal of \
her time with them.

On account of her bright blue eyes
she was calied the “blue-eyed pet,” a
name that she seemed to deserve.

About a month or 80 ago she went to
her father and told him she wanted to
go to work

He was surprised at her remarkable
request, as there was no need for her to
do anything of the kind. She had a
good home and all that a girl could
want,

“What do you want to work at?” he
asked.

“Ob, nothing very hard,”’ she said.
“I’ve got achance to learn to make
embroidery, and I would like it very
much, I know I won’t get much pay
at first, but I will get a lot when I

learo.”’

That is the way it began, and after
a considerable argument the girl had
her way and went to work.

Thatis to say, she left home every
morning at eight o’ clock and did not
return until seven in the evening.

But she never went to work.

Instead of that she was having a high
old time with the boysin a place that
was called & club room, and they used
to drink and carouse and have a high
old time from early morning until it
was time tor Daisy to go home in the
evening.

This kind of an arrangement might
have continued indefinitely had not a
friend of the father heard something
that aroused his suspicions, and forth-
with he went to the old man.

“*What is your daughter doing now ?”’
he asked. “She is learning embroidery somewheres
uptown and she is doing very good, too, for only last
week she got a raise in her wages.”’

‘“‘Would you be surprised if I were to tell you that she
isn’t working and never has been working ?”’

“What are you telling me?”

“The truth. Your daughter has been deceiving you,
for she has never had a position.”’

**Butsbe has been leaving the house every morning
and coming every night.”

“She has been carousing with a crowd of boys all day
long.”

“T can’t believe that,” said the father, ‘for my girl is
a good girl and wouldn’t deceive me.”

When the girl came home that night her father ques-
tioned her, and her answers did not quite satisfy him.
In the morning he talked to her again and finally he
said:

“Well, I'll go with you this morning to your employ-
er’s and see for myself.”

“All right, father,” she said, ‘‘but first I’ll go for the
milk.”

She hurried out of the room without any hat or coat,
and wearing a check apron over her plaid dress. The
minutes passed and she did not return. The father
grew impatiept and went to the stairs and called her.
Then he went down to the door. The inilk was there,
but Daisy wat not. He inquired at all the neighbors’.
Nobody had seen her.

The night came and went, but the girl did not return,
and then he realized the truth.

Now she is somewheres with her wild companions.

THEY GOT PAPA’S WAD.

(SUBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION.)

A fine old gentleman of New Orleans, of the old
school, is responsible for the statement that there are
giris in that city who would not for a moment hesitate
to rob their best friends. He fell in with two fairies on
Canal street the other evening, and after a short walk
they induced him to walk into their parlor on Custom-
house street and indulge in a glassof wine. He liked
the girls and he liked the wine, and in a very short
time he was doing the couchee-couchee in his stocking
feet. Then he got something stronver than wine, so he
lay down upon a convenient sofa to think it over. He
doesn’t remember how long he was there, but when he
awoke he was bustiled out of the house in a great hurry.
When he got home and went through himself he
found someone else hid been there before him, and had
tuned him up to the extent of $1,763. He has a
mourning band about bis hat now.

MOTHER AND DAUGHTER SLAIN.

(SuBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION.)

Mrs, Foley, a widow, and her unmarried daughter,
Fanny, were found murdered in their home, near Lib-
erty, Mo., early the other morning. No motive for the
crime is known.

William Foley. aged twenty-five, a son of the mar-
dered woman, had visited a neighbor and returning
home after midnight was the tirst to discover the dead
bodies. Motherand sister were found in their bed
room dressed in their nightgowns and bespattered with

blood. ‘Phey had both been shot, the mother through
the head and the daughter in the back. The assassin
or assassins had fired at Mrs. Foley through one of the
front windows. The bullet lodged in the head of the
bedstead. joth women evidently became frightened
and ran into the bedroom in the rear. The door was
then forced and the bloody work completed.

iTS HS ATER

James Harvey Says That He
Killed His Wife.

tin

AND HE MAKES AN AFFIDAVIT

Both Are in Jail and the Town Is ina
Fever of Excitement.

WHO WAS IT KILLED THE WOMAN?

The people of Wilmington, O., have had enough sen-
sations recently to last them a long while, and they are
notall over yet. A short time ago James Harvey was
arrested and lodged in the county jail on a charge of
murdering his wife, Ida. He said nothing about the
crime until the other day, when he filed an affidavit
before the mayor in which he charged his father with
causing the death of his wife by beating and striking
her about the head and body.

The mystery that has surrounded this case from the
begining has proved a puzzle to the authorities, and
the officials have been trying to get a solution for some
time. Atthe time the woman was buried, young Har-
vey, her husband, broke down and was on the verge of
making a confession to the sheriff, but he was told by
his attorney not under any ,circumstances to talk of the
matter.

On this occasion he remarked there was something
within him that told him he must make some state-
ments; that there was another implicated, and he was
not the guilty party in the matter, and he asked that
his attorney be brought to the Jail.

When he came he was warned not to talk more,
and he closed up likeaciam. He has been uneasy and
restless ever since, and dropped a number of remarks
indicating that he was going to take some decided steps
in the matter.

One night he went to Merrick F. Jones, another in-
mate of the juil, and asked bim which of the authori-
ties that had talked to him he could trust.

Jones told him he could trust Deputy Sheriff Ben
South. He sent for the deputy,and told him that
when his father was in the jall, the day of the funeral,
he said to him he was willing to take ten or twelve
years in the penitentiary; that he was an old man and
it would not matter so much to him, while Harvey was
young. The old gentleman does not deny that he
might have made sucha remark. A couple of days
ago James asked the deputy to go and arrest his father,
charging him with the killing of his wife, but not to let
his attorney know it, The deputy refused, telling him
he had no authority, and called the sheriff. Tne sheriff
informed him there must first be an affidavit filed, to
which Harvey replied that he did not know whom to
recommend todo this. The sheriff would not do it
himself on Harvey's request, Harvey then said:

“Could I make that affidavit?”

The sheriff informed him that he would consult the
prosecutor and notify him. He did this, learned he
could, and communicated the fact to Harvey. Harvey

was then brought in the front room of the

jaf. He was repeatedly warned by the pros-
} ecutor and sheriff that if his father was

innocent he should not make the affidavit,
but if he was guilty it was the proper thing
to do.
._ Hesaid he understood the significance of
the act aud wanted to record the affidavit at
once. He was persuaded, however, to desist
until after the action of the grand jury, but,
again repeating his request, he was per-
mitted to file the affidavit, and in the pres-
ence of nearly a dozen persons, and after
the signing of the affidavit acknowledged
the signing of it to be his voluntary act.

It is said now, however, that he has changed

his story somewhat, and says his father might
have murdered Mrs. Harvey. He says he
was upstairs; tuat his father had gone away
from the house some time before with his
stepmother; that they had started to his
sister-in-law’s, Mrs. Jennie Harvey’s; that he
heard heavy footsteps in the kitchen, and
going down found Idalying there across the
wood-box, unconscious and alone. He fur-
ther says there is a by-road leading from the
main road back to the house on another side than
the regular road, by which his father could have re-
turned and done the act.
- Inthé afternoon Marshal Will Sliker and Deputy
Ben South returned from the Harvey home with the
father in custody, and locked him in the upstairs de-
partment of the County Jail. He said:

“T am innocent of any such charge, and bad no con-

nection with the affair whi tever. When my wite and ~

left home at about 12:30 that day to go to my
daughter-in-law’s, Ida was sitting at the table eating
ber dinner, James had madesome excuse and gone
upstairs, and she was alone. We left, and about 4
o'clock was notified, when on the way home, of her
death. James bad not eaten his dinner before I lett.
We wentin a buggy.’’

The old gentleman was considerably affected, and his
eyes filled with tears while talking of the occurrence.
He is nearly sixty-nine years of age, and is one of the
well-known citizens of the county, having been a resi-
dent there almost all his life, living on a. farm about
seven miles west of Wilmington, He has been married
twice, his last wife’s maiden name being* Moore, a
member of one of the oldest and best-known families in

that locality.

ANOTHER VICTORY FOR LEON.

The ‘‘ Dago”’ Bantam Champion Wins a De-
cision Over Jack McKeck.

At the Union Park A. C., New York city, on Jan. 18, the event of
the evening was the bout between Casper Leon and Jack MoKeck,
both of New York city. They were matched to go fifteen rounds,
the weight being 112 pounds. When the bell rang Leon got to work.
He had the longer reach and got his left to the body repeatedly.
McKeck's blows were nearly all stopped, Leon taking things coolly
and waiting for a chance to put in a settler, Leon continued to do
the bulk of the work in the second and third rounds, but McKeck's
defense was clever. McKeck consented to do some leading in the
sixth round, and in a bit of infighting he caught Leon on the jaw
with a short left hook which made Casper slip down on one knee.
Leon got up quickly, however, and sailed im vigorously, Still Me-
Keck held his own. The seventh was even. When the eighth
opened Leon began rushing. Jack was a trifle groggy, but he
stayed the round. MecKeck came up strongly in the ninth, and
neither bad an advantage in the tenth. Leon showed signs of
fatigue in the eleventh, but braced in the twelfth and landed a
couple of heavy rights. McKeck rallied and made au even bresk of
the round, Leon cut loose in the thirteenth, but his an‘agonist did
just as well, the fighting growing fast and furious. Io the four-
teenth Leon again resorted to rushing, and soon staggered Jack.
The last round was all in Leon's favor, aud Referee Tom O'Rourke
gave him the decision.

Fitzsimmons is in New York, presumably waiting for news from
Stuart before establishing himself iu training quarters.

Corbett, on the other hand, is already training, following out a
line of action which began with a mild preliminary course at Asbury
Park, N. J., late in the summer, and continued carefully up to the
present time. His intention Is to goto California on a visit to his home
about the first of the month, after which he will locate his training
quarters within easy access to the battleground, D.n Stuart having
agreed to give Fitzsimmons and him a ‘‘quiet’’ tir sufficiently far
in advance to enable them to select desirable . ~- ‘.s for estab-
lishing training quarters.

As yet Corbett is just as much in ignorance of the precise locality
of the battleground as anybody else. When asked the other day
where he would train, he said:

“Well, I can’t answer that,as I do not know where Mr. Stuart
intends to have us fight. If be picks out a piace in the Seuth or io
Mexico I will train in Texas, as I like the climate and can arrange
matters there quickly. lam not anxious about the training part of
it, as I consider myself in very good condition now. I have been
taking the best care of myself for several months and have been
doing light work for nine weeks. I am now heavy aad feel as
strong and fast as I ever did, so the final preparation does not worry
me. Of course one cannot do himself justice in training when he
has other things on his hands, as I have, but I have made the best
of it and am satisfied with the result,”

The show will close about the first of next month and by that time
training quarters will have been selected.

For the past ten or twelve weeks Corbett has been undergoing a
course of light preliminary training. Even while “on the road’’ he
rarely allowed a day to go by without spending two or three hours
in a local gymnasium. While in New York he frequented Wood's
gymouasium daily. His method was, after alight breakfast at the
Gerlach, to repair at once to Wood's, accompanied by Manager Ed
Thurnaer, Sparring Partner Con McVey anda helper. Soon after
arriving the champion was busy changing to his gymoasium cos-
tume, and at 11:30 o'clock he entered the room.

First he tackled the flying rings to limber himself up some, and
then he hit the bag a few punches. He tugged ata chest machine,
then, taking a very smal! pair of dumb-bells, he began systematic
exercise, going through a number of motions until he felt the effects.
After this came the chest weight, with all the weight on, and he
worked hard for a few minutes. He seemed to change very quick!»
from one to the other, and did not drag his steps in moving about.
A skillful partner was there to play handball with him, and they
were at it.

Corbett is an adept at handball. He serves finely and his work is
quick and sure. He did not seem to tire in the least, and while the

TO SWELL THE SIDE WAGER.

kept up for over a half hour, and then Corbett tried the wrist ma-
chine, working at it for some time. Corbett then put on the gloves
with any of his friends who happened along, somet/mes with little
Johnny Bebrens, the 105-pound boxer, of Detroit. When the latter
put on the gloves the exhibition was amusing, the one towering over
six feet and weighing 185 pounds or so, and the other five feet three
inches and weighing about 110. The idea was Corbett's own, and
he coaxed Bebrens to hit him as often ashe could. The little fellow
found a bard undertaking before him and his leads fell short,
scarcely ever passing the gloved guard. Corbett was dancing and
jumping, the bout helping him in leg work.

The last feature was the sparring between Corbett and McVey.
They went three rounds, the first of five minutes, the second of
seven and the third of about twelve. Corbett was all over, out and
in, dodging and ducking, and McVey could not land on him, Me-
Vey tried for the face in the first round, but never reached the head.
Later they rehearsed blows, and Corbett iudulged in his drawing on
of his opponent. He would poke his head out, and a lead from Mc-
Vey meant an escape and areturn. McVey was thoroughly tired at
the end, while Corbett was fresh and ready to go another hour. In
all, he had worked fast for an hour and a half, and was distressed
but very little. Corbett followed with a long run on the indoor
track in the gallery and even this did not wind him. Meantime
McVey was relieving himself, having stopped in the t b se
of a blow on the stomach. McVey said it was in the close work and
the punch was a short right which made him very weary.

Corbett at work and Corbett at play are two different individuals,
On the stage and in talk he is very mild-mannered and easy-going,
but there is a set look about him when he starts working. Jn the

| sparring he did not give a stage exhibition, but with set eyes and a

vicious look, he was business throughout. In his fight with Sulll-
van it was said that he had the look of a fiend as it progressed, and
it is easily understood that such a thing is right.

As far as Corbett going back is concerned, that is the veriest rot.
He is as fast as ever, is stronger and his wind now seems strong
enough to stand him good in a longer fight than was that with Sul-
livan. He has developed about the shoulders and neck and his fists
shoot out quickly when he lets go, his aim, too, being excellent.
There are no wasted swings, the entire work showing science, and
there is a reason for his every return. In the clinches he is strong
and can give McVey, who is a big, strong wrestler, all he wants in
the breakaway. And Corbett is very handy with a punch when
they come to close quarters.

His work was surprising forthe speed and stamina shown. The
hard part of the game will come during the month preceding the
fight. Then it will be no child's play, but stern, rigorous devotion
to duty under Charley White's direction. The latter prepared Fitz-
simmons at Coney Island and Corpus Christi for the meeting with
Corbett at Hot Springs, and bis aid will be invaluable to Corbett
now.

Speaking about the site of the proposed battle ground the other
day, Corbett said:

“I only hope Mr. Stuart will not be troubled ia locating the place.
This thing has been prolonged until the people are naturally tired,
and you can say for me that I will be on hand and ready w fight.”

Regarding the complaint made by Fitzsimmons in relation to the
outside privileges, such as photographing the battle, Corbett said he
did not blame Fitzsimmons, as he had objected tolt. If there is to
be any more money than the purse in the match he wants his part
of it, and the statement that Stuart had agreed to do the right thing
in case he let any privilege of the sort seemed to suit him. But as
to the amount of the stake he did not like the intrpretation from
the Fitzsimmons side.

“I put up $5,000 for my share of the stake when I signed the arti-
cles,"’ he observed, ‘‘and also gave Mr. Smith $2500 to guarantee
my appearance in thering. AsI before stated, that was when I
had a match with Sharkey in view, and did not want to put up
$10,000 in each affair at the same time. He now says he fs willing to
make it $10,000 a side, and all I can say in reply is that I will at-
tend to that ina short time. When I was in New York and wrote to
him about making it $10,000 he never answered by letter, but now
that 1 am in the far West this is «prungon me, There is no ques-
tion about the stake if they really want it twice the amount I have
deposited, but I want to see their $5,000 up first. When itis in Al
Smith's hands I will talk business."’

M’KEEVER NOT SO GOOD.

Jack Daly, of Wilmington, Gave Him a Warm
Argument.

Charley McKeever the other evening adopted such foul tactics in
his bout in Philadelphia with Jack Daly, of Wilmington, that had
the contest been for a decision he would have been disqualified.
There were nearly 3,000 persons present, and the man who has de-
signs on the lightweight championship aroused the indignation of
the spectators to such a pitch that they hissed and hooted him to
such an extent that twice im the fourth round the referee had to stop
the boxers and threaten to end the go at that stage. The set-to was
ot the hurricane order all the way through, and while Daly had the
advantage of the first two rounds, McKeever had the better of the
last four. McKeever's fouls were committed iu the breakaways, and
were so palpable that every one in the building saw them, one being
committed while Daly had both his arms outstretched and was
breaking as clear as possible. Although McKeever had the better of
the bout, Daly was wildly cheered by the spectators as he left the
ring, while a wave of hisses swept over the house and not one man
applauded when McKeever moved toward the dressing-room.

There were several preliminary bouts. Danny McMahon, of De-
troit, bested Paddy McPhillips, of Philadelphia, and Stanton Ab-
bott, the English lightweight, and Jack Bennett, of Pittsburg, boxed
six rounds with honors about even.

In the absence of anything more important
the idle persiflage of current comment seems to be directed to the prob-
able location where the big fight will take place rather than the more
perplexing one which involves the possibility of it not taking place
atall, Strange as it may seem, Dan Stuart's efforts to locate a
battlegrouud are affording the sporting fry, big and little, more con-
cern than the question whether Bob and Jim will be there when the
eventful and auspicious time arrives. As I have said before, there
seems to be a settled conviction in everybody's mind that the two
mean business, aud that if any bitch occurs this time the fault will
be laid at the door of the big Texan projector.

Certain it is that that worthy gentleman is doing all he can to
mystify the public regarding his ultimate intentions in the way of
selecting a spot upon which the long-deferred and anxiously awaited
settlement of the controversy may be effected. One day the story
emanates, from some presumably reliable source, that Mexico will
have the hovur of entertainiug the two fistic celebrities and their
friends on St. Patrick's Day. Stuart hardly lets the types grow
cold before he is out with a denial, backed up with a significant
refusal to aid in solving the problem. If Nevada is suggested an
equally strenuous denial comes forth, corroborated in a by

prize ring record that might be cut off in yard lengths. It took
Creedon four rounds to put acrimp in bis career, and the cham
piouship aspirations of the man from Salt Lake were nipped in the
bad.

Since that eventful episode Creedon has been ‘resting,’ as they
say in theatrical parlance, in expectation of getting something
definite in the way of news from the gold country in response to the
acceptance of McCoy's challenge, which I cabled over early In the

ship honors he needn't go so far away from home in search of it.
John Quinn, who is Peter Maher's financial man, has a middie-
weight unknown whom he will match against either Creedon or Mo-
Coy, at weight, and bet §2,500 on the side. There is also seme talk
of matching Peter Maher against Creedon, but I do net believe
the latter or his backers would seriously consider such a propo-
sition.

Strange as it may seem, Creedon has not evinced any very great

t of enthusi over the offer to meet McCoy in Johannesburg.
His acceptance was something of a compromise affair, occasioned by
the fact that the local followers of the game were woodering why he
hesitated almost two weeks before giving the slightest inthaation
regarding his intentions. It may be that he regards a $5,000 purse
in London with more favor than a purse of three times that size iu
Jobannesburg. MoCoy is evidently anxious to get on with
Creedon, and if the latter is really as anxious to meet MoCoy as
he professes to be, it should rot be very long before they come to-
gether.

Some pugilists seem to know when they
have had enough. Steve O'Donnell is still talking fight, or rather
his energetic, but voluble, manager is, which is about the same
thing, only more so. Last week when the latter was making another
determined effort to inject Steve into the pugilistic whirl, he coupled
the latter’s name with Joe Choynski with such persistency that
“Parson” Davies felt it becoming in him to “get into the game.”
He replied with an offer to match Choynski against O'Donnell for the
entire gate receipts, with the additional consideration of authorizing
a convenient friend to wager $1,000 with another convenient friend of
the opposing side on the result. He also offered to match Bob Arm-
strong against O'Donnell for the entire purse or gate receipts. Up
to date nothing further has been heard from the O'Donnell end, a
fact which leads me to doubt the sincerity of his intentions.

In the midst of the controversy Stuart calmly moves his traps and
belongings to Reno, Nev., and proceeds to attend to the preliminary
details of the impending affair from that remote centre.

Surface indications wouldn't any more point to Nevada being the
theatre of action than any of the bordering States or Territories, but
recalling certain correspondence which I was permitted to see at
the time negotiations were pending for Corbett and Sharkey to meet
for the second time, [am now impressed with the belief that the
city of Carson, Nev., will figure upon the pages of contemporaneous
history as the scene of the most important fistic event the world has
ever seen.

When Corbett and Sharkey were negotiating for a second meet-
ing the National Club of San Francisco startled the fistic world
with an offer of a $20,000 purse. The receipts for any boxing show
given in the Californian metropoiis failed to justify such seeming
extravagance, and the authenticity ‘of the offer, and the responsi
bility of the projectors were questioned until it trauspired that the
leading citizens of Carson were at the back of the proposed affair.
After figuring out the boom value to the city and the financial profit
to be netted from the visitors who might be counted upon to come in
by the thousands, the Carsonites saw their way clear to giving a
bonus of $15,000 to the National Club people, leaving the latter to
manage the affair and make whatever surplus there was over and
above the $5 000 additional toward making up the purse,

Everything went along swimmingly for a time and it looked
mighty like as if Corbett and the Sailor would have it out. How-
ever, before things got down to a business point some one had an at-
tack of ‘‘cold feet." Fitz cut in and busted the conuecting thread
with an offer to fight Sharkey; it looked like casy money to the
Californiaus and they took iton. Then came the talk about Fitz-
simmons and Corbett. Just prior to the time they got ready for
action | happened one day to drop something to Wheelock, Stuart's
Fidus Achatcs, about the Carson City bonus, and in his suave, un-
compromising and seeming indifferent way he remarked that it
was worth looking into.

The way he said it didn’t indicate much interest in the matter,
but he evidently didn’t lose any time in letting Stuart know all the
facts, for a few days after the latter made a hurried visit to the
metropolis and we talked it wver.

Having no personal interest in the affair, I dismissed the subject
from my mind uutil it was recalled the other day when I learned
that Stuart bad established his headquarters at Reno, Nev., within
striking distance of Carson, and that the telegraph companies were
planning the erection of an independent line between the two cities
for the purpose of giving increased telegraphic facilities.

If I am correct in surmising that Carson City, with the bonus,
etc., ete., is part of Stuart's scheme, I can oaly reassure him of my
best wishes in his success. He is deserving of all the profit to be
made out of the venture. He proved himself to be a daring, cour-
ageous sportsman when, in the face of the Hot Springs flasco and
the losses entailed in bringing Fitz and Maher together, he devoted
his time, labor and energy toward bringing Fitz and Corbett into the
ring, a scheme the mere contemplation of which, under the circum
stances, would have thrown more experienced promoters into
hysterics.

was afforded him to “‘turnitup." That was the opinion of Referee
Roche and hundreds of others who sat up close to the ringside and
in a position to see in minute detail everything that was going on.
In the third round he looked as if he didn t want togo any further, but
Dixon, who expressed a determination to give hin: a good walloping
in return for past offences, ‘‘pulled a bit’ to enable Murphy to steady
himself. The affair was too one-sided to deserve any extended ref-
erence.

duced it at Albany, where it is now under consideration by the law
makers, The amendment Is as follows:—

“But no »erson shall take part, as a principal, in a sparring exhi-
bition except on the certificate of two duly licensed physicians,
stating that they have examined said principals twice; once three
days and once two hours previous to the exhibition, and that such

The full bill will then be as follows:

“Prize Fighting and Sparring Exhibitions, Aiding Therein, etc.—
A person who, within this State, ergages in, instigates, aids, en-
courazes or does any act to further a contention, or fight, without
weapons, between two or more persons, or a fight commonly called a
ring or prize fight, either within or without the State, or who en-
gages in a public or private sparring exhibition, with or without
gloves, within the State, at which an admission fee is charged or re-
ceived, either directly or indirectiy, or who sends or publishes a

bition or fight, or carries or delivers such a challenge or acceptance,
or trains or assists any person in training or preparing for such a
contention, exhibition or fight, is guilty of a misdemeanor; provided,
however, that sparring exhibitions with gloves of not jess than five
ounces each in weight may be held by a domestic incorporated ath
letic association in a building leased by it for athletic purposes only
for at least one year, or in a building owne1 and occupied by such
association, but no person shall take part,as a principal, ina
sparring exhibition except on the certificate of two duly licensed
physicians, stating that they have examined said principals twice;
once three days, and once two hours previous to the exhibition, aud
that such principals are in proper physical condition to take part in
a sparring exhibition,

“This act shall take effect September first, eighteen hundred and
ninety -seven."*

The hullabaloo and cry raised by pulpit and press against the so-
catied boxing evil seems to necessitate the amendment to the law
going®into effect at once. As it is, all the leading clubs are employ
ing physicians for the purpose suggested, and a prompt and ready
acquiescence to public demand to prevent a repetition of the previous
unfortunate occurr¢hce will soften the now prevailing sentiment
against the sport. .

John L, Sullivan will join a vaudeville company, with
which be intends to playin this country, England, Ireland and
Scotland. Manager Frank Dunn will furnish | the capital, and the

company of vaudeville artists, and in addition to their turns Sulll-
van will appear in ove scene taken from “The Man From Boston’
and also do statue posing.

Corbett intends to bring out something new in the line
of pugiliem. It has been said that he cannot hit, but he intends to
show that he can, and while training wili have somebody in front of
him to take the stiffest punches. He is having made in Chicago »
pneamatic sbieid which will protect his opponent from injury, aud
he will employ some strong fellow to wear It. McVey will be too
busy wrestling and sparring with him, and the plan is to engage
someone equally strong to take the punches. There will be guards
for the face and jaw, and for the heart aod wind, and Corbett will
be able to punch as bard as he sees fit.

THE CRONIN TRAGEDY in Chicago is gradually
being transformed into a farce-comedy. Mr.

- Woodruff shows up as the low comedy man and

he is earnestly fitting himself for the posi-
tion of snake editor on some ono of our great

dailies. It will be so cold that it will snowin
‘bed on any day when Mr. Woodruff’s fecund

brain does not originate a new Munchausenism,
aliasa “confession.” As a champion dodger
of the truth Mr. Woodruff can have our piece
of cake and the ‘‘Poiice Gazette” belt.

JAKE KILRAIN, the “Police Gazette” cham-
pion, showed his kindnéss of heart by appear-
ing at the Madison Square Garden last week
and sparring for the benefit of the. Johnstown
sufferers. Charley Mitchell also came on from
Baltimore and appeared as: Jake’s opponent

protempore. From the manner in which Kil-
rain: was received there was no mistaking the
feeling of the multitude of sporting men

present. eee Se

Txat fateful Black Friday on the Conemaugh
will never be forgotten by the residents of the
once peaceful valley. Sunday witnessed dis-
heartening scenes there, and our correspond-
onts and artists have pictured them true to the
life. .The werk of reelaiming the bodies still
goes bravely on, and the section is now under
military espionage, and will remain in that
state until all danger of dissatisfaction on the
part of the laborers is over. There is no
way of telling exactly how many lost their lives
in the horror, and the roster will not be made
until the Judgment Day rolls around. Let us
hope that it has been overestimated, and let us
pray that the world will never again witness
such a calamity.

‘THE summer season has opened at Coney
Island, Rockaway Beach, Gien Island, Long
Branch, Fire- Island. Newport, Saratoga, and,
in fact, all over.. Soon myriads of citizens, male
and female, will be disporting themselves in
the surf or seeking secluded nooks in moun-
tain morasses, forests and fens, where they
may give dull care the go-by and whoop up en-
joyment to its altitudinum. May they all en-
joy themselves! This cannot be done, how-
ever, unless they subseribe for the PoLicE Ga-
ZETTE.ere they start. Good luck to everybody,
except the man who puts a high shirt collar on
the top of his beer glass. and the cheeky ram-
rod who charges 25.cents for a milk punch
made of alleged milk and perhaps Santa Cruz!

PAUL POTTER’S PARAGRAPH.

I sit and wait the curtain’s rise, and watch the sea of faces
That sparkles into laughing waves beneath the gasalier,
I sce the variegated craft towed safely to their places,
By busy little ushers, gliding swiftly far and near,

I hear the buzz of voices, and of the boy who nefits us
* Librettos of the opera!’ —the swishing of the fans—

The rustle of the programmes, and the manager who tells us
With depreciating bow, the dismal failure of his pians.

The orchestra begins to wheeze an antiquated mediey—

The curtain rises with a hiteh—the hero rolls his eyes—
The chorus gambols through its part—the faring gas burns
redly,

As in a blaze of colored light tho villain falls and dies.

I gaze upon the funny man—but dreamily and sadly—
My laugh is forced and hollow—

Yes, my laugh. if there is a laugh at all, is forced
and hollow when Mr. Fred Solomon, who is now the

crack comedian of the Casino, tries to get off a —
a vayilet or asonglet.

He is so labored, the good man, and his accent
smacketh so decidedly of Petticoat Lane, and his hu-
mor is so plainly much manufactured.

Edwin Stevens, whom I praised when in “Said
Pasha,” disappointed me as the chief of “The
Brigands” at the Casino the other night.

There is something lacking in his performance, a
dash, a brio, an entrain, an I don’t know what you'd
call it.

We are used to seeing Urquhart stick-like and Rice
monotonons, but Stevens, whom some compare with
Hopper, truly here was a disappointment. -

But, as Shakespeare, alias Bacon, remarks:

“Expectation fails,
And most oft there where most it promises.”’

Lillian Russell almost makes up for all the short-
comings of all the rest.

The stage presence of Russell is so fine, her voice is
of such magnificent vol-
ume and quality, her
acting even, strange as
this may appear, is r0
free and debonair in
this operette that the
silly sallies of Solomon,
the foghorn toot of
Urquhart,the cavernous
snile of Rice are alinost
forgotten in the shower
of melody and glow of
radiance that emanate
from her.

There are a number of
pretty girls up at the
Casino just now.

They look pretty from
front, atany rate, how-
ever seedy they may
look with their make-up
off and their everyday smile on.

Sylvia Gerrish has a good pair of legs.

Anna O'Keefe is a better singer than a looker.

Georgie Dennin is getting too tat.

Laura Russell looks like a good one.

Emma Lawrence, Edith Edward and Gertie Silver-
thorn have admirers.

I regret to record another fizzle at Niblo’s Garden.

somme there.

**A Noble Son” did it.

tier,” an old-fashioned .

atale incidenta.

The play is all abonta
murder committed by a

And Percy Aunting, John Burke, R. A. Koberts, Fred

like all the rest of the characters in the play, assumes

I can’t understand why all the members of the cast
didn’t take the trouble to get,the pronunciation of
that simple word ‘‘monsieur” straight and clear.

It was ‘‘monsoor,” and ‘‘munsoor,” and ‘“minsir,”’
and ‘‘munsir,” and everything but what was correct.

which Hubert Wilke, as

Apropos of the success Paul Potter has had with
“The Directory,” in which Donnelly and Girard ap-
peared, I am reminded of oneof the brilliant news-
paper exploits of that very clever writer. It illustrates
the value of a pertinent paragraph to an actress.
**There is nothing like a short paragraph,” said Mr.

Potter to me some time ago. ‘I remember when I haa |.

charge of the foreign news of the Herald, Mary Ander-
son made her debut in London. I received a long dis-
patch from London telling me of the actress’ triumph.
The dispatch was not signed, and I thought. it was a
bogus puff, so I killed most of it. A few weeks later I
sailed for London to take charge of the Herald office
there. ‘Say, Potter,’ said Mr. Bennett to me one day,
shortly after my arrival, ‘what made you kill that
Anderson dispatch? I had that dispatch cabled ex-
préssly. I wanted it to go.’ ‘Well,’ said I, ‘Mr, Ben-
nett, the dispatch was not signed. I was suspicious as
to its authenticity. But if you really want to boom Miss
Anderson, if you'll give me carte blanche, I’11 manufac-
ture and cable an item to New York that will go the
rounds of the press of the United States, and it won’t
cost you much either.’ Bennett told me to go ahead
and doit. A few weeks later 1 sent on the following

laconic paragraph:

Sa ‘Mary Anderson, who
Sage was seen in the Duke
of Portland’s box at the
_- Opera last night, ie now

creditably reported en-

gaged to that wealthy

nobleman.” You remem-

ber how that item went

the rounds. That’s how
itonginated. I promised Bennett to advertise Ander-
son and I did,”

Tommy Rassell, who played Little Lord Fauntleroy
80 well at the Broadway Theatre this winter, laid the
corner stone of the Weat End Theatre, which Mr. A.
H. Wood is now building up in Harlem.

Tommy Russell got on the platform quite boldly,
seemed cool in spite of the broiling sun, and said :

“(LADIES AND GENTLEMEN: I propose to lay the cor-
ner stone of the West End Theatre. [Applause.] This
is a very hot day, but I can say I am glad to be here.
(Renewed applanse.] In laying the corner stone of
this theatre I hope it will meet with every success,
and I hope Harlem will be some time the centre of
New York.

Langtry, in her new play, seems to have caught on
in Chicago,

The play, “Esther Sandraz,” isa dracentiention by
Grundy of a novel by Adolphe Belot.

Esther, the heroine, is a Portuguese beauty, an,orphan,
who has established herself in Paris, and by her
charms and talents readily makes her way into the
most exclusive circles.

“Henri Vandelle, the hero, is a young man of affairs,
who loves her devotedly. Their courtship is a dream
of heaven. Henri becomes financially involved, and,
in his extremity, turns to Henrietta Dounay, whom he
courts,while Esther, unconscious of treachery, lavishes
her caresses upon him: Henrietta is immensely rich
and‘encourages his advances, and finally weds him,

the affair being hastened by the bridegroom, who dex.

teronsly assigns false reasons. Esther first learns of
her desertion the evening of the marriage, and direct-
w following the revelation comes an infuriated quar-
el between Vandelte and a former rival for Henrietta’s

i hand. .In the melee Esther Sandraz is shot by Vandelle,

the pistol having been aimed in self-defence at his
‘vanquished rival. In the denouement the grieffemitten
‘Vandelle caresses the lips of the only woman he has
loyed, revealing in the passion that rends him all the
plot by which hesacrificed his bonor and the woman
of his choice. Henrietta, with others, is a witness of the
scene, and prompted by Esther, who gasps her pardon
with her last breath, forgives her faithless huaband,
relinquishes the half of
her fortune to him, and
dismisses him forever.

HANDSOME BILLY BURNETT.

(WirH PortralrT.]}

In this issue we publish a portrait of Billy Burnett,
the leading sporting man of Washington, D. C.
Burnett hails from Rochester, N. Y., and his name is
a by-word with sporting men in all partsof the conn- ©
try. Heisa backer of billiard players, oarsmen/and

HIS ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION.

nina eas

Jake Kilrain, under the mentorship of Charley Mitch-
ell. is in training near Baltimore. and he is working
hard to reduce his weight so that he will be in first-class
condition when the all-eventful day arrives. Kilrain’s
modus operandi of training is as follows: Long walk and
the regular daily breather of ten or twenty miles, after
which he is thoroughly rubbed down. He then takes a
shower-bath and is again thoroughly rubbed with
coarse towels until his skin resembles a rosy peach.
He dons clean sweaters and then takes his morning re-
past with arelish. Kilrain’s breakfast consists of dry
toast, a pint of tea (which is drunk from a bottle), mut-
ton chops and boiled fresh eggs. :

After breakfast he reads the PoLiIcE Gazerre and the
daily papers and then goes to his improvised. gymna-
sium, swings clubs and lifts dumb-bells, and then goes
on a long tramp cross-country at a quick pace. He is
again rubbed down, puts on clean flannels and sits

REPORTERS VISIT THE CHAMPION.

down to his dinner, which consists ot porterhouse
steak, spinnach, toast, rice pudding aud a bottle of
Bass’ ale. *4
After the noon-day meal he rests for an hour, and
then wrestles with Mitchell, boxes, and spends the
interim in fighting the bag or the foot-ball until supper
time arrives. His supper consists of mutton chops,
tea in a bottle and toast. After the evening meal he
takes a stroll or plays billiards, and at 9 P. M. he goes
to bed and does not arike’ until 5 A. M. Kilrain isa
first-class man to attend to his training. and there is
not the least doubt but that he will be in tiptop condi-
tion when the time arrives for the fight.
John L. Sullivan is being trained by Jack Barnett and
Mike Cleary. On June 13 he weighed 220 pounds, and
looks to be a perfect mass of muscle. Sullivan says he
will step into theringin the finest condition he was
ever in, and would make the fight of his life.
Sullivan gets up at 6, and he takes light exercise and

a short walk, and has breakfasted at 8 o'clock, At 10
his trainers put on him three heavy sweat shirts, a
heavy double-breasted coat and vest and heavy shoes,
and he starts on his daily walk. He carries while walk-
ing a club weighing six pounds. His walks consist of
twelve miles over the hills, through the woods, getting
back abont 1. ri
After dinner and after resting a while he exercises at

putting the shot, using iron balls weighing 18 pounds

and 12 pounds. At4he strips and punishes the. ball.
I saw him pound a ball for nine minutes without a
stop, and he appeared fresh when he stopped. This is
the longest I ever saw a man punch a ball, and he Lit
it with terrific force. He is put to bed promptly at 10.
He will enter the ring weighing about 2065 pounds.

Jake Kilrain came to town to attend the boxing tour-

the Johnstown snfferers, on June 13, and it was a finan-
cial success. Nearly three thousand persons attended
the affair, and many expected to see John L. Sullivan,
who been advertised to appear, and who had con-
sented td lend himeeif as an attraction to bring dollars
into the charity fund so needful to assist the unfortu-
nate sufferers of the great calamity. Jake Kilrain, the
champion of America, and Charley Mitchell, the box-
ing champion, had also volunteered, and Kilrain had
agreed to pay his own expenses from Baltimore and
leave his training quarters in order to assist in bring:

Sheedy, the handsome, witty sporting man, was the

Tremendous cheering and no hisses followed this
