down from the mountaio side. It will be mon Byet
before Johnstown proper can be reached’ sufficiently
for people to begin to build with’ ‘any certainty as to

the exact location of their lots. Meanwhile, they are :

living with those who survived, while all are depend-
ent upon the alms of the world.

There is no more sickness than there was a week ago,
a gratifying and surprising fact when it is considered
that the breaking up of the houses and the digging into
the debris might naturally be supposed to stir up
germs that would lead to contagion. The medical gys-
tem is well attended tu. The only department in which
it is not thorough, and, to do it justice, in which it

does not pretend to be thorough, is in the statistics of
the dead. H
There is really no method whatever in this. All bodies
found are supposed to be reported, but the rule has
not been enforced, and until the canvass of the living
is made it will be impossible to ascertain the exact

number. It will not fall much under the estimate
formed by the newspaper correspondents who were
here through the worst of the scenes. The regime!

mauistracy insist that the loss is less, but they ot
be induced ‘to revee! the reasons which lead them to
their belief. “

The charitable organizations with headquarters here
are doing magnificent work. Their doors are open
to all the sufferers, and the attention bestowed upon
them by the voluntary workers is worthy of all praise.

There is a great drift yet of the wreck and the dead
about Stony Bridge, and, although dynamite has t
freely used, it will be a long time before the chamel
of the river will be cleared and the sickening sight’ re-
moved.

Asurvey of the valley of death discovers mapy
strange scenes. Yesterday an unknown girl, alinost’
nude, was found in the woods near Cambria City, wan-
dering about aimlessly. She had been crazed by the
cruel blow, and kindly hearts led her to a place of
safety.

Our artists have depicted other strange scenes that
can be witnessed hereabouts any day in the week.
They are strange, weird scenes, and they make the on-
looker weary and sick at heart.

There is no telling when the last body will be recov-
ered. TheJudgment Day .alone will reckon up the
final counting.

_ FORTUNE'S FAVORITES.

Two Families ‘Made Happy by the Louisiana State
Lottery.

“I think you are foolish not to keep at least one
whole conpon for youreelf,” said a friend to James
‘Adams, a well-known hay and grain dealer, who, hav-"
ing purchased: a half dozen tickets for the May draw-
ing of thé ‘Louisiana State Lottery, was engaged in die,

posing ot half interests in each.to some of his acquaint |
| ances.

“It seems to me,”’ continued the fnend, “that
you are sacrificing your luck; try for the whole prize.”

“I will for once,” laughed Adams; “but I’ve no luck
in that direction; never had.”

He did as he said. ensconsed the ticket, a twentieth
of 50.416, in an inside corner of his pocketbook and
walked off thinking no more of it. May l4th, the day
of the drawing, came, and with others Mr. Adamb
pressed up to the bulletin board whereon the lucky
‘numbers were written. Much to his delight he recog:
nized on the first line the figures of bis own ticket,
entitling him tothe handsome sum of $15,000. With-
out an instant’s delay he placed the lucky coupon with
Wells, Fargo & Co. for collection, and a few day? ago
he received his money. Mr. Adams possesses consid-
erable property in various parts of the city, a portion
of which was mortgaged. His first application of the
windfall was to relieve hiinself of these incumbrances,

and with & portion of ‘the remainder he proposes to ‘

take a trip to‘Europe.

A lottery ticket has often enough enabled twé lovers
‘to unite their lives, but one seldom hears of a: similar
office being performed by the same agency for a mar
ried couple. This has been the experience of Mr.

Alfred ‘and Mra. Margaret Friot, who. a few days be- |

fore May léth, were at daggers drawn. They kept Stall
57, Washington market, as a cheese and butter stand,
and both wereso thoroughly dissatisfied with the other
that each applied for a divorce. Their applications
were denied. atrange to say. but they continued to live
separate. One day after the drawing of the Louisiana
State Lottery, the two met, and the husband proudly
exhibited a coupon numbered 50.416. entitling him to
one-twentieth of the capital prize of $300,000—$15,000.
“Come to my arms.” said the erstwhile disgruntled
wife, and they embraced exuberantly. The next thing
was to collect the money, and the pair descended on
the Wells, Farzo Bank post haste, sent their coupon
throngh to New Orleans, and a few days ago they re-
ceived their prize in gold coin. They are now on their
way to Enrope, with hearts that once more beat in
unison.—San Francisco (Cal.) Call, June 5.

Sy ENGLISH 1 MIDDLE-WEIGHTS.

“the prize fight between “Alec Bur Burns and Ted Pritchard, for
a4 and the middle weight championship of England, has
i Bocsead the topic in sporting circles in England for some time, and

dependent of the large stakes hundreds of dollars were wager-

Hon the result. Burns is twenty-eight years of age, and he is
tane of a family of tour brothers who have followed the trade of
“engineers, and also the pastime of boxing. An elder brother,
- dohn, was, before he turned Socialist leader and County Coun-
selllor, a well-known performer with the mittens, though his rec.
“ord is nothing compared with that of the subject of this notice.
[-Alec has been before the public for some years, and has engaged
Ain numberless cappetitions and matches of this class, though he
‘never, to our knowledge, fought a knuckle fight for a money
stake.

Ted Pritchard is younger than his opponent by some years,
and has been known in London for a much shorter period. His
‘knowledge of the art, which he has up to now practised so well,
‘was-gained by traveling with young Bub Webb as one ot the

; [2 latter’s troupe of boxers, an occupation that affords plenty of

Opportunity for acquiring proficiency.

Pritchard made his first bow in a competition before a London
audience at Frank Hinde’s
Christmas show at the
Aquarium, wherein he de-
teated Dave Galvin, Dick
Leary and Dave Burke in

Another case was the Bon Soir affair at the Ameri-

It is my opinion that the tonnage: for Custom ‘
House purposes has about &s much reference to the” power ofa
yacht as has the size of her rudder head as ‘to her speed. ” This .
tonnage, theoretically, represents the interior capacity of a
yacht, but in my upinien, practically, it does hots t any-
thing. Thus the English. cup-hunter, Valkyrie,. by the ald of
her long overhangs, tons more than the Galatea, a yacht 17 feet
longer on the water line. The tonnage is based upon the length
on deck from the bow to the rudder post, the extreme beam,
and the depth from top to deck beams. To iliustrate how little
can be learne:i from the tonnage, it is only necessary to com-
pare Yarana and Petroniila. Yarana is four feet longer on the
water line than Petronilla, yet the latter shows 85'tons, while

Yarana was almost uniformally successful in beating the

-SERGT. MICHAEL McCARTHY.

K Police Officer of Whom Brooklyn,
N. Y., May Well be Proud.

Sergeant Michael McCarthy, of the Second Precinct,
Brooklyn, i8 a born policeman, and has friends by the

hundreds on the other side of the river. The genial
sergeant, who i8 in direct line fora captaincy, was ap-
pointod patrolman in 1871, and in 1875 a roundsman.
He is one of the brAvextand most efficient officers on
the police force. Me has rescued a number of persons
from drowning and from burning buildings at the
risk of hisown life, and in February, 188%, duringa
fire that occurred at No. 2 McKinney street, Brooklyn,
he rescued atamily consisting of the father, mother
and five children. For his services rendered on this
occasion and others he was highly complimented by
Superintendent Campbell and ex-Commissioner Part-
ridge, allof which is duly recorded in the books of
the department. The sergeant is as moder’ as he is
brave and efficient, and enjoys equally the confidence
of his superiors and associates. Sergeant McCarthy
isa veteran of the Fourteenth Regiment, N. G.8.N. Y.,
‘otherwise known as the ‘Red Devils,” is a member of
Odell Post. G. A. R., and of the Society of the Army of
the Potomac, and president of the Officers’ Association
of the Brooklyn Police Department. In addition to

this he is a good fellow.

WILLING TO WRESTLE ANYBODY.

{Wira PorTRAIT.]

Jas. H. Falkner was born in Manchester, Eng.. in the
year of 1857, stands 5 feet 4 inches high and weighs, in
condition, 135 pounds. He commenced wrestling when
sixteen years of age, and when twenty-one
years of age won the light-weight champion-
ship of England from Jack Eckersly at Farnsworgh
recreation grounds, near Bolton, the match lasting
two days. Since his arrival in America he has proved
himself to be atertor amongst the leading wrestlers
of this country. Mr. Falkner arrived in New York
Dec. 16, 1884, since which time he has downed Tom
Caunon, Sam Barry, Jack Hart, William Coupe, Ben
Jones, Owney McCarty, Andre Christol and Edward
Bibby, and has wrestled a draw with the famous Acton.
He is open to all comers.

A MANIAC’S DEED.

‘(SUBJECT OF ¥ ILLUSTRATION. ]

“A farmer named Lucien Freeman, aged thirty years,
who lived with his mother at Meriden, N. H., became
temporarily insane one night recently, and while in
that condition took an ax and went to a room occupied
by a friend named John Morgan. Seeing Morgan
asleep, he struck him two blows with the ax on the
head, killing him instantly. He then went to his moth-
er’s room and, overpowering her, killed her in a like
manner. After this he walked two miles, in almost a
nude condition, to the house of Orrville Eaton, and,
arousing Mr. Eaton, told him what he had done. The
sheriff was sent for, and he put Freeman under arrest.
Freeman is subject to hereditary insane spells, and
Morgan had slept in the house to look after him.

SHOT THE BURGLAR.

[ScBJEcT OF ILLUSTRATION. ]

"A ‘wanda entered the store of Mr. Edward Kimball.
of Saccarappa, Me.. one night recently, but in so doing
he awoke- Kimball, who sleeps inthe store. Kimball
waited until the intruder got inside and then shot at
him. He nrissed the burglar, who jumped through a
window. Kimball fired another shot, which hit the
marander in one of his hips, and brought him down.
He gave the name of James White, and is badly in-
jured. Kimball had his place robbed several weeks
ago,

DRAGGED TO DEATH BY MASKED MEN.

|SuBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION.,

Albert Martin, a mulatto, assaulted Mra. John Gillis
about four miles outside of Port Iuron, Mich., two
weeks avo. He was caught and locked up. Ever since
he committed the crime there was much talk of lynch-

ing, but the threats were made so loud that it was |

thought the rage of the people would easily cool, and
so the police did not pay much attention to the threats.
A crowd of masked men approached the jail early one
morning recently, bound and gagged ‘lurnkey La-
rocke, battered down the jail door, grabbed Martin,
put a rope around his neck and dragged hii out of the
jail, down the stairs, and-so along the street. where
they hanged him and then riddled his body with bul-
lets until he was dead.

AN EXPLOSION IN A SQUIB FACTORY.

[Subs OF ILLUSTRATION. |

Shortly after 12 o’clock on the afternoon of June 13 a
squib factory located at St. Clair, three miles north of
Pottaville, Pa., was totally wrecked by an explosion of
several kegs of powder kept in the storage house. The
building took fire after the explosion, and Mamie Mail,
aged about 19 years, was burned todeath. Her charred
reinains were found in the debria after the fire wua ex-
tinguished. The manager of the factory, Harry Hayes,
escaped fronf the building after the explosion, bus he
is 80 badly burned that he cannot recover. Heisa
married man, with two children. The factory em-
ployed about fifty girls, who had gone home for din-
ner when the terrible explosion took place. Tne cause
of the explosion is a mystery.

SAVAGE FIGHT WITH TRAMPS.

[SUBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION. |

For some time past a gang of tramps have been raid-
ing on the farmers of Greenbrook, N. J. A few days
ago a detachment of the Elizabeth police surrounded
a sand-house at the above-named place and surprised
the gang asleep. A terrible fizht ensued, which ended
in the capture of Pete Murray and the ringleader of
the gang, named Robert Barry. Barry fought savagely
and had all his clothes torn from his body. He had to
be knocked senseless before they conld master him.
The rest of the gang escaped to the woods near by.

For ten years the waters of the rapids knew no
seekers after fame, untilon June 9, 1900, Peter Nissen

Ilis dog

In 1886 he announced at Philadelphia that he would |

go through the Whirlpool rapids in a barrel of his own
construction. The time was three years after Capt.
Webb, the English champion, had gone down to death
in the terrible currents. Graham’s statement caused
people familiar with the Niagara River to laugh.

The steamer Maid of the Mist bad previously to this
been the only craft to carry human freight through
the gorge in safety, and to think that a man in a barrel
would excel the feat of Joel Robinson and his boat on
June 6, 1861, seemed ridiculous. The conclusion was
that the body of a dead Philadelphia cooper would
have to be searched for between the rapids and falls
should Graham attempt the feat.

When Graham and his barrel reached Niagara he
was told this, Everybody said he was foolish; that he had
no idea of the terrific force of the waves that tumble
between the mighty cliffs of the narrowest part of the
famous gorge, just below the great railway bridges.

Graham looked the rapids and the gorge over care- |

fully and determined to make the voyage. He selected
the afternoon of Sunday, July 11, 1886, for his per-
formance. <A great crowd gathered, many of them
remembering how Webb went down to death and ex-
pecting to witness another and similar tragedy.

Graham was on time to the minute, and, protected
only by bis barrel, a boat towed him out into the main
current and set him adrift. It was 4:50 P, M., and
eight minutes later he wasin the Whirlpool. Within
two minutes the barrel had passed out of the pool and
was enroute to Lewiston, where it was picked up and
Graham was found to be alive and uninjured.

This performance amazed everybody.
also to belittle the power of the great rapids and the

It seemed |

Whirlpool. Elevator owners, hackmen, and those who |

made «# living through the coming of visitors to see the
“nastiest bit of water in the world” began to call for a
stoppage of such performances in the rapids, realizing
that they could no longer tell peoplethat the waters
were unconquered, Webb’s death had brought money
to their coffers, for many people longed to look upou
the waves that had beaten the life out of England's
champion swimmer,

Undaunted, Graham showed that he still had his
nerve by announcing a second trip through the rapids
for Thursday, Aug. 19, 1886. He said he would keep his
head out of the barrel, so that all who came to witness
the performance might see him, There was a bigger
crowd than at his first exhibition,

It was a remarkable sight to see the barrel boat with
a buman head above it bob up and down through the
One moment it would be high in the air, the
next out of sigint under the foamy wash of the rapids.

This time Graham landed in the whirlpool on the
Canadian side, the stream failing to shoot his barrel
into the currents of the outlet. In the passage through
the rapids tne wave that killed Capt, Webb struck
Grabam a terrible blow on one side of his head, and
from that day to this he has never heard a sound in
that ear. Thus did the rapids give Graham something
to remember,

waves,

On June 15, 1887, Graham made a third trip through
the rapids, and on Aug. 25, 1889, be used a much
smaller barrel in making a fourth trip, passing entirely
through the gorge to Lewiston.

Graham ’s performances attracted others to Niagara
in search of fame. Among them were George Hazlett,
William Potts and Sadie Allen, all barrel navigators.

From Boston came William J. Kendall, a policeman,
who made the swim through the rapids wearing a life
preserver. James Scott of Lewiston went down to
death in trying to swim from the Whirlpool to Lewis-
ton. Charles Alexander Percy made several boat trips,
on one of which from the pool to Lewiston he was ac-
companied by William A, Dittrick.

THIS WAS A FAKE KID MURPHY.

Oue of the rankest counterfeits that was ever thrown
before the public as a pugilist, was handed up before
the Eutaw A. C., at Baltimore, Md.,on April 27, by
Sam Solomon, of the Capital City, in the shape of
Young Murphy, of Chicago.

Murphy was scheduled to go fifteen rounds with
Tommy Lowe. also of Washington. The so-called
Chicagoan lasted exactly two minutes and twenty-five
seconds, Inthe brief time that he lasted, he demon-
strated that be did not know the first rudiments of the
boxing game,

Bobby Dobbs was knocked out in the eighteenth
round of his bout with Young J. L. Sullivan, at Liver-
pool, England, on April 27. The original contest was
scheduied tor twenty rounds for a purse and $200 a side.

A HOT BOUT AT POTTSVILLE.

In the hottest contest ever pulled off at Pottsville,
Pa., Nick Hollywood, of Coaldale, received the decision
over Joe Wagner, of New York, before the Twentieth
Century Physical Culture Club on April 27.

It was Holiywood’s fight for fully ten rounds, It

looked serious for Hollywood, who was the aggressor
throughout the contest, in the fourteenth round, when
Wagner by a remarkable recovery, shot right and left
into him, knocked him down twice and once through
the ropes into the audience. The gong saved Holly-
| wood from a defeat inthis round. In the final round
Hollywood recovered and finished strong.

DEAD HEATS ON THE TURF

WHEN

THEY OCCUR ARE

EXCITING, BUT UNUSUAL

How the Judge of Position at an American Race

Course Picks Out the Winning Horse.

WHEN HENRY OF NAVARRE

A Remarkable Race in Australia When Three Horses Ran Together, and Sent Over

AND DOMINO BROKE EVEN.

the Gourse Again, Finished Together a Second Time.

NE frequently hears of dead heats on |
the turf, but few bave any definite
idea concerning them, or what they
represent other than two or more
horses finishing abreast. The term
undoubtedly came from the old days
before the war, when the bulk of

racing was in what were termed heats of stated dis-

tances, This meaning that the full distance had to be
covered three, or possibly more times before the win-
ner was finally selected. Therefore, asthe loser in each
contest was ruled out of further competition a heat
which resulted in no definite winner was dead so far as

utility went,and had to be run over again for a

decision.

What is not generally grasped, however, Is the cir-
cumstances surrounding such a race, Two or more
horses start from a given line and race to the first turn,
the majority of races being run on an elliptic, and prac-
tically all the dead heats occurring there. At this turn
certain advantage must be gained by one of the horses
getting around close to the rail, the outside horse travel-
ing 80 much further. Two horses seldom run head and
head allthe way. Then, asthe finish approaches, the
two draw closer and closer together, and finally flash
past the Judge so aligned he cannot tell which was in
front.

The judge does not look at these animals as does the
spectator. In his box on a level with the head of the
horses. he stands, Far across the track is A perpendicu-
lar white line down the centre of a broad blackboard.
On the further side of the track, in line with the black-
board, is an upright lance, 10 feet high. A similar lance
appears on the near side of the track, also aligned with
those two, and eight feet further away, where the pub-
lic cannot see it, is still another lance, also in line.
When the race starts, the Judge places an arm chair
with its back to this fourth lance, and, leaning on the
arms with both hands, waits for the norses to enter the
stretch. As they near the finishing point he leans for-
ward, placing his left eye aguinst the lance so that the
sight is obstructed, while with the right eye he brings
the other two lances and the while line on the black-
board into one blended mark. The first nose ACTOSS
that line of vision is the winner, and the difference of
a single inch is clearly shown tothe practiced eve. This
is what the great mass of the visitors do not under-
stand. Itis also impossible to overlook a horse. No
matter where on the track it may be running, close
under the Judge’s nose or right across at the outer rail,
it is equally in view as the animal in the middle of the
track.

The truly marvelous quickness of the human eye is
shown by the fact that a nose finish of, say, four inches,
the breadth of a man’s hand, is represented by about
the one hundred and fiftieth part of a second. The
average length of a horse is nine feet, and the speed
traveled reaches 53 feet to the second, witness the 0:5634
record at Morris Park for five furlongs.

Strange to say, it is not always the leading horse
which first catches the eye of the judge, this being an
apparent contradiction, due to a factor which misleads
many people who see differently from the judge, and
are not slow in insisting he has made a mistake
where the official placing was absolutely correct. This
is because two horses running together constantly vary
as to the leader, unless they are both striding instep.
Thus an extended horse’s nose will show distinctly in
front of the nose of a horse which is gathered fora
stride, with all his feet under him. Yet, at his shoul-
ders, the gathered horse may be distinctly in front.
Thus individuals immediately to the left or to the right
of the finish line, and some distance back from it, may
feel positively certain that their eyes saw so and so, and
be perfectly correct, while the line of the judge’s vision
shows exactly where the horses finished as they flasbed
past the judicial finish line of the race. This may per-
haps be emphasized by the fact that dead heats appear
to be much more frequent in England than in this
country, this being apparently due to the fact that the |
English judge bas no lance arrangement, that he stands
at some distance irom the horses, and that the one
man places the first, second and the third horses, in-
stead of only the first, as does the judge in the metro-
politan racing circuit.

It is, therefore, interesting to note that while there
were no dead heats on the Eastern race tracks in 1903,
there were three in 19094. This isa marked change, as
was shown by a friendly dispute which arose during
the past season on the occasion of one of the dead
heats.

A sporting man made a statement as to such finishes,
and was contradicted by another man, and finally the
matter was reserved for investigation. The records
proved that in the last ten years there had been 20
dead heats, two at Aqueduct, two at Baltimore, seven
at Brighton Beach, two at the Brooklyn course, one at
Morris Park, three at Saratoga, two at Coney Island,
and one at Washington, D.C. the last
from 1884, there have been 163 dead heats in the United

A DEFENSE OF JIU-JITSU

Higashi, the Famous Expert, Issues a Challenge to
All Rough and Tumble Fighters.

WOULD BE A GOOD DEMONSTRATION.

Saito Answers Those Skeptics Who Don’t Believe in a Science Which Has
Stood the Test of Thousands of Years.

By K. SAITO of Nagasaki, Japan.—No. 9.

NLESS the challenge of a well-known
Japanese jiu-jitsu expert is ignored,
there will be a demonstration before
long of the practical value of that

science that will convince the most

skeptical. Higashi has announced
that he will meet any man inarough and tumble en-
counter, everything to go, and he doesn’t draw the line
at size or weight. He is perfectly willing to compete
against any man who may be produced for the purpose.

When Higashi’s actual weight is taken into consider-
ation, the challenge, to the crdinary man, would seem
lixe a most ebsurd one, and there may be those who
will scoff at it, but the fact remains that he has chal-
lenged in good faith and stands ready to make good at
any time,

Up to the present no man has taken up his defy, even
though many have said that Higashi stands no chance
whatever with such an opponent.

At any rate his sincerity, his belief in himself nor his
physical courage can be questioned.

The commonest argument against Jiu-Jitsu is that the
expert cannot secure the holds necessary to a victory,
although it is conceded that the holds themselves are
all right. I have received many letters on the subject,
and the general tenor of them has been:

“Do you expect a man to stand still while you get a
bone-breaking or joint-dislocating
lock on him? What will he be
doing all the time ?”’

There are several ways of an-
swering that.

The average boxer can deliver a
particularly hard blow with his
right hand, sufficient, if landed on
the point of the Jaw, to produce a
knockout, and any good boxer can
knock out an opponent if he lands
right. But isthe other man going
to let him do it? If the blow is
tried and doesn't land on the vul-
nerable spot, does he conclude that
his system is all wrong, and give
upin despair? Does he keep on
trying to land the same blow in
the same place ?

Certainly not.

If he fails to land on the point
of the jaw with his right, he tries
his left for the stomach, or he
upper cuts, or he crosses, or he
tries for the kidneys. He has
many different feints and punches,
allof which be tries until he finally
succeeds in doing what he started
out to do, or succumbs to the
superior cleverness or hitting
ability of his opponent.

So with jiu-jitsu.

The Japanese has no one par-
ticular invincible hold. He, too,
If he fails

to secure a certain hold he tries for

like the boxer, feints.

another one, equally eflective, and
if that also fails, he has many
others which follow in quick suc-
cession. He relies for victory upon
superior speed, cleverness, and a i ea
in detail in
complete knowledge of the human
anatomy. The tender, sensitive
points of the human system are as :
. inevitable.
an open book to him, and he
knows how to take instant advan-
tage of every one. He doesnt as a rule want instant
victories. Ile is taught to allow his opponent to believe
that he (the opponent) is gaining the victory. He per-
mits his man to become over-confident. Just as clever
boxers have simulated grogginess or injury in the ring
for the purpose of courting attack from the man who |
thinks he cannot lose,

I could cite many such cases, but it is not necessary,

READ ALL ABOUT AN OPIUM JOINT IN CHUCK CONNORS GREAT BOOK, BOWERY LIFE---29 CENTS

for even the mention of this must bring instances to
the minds of POLICE GAZETTE readers.

I don't feel that it is necessary for me to attempt to
influence to my way of thinking any man who doesn’t
believe. All I ask is that a closer and more conscien-
tious study be made of this art.

Get the book on Jiu-Jitsu, by M. Ohashi, of Tokio,
which is published by Richard K. Fox, the price of
which is ten cents. It shows a preliminary course of
training, as well as many practical holds. Get yourself
in shape and practice them. Then look my lessons

Government officially recognize it, and engage instruc-

tors for the cadets at Annapolis and West Point.

That point alone ought to be quite enough to convince |

the most skeptical.

I shall be glad to answer any questions on the subject

if they are addressed to me at the PoLIce GAZETTE
office.

JOHNSON TOO GOOD FOR JEFFORDS—

Jack Johnson, who recently lost the decision to

| Marvin Hart, met Jim Jeflords, of California, in the

windup at the Knickerbocker A. C., Philadelphia, on
April 25, but up until the fourth round be gave no indi-

cation that he regarded the stuntin hand very serious- |

ly. Inthe second round, for instance, he dropped Jef-

fords with a short joit to the chin, and while the referee |

was industriously engaged in clocking off the seconds,
Johnson leaned over the ropes and engaged in con-
versation with one of the spectators.

It was not until the fourth round that he showed any
disposition to extend himself, and then it was all over.
Jeffords made a swing with his right and it landed
around Johnson's jaw. The smile which had illumin-
ated Johnson’s face all through the bout vanished, and
then Jeffords was in trouble. Johnson stopped his
phony tactics and let out a few links. He swung his
left viciously into Jeffords’ body. There was a lot of
heft behind the punch, and Jeflords showed a disposi-
tion to hug. Afterthe breakaway it was evident that
Jeflords was willing to apologize for his indiscretion.
He boxed very coyly.

Not so with Johnson. He waded in and before the
spectators realized what had happened he shifted and
planted his left in Jeffords’ works,and the latter went
down and out. Johnson made it clear that there is
nobody in this vicinity who has any business with him,
He simply stalled with Jeffords.

In the semi-windup Jackson ‘and Mississippi evened
up things at the finish.

PHILA. JACK O’BRIEN WHIPPED.

Philadelphia Jack O'Brien lost to Hugo Kelly, of
Chicago, on April 2, in a ten-round bout at 158 pounds.
The match was under the auspices of the Indianapolis
(Ind.) A. C., before one of the largest crowds ever
drawn to the Auditorium by such a contest.

While it was not a clean fight, Kelly earned the de-
cision fairly by earnest, steady fighting and a perfect
willingness to carry the gameto any corner. His work
in the last four rounds overcame O'Brien's slight ad-
vantage gained by shifty tactics early in the fight. The
decision met with the approval of the crowd, Referee
Ryan said that he gave the fight to Kelly because at
no stage of the game did O’Brien show a great willing-
ness to fight, and at the last hung on and clinched to
avoid punishment. After the decision, when O’Brien
made a protest to the referee, he was compelled to
hang on to keep his feet and had to be assisted from
the ring.

In the early rounds O’Brien gained a slight advan-
tage by keeping out of Kelly’s reach, and landing
single blows almost at will, After the fifth round he
was visibly tired, asa result of hard work, and Kelly

NOTHER bomb was thrown
into the colored camp the other day,
when no less a star in the pugilistic
constellation than Battling Nelson,
announced that he would never again
meet a black man ina ring en-
counter; of course, this presumable

slight was intended for Joe Gans, and the supposition
is that the Battier figures bim to be a pretty hard
proposition, too hard, in fact, to involve his reputation
on the outcome of a “go."’ This interesting bit of in
formation cropped out as the result of Joe Macias’
effort to induce the Nelson person to go to Philadelphia
and meet three men of his own choosing, In a series of
six-round bouts. Macias offered Nelson $5,000 for three
contests. Nelson, in accepting, asked that the names
of his prospective opponents be sent him, and Joe
Gans, Willie Fitzgerald, Willie Lewis, Kid Herman,
Adam Ryan and Harry Lewis were named,

Nelson wired back that any white man would do, but
he drew tbe color line. Macias then named Willie
Lewis, Willie Fitzgerald and either Kid Herman or
Adam Ryan gs the men, Nelson accepted them.

The first contest will probably be held on Monday
night, May 15, with Fitzgerald or Willie Lewis as the
Dane’s opponent, and the others on the Monday nights
following.

Another victim for Bob Fitzsimmons has
been found in the person of Mike Schreck, of Cincin
nati, who has agreed to fight the former champion
twenty rounds in San Francisco the first week in July.
The match was made the other day in Chicago, Charlies
Easig was made the stakeholder of the contest and each
man placed $1,000 in his hands as an earnest of his
signature. The men agree to box at catchweights with
five-ounce gloves, the only stipulation being that the
contest must be at least twenty rounds, with San Fran
cisco clubs being given the preference as bidders. Both
men agree not to engage in a championship contest of
any kind prior to their meeting.

Fitzsimmons signed for himself, and Billy Hogan,
manager of Sehreck, signed for the German boxer, al-
though the latter was present at the meeting. Schreck
recently knocked out George Gardiner in Salt Lake
City and gained a name for himself by doing this, al-
though shrewd Judges of boxing have figured for some
time that Gardiner was about done as a first-class
fighter.

Fitz said after signing the articles that be thought he
could solve the Schreck puzzle easily and in short order.

Strange as it seems the devotees of boxing
in New York City are not wildly enthusmstic over the
Frawley bill which wi!l vive amateurs the right to en-
cage in boxing contests. Although it does not offer
much in the way of sport forthe lovers of good hard

fighting, the measure is the entering wedge, and
many special matches between “amateurs” who will
quickly develop will likely figure as the tempting at-
tractions which the athletic clubs wil furnish The

bill limita the length of a contest to fiftee® minutes and

the same men can compete only once in twenty-four |

hours,

This is to prevent a match between “amateurs’’ with
a giudge for fifteen minutes, and after a brief rest have
a fifteen minutes additional assault. Under the old
order of things, before the Horton law, the writer sat
alongside Mayor Grant in the New York Athletic Club
gymnasium, witnessing a special contest between two
lightweight “amateurs."’ Denny Butler, the noted
swimmer, now on the police force in this city, was
master of ceremonies. He announced that the men
would box five rounds. and If at the end of the fifth
round the referee was unable to arrive ata decision he
would order five additional rounds, and so on without
limit. The fight resulted in a knockout at the end ot
the thirteenth round. Thus the members and guests
of New York’s leading athletic club had witnessed a
finish fight under the guise of a limited-round contest.
Should the Frawley bill become a law the fifteen

minutes of boxing is apt to be divided up, either in four |

three-minute rounds, with a minute’s rest between
rounds, or six two-minute rounds, with thirty seconds
rest between rounds. The latter would make a whirl-
wind go replete with action, and would give the
Gothamites something to rave over.

A negro of promising quality who is cutting quite a
figure in lightweight pugilistic circles is Jack Black-
burn, whose extreme cleverness and ability to hit a
knockout biow with one punch has caused nearly all
the lightwe ghts of the country to avoid meeting him
inthe ring. Hew the first American boxer to come

JACK BLACKBURN,

He has driven champion Joe Gans to the
woods, and Eddie Hanlon, Young Corbett, Jimmy
Britt, Willie Fitzgerald, Battling Nelson and other
lightweights of lesser ability have practically confessed
they do not wantany of his game. Blackburn made

| thesame offer to all—133 pounds ringside, or weigh in at

3o0r6 P. M.—but tbey either bad lame shoulders or
were too busy in other directions.

For the reason that the coffee colored Kid from
Indianapolis has fought his way gradually from the
bottom until he is now within striking distance of the
lightweight goal will cause the devotees of the sport to
demand that he receive recognition. When little George
Dixon commenced his championship aspirations fifteen
years ago the mild-mannered, modest mulatto met with
considerable opposition from ring patrons. The ban-
tam and featherweight classes up to that time had not
been invaded by the negro. Dixon went down the line,
and beat every man he was asked to meet. There was
no bluster. His first real championship fight was with
Cal McCarthy, and was declared a draw after seventy
rounds. The men had been four hours and forty min
utes in the ring, and some of the spectators on that
memorable night in February, inthe Boston Club, were
almost as tired as the boxers. Dixon met McCarthy

| one year later, and beat him decisively in twenty-two

rounds, For twelve years he was the unbeaten cham-
pion of the world, and in all those vears was a credit to
the ring, despite his color.

Blackburn possesses many of the characteristics of
Dixon. He is modest, unassuming, rarely quibbles
over conditions and is determined to prove that he is
the best lightweight in this country, if not in the world.
Who will dispute his right? Gans says no, while all
the rest offer excuses too flimsy for consideration.
When the Indianapolis lightweight first came East his
work, which was of the finished Order, did not please
the Philadelphia crowds, When he began to let out a
link of his punching ability, then all other aspirants
took fright. His decisive victory over Fighting Joe
Allen recently, the punishment he administered to
Grim when they met and his victories over scores of

| lightweights, stamp him as one of the most dangerous

to cover postage, and when I tell you that 50,000 of them

have already been sold to POLICE GAZETTE readers, its
value may be readily determined.

Cc. D. B., Harrisburg, Pa.—During a game of base-
ball; A bets that the man at the bat will make a hit; B
bets he will not. The batter knocks a grounder out to
shortstop, who picka it up, throws it to first base and
puts the runner out; who gets the money? Now in
rendering your decision on this question please bear in
mind that there was nothing said about what kind of a
hit he was to make, and A claims the money inasmuch
as the batter made a fair hit, asdescribed by J. J. Me-
Graw, on page 97 of his Book of Rules for 1905. B
claims that a hit in baseball talk means that a batter
must hit the ball safe and make his base before it is a
hit, and he was betting under that impression, although
he said nothing at the time he accepted the bet. A
claims, however, that he is technically wrong, for
when a batter hits the ball safe and makes his base it is
then a base hit, as described by McGraw on page 110;
and tie fact that newspapers or others abbreviate the
expression or term by dropping the word base from in
front of the word bit for their own particular con-
venience, expecting others to take for granted what they
mean, does not make it right or proper? .....B wins. A
hit in betting or in the phraseology of the game is a
“safe hit.’”’ A’s claim is foolish.

c. P. D., Gary, W. Va.--A runner on second starts
for third just as the pitcher delivers the ball, and the
batter holds out his hand allowing the ball to bit it and
roll away from the catcher. The umpire allows the
runner, who moved from second to third, to remain
there, but calls the batter out? There is a runner on
third base, and a man at bat, who is in the box to bat
right handed, and the next batter up, who was near
there, steps into the left hand batters’ box to ask about
a decision that has just been made, The pitcher, in-
stead of holding the ball until be was removed from the
box, delivered same, which the catcher did not attempt
to field, allowing it to pass him and the runner on third
came home, The umpire called it a ball, as it was not
fairly delivered, and allowed the run to score, explain-
ing that it was a passed ball that the catcher did not
attempt to field. and the player in the left hand batters’
box did not interfere in any way? The batter knocks
a ground ball between first and second, which is fielded
by the second baseman, who throws the ball to first,
which is covered by the first baseman and he catches
the throw, or in other words, holds the ball just a
moment before the runner reaches first, who bumps
into the first baseman, both men falling, and the first
baseman dropped the ball. The umpire called the run-
ner out ? 1. The batter was out for interterence, and
the runner should have been sent back
The runner should have been sent back, and neitnera
ball or strike called. There is no rule for any such
play, but the umpire should bave used common sense,
Both the pitcher and catcher were interfered with, and
the offender could have been put out of the game, as it
was obviously an unfair advantage taken. The easiest
way out of the difficulty was for the umpire to make
the pitch null and void and begin all overagain. 3. It
was up to the umpire whether the collision was inten-
tional on the part of the batter. If he thought so, the
batter was out. If the ball and runner got to the base
at the same time,and the collision unavoidable. the
batter should have been decided safe.

RECORDS SMASHED.

Two new world’s records and sensational perform-
ances in neurly every of the events marked the
University cf Pennsylvania's tenth annual relay carni-
val on Franklin Field, Philadelphia, on April 29.

In the four mile relay race for the championship of
America, the University of Michigan won for the third
time in succession, setting anew mark of 18 minutes,
25 3.5 seconds, an average of 4:36 for each mile. The
second world mark to be bettered was in the discus
throw, which again went to Michigan. Garrelis hurled
the missile 135 feet, 44 Inch. Although this beats the
world’s record it was not allowed to stand, because the

KRALL’S HUGGING SAVED HIM.

Charley Knox, of Altoona, and George Krall, of
Philadelphia, met before the Bellevue A. C., at Altoona,
Pa., on April 26, in a six-round bout, the latter staying
the limit only because of his persistency in clinging to
Knox,

The semi-windup was a grueling mill between Kid
Ryall, of Chicago, and Young Nelson, of Denver, the
lads going six rounds to even honors,

TWIN SULLIVAN HAS THE PUNCH.

After three rounds of very fast fighting Mike (Twin)
Sullivan, of Cambridge, knocked out Tommy Coch-
rane, Of Philadelphia, with a right solar plexus punch
after two minutes of fighting in the fourth round of
their scheduled twelve-round bout at the Eastern A. C.,
Portland, Me., on April 26.

It was a fight that brought the spectators to their
feet, and Sullivan’s great experience and ring general-
ship won it amid a wild demonstration.

HERMAN AND LEWIS DRAW.

Kid Herman, of Chicago, went on off the reel against
Harry Lewis, of Philadelphia, and putup a remarkaLle
fifteen-round battle to a draw atthe Fourth Regiment
Armory before the Eureka A. C., on April 28.

It was one of the hottest fights ever seen in that city,
and there were many in the large crowd who thought
that the Western lad should have had the verdict be- |
cause of his cleaner work at all times.

Lewis was ten pounds lighter than Herman and was
ureatly cheered for his fine showing.

Kid Sullivan, of Washington, who was to have fought
Lewis, sprained his ankle white training and Herman |
was Called in at the last moment.

Herman floored Lewis in the eighth and was himself

COLE WAS THERE.

The windup at the Keystone A. C., Philadelphia, Pa.,
on April 29, was a fiercely fought battle. The contestants
were George Cole, of Trenton, N. J., and Walter John-
son, of Boston. The latter outweighed Cole by many
pounds. He has a punch, which fact he demonstrated
in the second round by dropping Cole for the full count.

Cole recuperated quickly, and from there on he took
the upper band, his cleverness being very apparent.
Cole had Johnson very shaky in the fifth round, and
the bell must have been a very welcome relief to him,

Cole continued his aggressive tactics in the sixth,
cutting Johnson up badly and dropping him. The
Boston man wisely took the count, and when he came
up he was bleeding bacly and was allin when the bell

ended the hostilities. Cole was a winner.

A VICTORY FOR COMMON SENSE IN IOWA.

By this time everybody knows and under-
stands who wants to be honest and means to be
square, that the PoLIcE GAZETTE is the people’s
illustrated weekly. It represents nothing but
lawful news, and its pictures are not only
accurate and artistic but morally irreproach-
able.

In the city of Des Moines, Iowa, reside two
fellows whose actions are a public scandal and
a disgrace to American civilization. One of
them is named Potts, and the other Pierce, and
itis safe to say of them that the record of Titus
Oates or of Jonathan Wild is fragrant reading
compared with their careers as spies, sneaks
and informers. These two men, for example,
while “operating” in behalf of Prohibition, have
committed outrages on sick and defenceless
women and children which, if perpetrated on
Americans outside of the United States, would
have spurred our government to declare war.
The worst and most infamous acts of British
tyranny in Ireland are deeds of gentleness com-
pared with the atrocious performances of these
two abhorred and detestable Iowans.

Some time ago Potts, acting in concert with a
little petty Jeffreys, Johnson by name, who
scandalizes law by acting as a justice, scared
and intimidated a newsdealer named Mose
Jacobs into surrendering his entire stock of
Pontice GAZETTES. At the same time one W. G.
Higiey, a newsdealer doing- business in the
Kirkwood, Des Moines, was not only arrested
for selling the PonicE GAzETTE, but his home
was searched without warrant or authority in a
manner which would have legally justified him
in shooting the invaders like the dogs that they
are,

In spite, however, of the conceited Pharisaical

malignity of ‘Titus Oates Potts and his “pal,” |.

Johnson, the Grand Jury, before whom Higley’s
case was sent, including such typical Americans
as Foreman Daniel Gerberich, T. W. Havens,
E. 8S. Sayre, James Crabtree, A. G. Nye, Peter
Ringgenberg and Ellis F. Randolph, threw out
the charge and indignantly ordered Mr. Higley’s
release. To those honest and courageous gen-
tlemen, for it requires a rare courage to oppose
malice and hypocrisy disguised in the garb of
religion and morality, every liberty-loving
American in Iowa ought to raise his hat.

But Titus Oates Potts and Jonathan Wild
Pierce were not abashed by their crushing de-
feat at the hands of the grand jury. Other men
would have either transferred their sneaking
energies elsewhere or else stolen in the middle
of a dark night to some neighboring duck pond,
and by a commendable act of suicide relieved
the State of Iowa of the odium of harboring
them. Instead, these two lineal descendants
of Judas Iseariot went out of town to Capitol
Park, a suburb of Des Moines, and obtaining a
search warrant (to which they had no earthly
right), raided the premises of a barber named
Reeler and seized his solitary copy of the
POLICE GAZETTE!

To sucha depth has the Pharisaism of Des
Moines deseended!

Now what.we want to say 1s this—and we
mean every word of what we say—unless the
action of the grand jury in the Higley case is
sustained and the “operations” of Titus Oates
Potts and Jonathan Wild Pierce promptly sup-

pressed, we will take bates to employ the same
doctrine of law, so-called, against the daily
papeets of Iowa as they allow to be used against
the PoLICE GAZETTE.

to put the daily press of Iowa on our side by
making a pretty effective demonstration of the
fact that they are just as much at the merey of
creatures like Potts and Pieree as w e are,

T his is what sporting men eal] “a straight
tip.” and our Iowa friends can bet their money
on it.

Editor and Proprietor.

STAGE SKIMMINGS.

THE INDIFFERENCE of raneptiitelion companies to
the convenience of the public is indicated in the expe-
rience of two young ladies, members of the ‘‘Adonis”
company recently onthe road. Miss Leila Cavanagh |
and her companion were passengers on a through train
from Buffalo to Philadelphia to go over the Erie and
Phil: Sea and Reading railroads. .When nearing
Jamestown, N. Y., the conductor came to them with
directions ae they must change cars at that point for
the balance of their journey, They left the cars in a
pouring rain, and just as the train drew out the station
agent rushed up hurriedly saying there was a mistake,
thev should have remained where they were. Of course
it was too late to do anything but wait for twelve hours
for another train, being put to an expense withal for
the natural requirements of the day. The ladies were
indignant and inconvenienced, and felt as though some
redress should be given. When they finally reached
Homellsville they encountered the superintendent,
Henry 8S. Billings, of. the Mills Building, to whom they
poured forth their grievances, and who told them he
had already heard the particulars by mail and the con-
ductor was to blame. ‘“‘But what are you going to do?’
asked Miss Cavanagh, “I will give you a berth on the
sleeper teenight,” he replied. ‘‘What about our loss ?
we were to play to-night, what about our expenses to-
day ?” “Oh, we can’t do anything about that.” ‘‘Do
you live in Philadelphia?” was his next query. “Ido
not; I go there to play,” Miss Cavanagh answered,
“Oh, then it will save you to-night’s bozrd,” the super-
intendent said. ‘it is outrageous,” she continued.
“Well, there’s no use talking.” Mr. Billings spitefully
observed, “‘it’s like a drowned man, if he’s drowned
he’s drowned, and there is no help for it.””, *“‘Then you
should put on your tickets that any one is liable to
drowning on your road,” rejoined Miss Cavanagh. This
is all the satisfaction they could obtain.

Fanny Rice, of the Carleton company, is a Boston
girl, and after the manner of the girls of the hub of
**culchaw,” she affects quill pens and large penman-

ship. The
other eve-
ning a gen-
tleman
connectéd
with the
local press
sent an au-
tograph al-
bum back
on the
stage with
@ request
for the au-
tograph of Miss Rice. She was playing ‘““Nanon” at the
time, and in her artless manner said that she would be
happy to write her name, but she couldn’t do so without
a quill pen, and she couldn't possibly go to her hotel
and get one. Thenit occurred to her to send to the
property man and ask fora quill. That functionary
thought the lady was jesting, and he obligingly said he
would bring her a dozen, He was as good as his word,
for he brought her the big, white, live goose which is
used in *‘Nanon.” ‘Props’ is a handy man himself,
but his eyes fairly stuck out when Miss Rice coolly
plucked a feather from the tail of the goose, and then
with a knife deftly made her pen, and a moment later
her name graced a snowy page in the album.

HE I8 A PATRON OF THE DRAMA, is the United States
Marshal at Louisville. In a practical way and un-
mixed with any self-seeking, as became a modést man,
this official the other day furnished a triumphant ex-
ample of the esteem in which’ he holds the theatre. By
the operation of law the gentleman was made cus-
todian of the liberty of certain Kentuckians. True
bills had been found against them, and though the
proof was overwhelming the nature of the alleged
offense appealed with irresistible pathos to the right
feeling of the community. The prisoners were
in custody for making moonshine whisky. They
had been ‘arrested away up in thse ;mountains,
and there they were, in the city of ‘Bourbon
Belle” and Mary Anderson, pining in confinement,
guarded by many hirelings, cut off from the society of
friends, and all the while wanting to go to the theatre.
Artless children of the wild solitude! They loved the
drama, For years, and remote from the haunts of man,
they conducted a manufacturing business. They were
producers—hard toiling men in an industry that is
native to Kentucky soil. Small wonder then that the
large-hearted official should provide them with some
relaxation. The exciting ‘‘Ranch King” was to be seen
at a play-house, so the captive moonshiners were es-
corted to the performance. But the marshal didn’t
stop at that. He took the moonshiners’ fnends to the
theatre and all the witnesses, too, and in the party
there were exactly 400 men. The marshal paid for it
all out of his own pocket, and all over Kentucky his
fame rings as a gentleman, a scholar and a good judge
—of the drama.

I HAD A DELIGHTFUL EVENING of it at Wallack’s thea-
tre the other night. Ihad taken my seat comfortably
prepared to enjoy *“‘Mr. Grundy’s Mouse Trap’’—at
least prepared to try and do so—when a rather flashy,
large-sized woman pulled down the seat in front of me,
and then taking an air cushion from under her arm,
she blew it oat—apparently with some difficulty—
screwed it up and sat down. Presently, after the cur-

WHAT IS THE SHOW business coming to? The latest
addition is Binns, the ex-hangman, who is “doing the
British provinces,”’ and reveals his art for the enter-
tainment of crowds who collect to see him perform the
final trick. The subject is a wax figure. The showman
first gives a biographical sketch of Binns, and then the
curtain is run up, revealing a scaffold with the regular
cross beam, and the subject standing on the drop,
&trapped hands and feet. A surpliced chaplain stands
on one hang and a uniformed jail governor on the
other; while the reporters watch the grim proceedings.
Binns, black bagin hand, steps forward, arranges the
rope, places the noose round the subject's neck, and
when the feeling of the spectators has been wrought to
an intense pitch, draws the bolt, and the wax figure
disappears into the pit beneath. Then Mr. Binns holds
a levee, during which the band plays, ‘‘Hark! I hear an
angel sing.”

CLARA MorRIs excessive and presumably unneces-
sary stage waits continue to be a source of justifiable
complaint with her audiences. On Monday night at
the Grand Opera House the curtain remained down
twenty-five minutes between Acts two and three and
twenty minutes between Acts three and four. These
delays are an annoyance to the public, which is begin-
ning to believe that there is no need of them. An ac-
tress who was with Miss Morris last season tells me
that the aggravating waits between the acts in her per-
formances are solely due to the whimsical moodst%tof the
star. If the trouble lies, as has been managerially given
forth for years past,in the direction of physical ail-
ment, Miss Morris has my sympathy, as well as her
spectators. If she is not strong enough to perform her
duties as other actresses are expected to do, it wouldsbe
far wiser for her to retire. She has sufficient means to
leave the stage comfortably.”

A SINGULAR ACCIDENT HAPPENED to Mr. Osmund
Tearle on the stage of Wallack’s recently. It was a
matter of dressing, or I should rather say, undressing,
which set the audience to tittering without the actor
having the remotest idea of what it was allabout. The
mistake was, of course, rectified as soon ashe got off
the stage from his “scene.” Precisely the same thing
happened to W. H. Crane on the second night of the
*‘Henrietta” at the Union Square, and what added to
the mortification of the actor was that he had to re-

r main in view of the audience for halfan hour. When

Crane heard of Tearle’s misfortune, he wrote him a
note accusing him of stealing some of his original busi-
ness, and requesting that, as a matter of professional
courtesy, Tearle should not do it again. There is no
danger. .

Mu, ABBEY HAS AN UNDERSTUDY for every part in
“The Mouse Trap,” and it isa partof the duty of the
ladies and gentlemen thus engaged to report every
evening at the stage door of Wallack’s theatre and sign
a book. The system is an excellent one, because if
carried out to the letter—and I understand it is—it be-
comes almost an impossibility for an audience to be
disappointed. Mr. J. W. Pigott, who happens to be en-
gaged at Wallack’s theatre, although out of the bill, is
one of those who have to sign the book as. understudy
for Charles Groves. That done,he rushes off to his cozy
little room at the Lotos Club and works on one of his
plays. I believe he does a good deal of this sort of work,
and does it well, although none of his plays have yet
been produced.

IN HIS NEW PLAY, ‘‘Monbars,” R. B. Mantell is not al-
ways that splendid specimen of masculine beauty he
has made so familiar to American audiences. In fact.
it is only in the first act that he is the elegant gentle-
man of the handsome countenance and stunning at-
tire. Afterward the prettiness is laid aside and Mantell
is seen as a rough-featured man in whom the evidences
of mental suffering are depicted. In the latter make-up
Mantell will be a novelty to the public, but the ladies
will find it difficult to forgive him for subordinating
his good looks to the demands of dramatic art. Still,
so imposing is Mantell in stature and mein, that he is
fully as striking in one phase of ‘*Monbars” as the
other. It is one thing to be the ‘‘pretty” actor of the
genus ‘‘masher’’ and quite another. to .be a genuine
dramatic artist who succeeds by dint of sheer histriovi>:
talent. WOODEN SPOON.

They Did the Job Themselves.

The ladies of Terre Haute, feeling indignant over the
condition of the village cemetery, assembled the other
day, and, arming themselves with axes, sickles and
similar weapons, repaired thither and commenced cut-
ting out the thistles and weeds that had been left to
ripen there. The sexton felt so scandalized that he
agreed to finish the bch if pases would leave.

Impaled on an Iron Target.

A special from Indianapolis, Ind., Oct. 17, says: Ernest °
Tendleman, a Bee Line employee, while standing on a
platform loading coal on a locomotive tender yester-
day, slipped and fell, striking a switch target, which
was driven through his body. There was a knob on
the end of the target which had to be filed off before he
was extricated. It took thirty-five minutes to remove
the knob and the accumulated rust before he could be
lifted off the target, and during the entire time of this
horrible impalement the man withstood the excruiat-
ing torture. The target was about an inch and a half
in diameter. He was removed to the hospital, and not-
withstanding his horrible injuries the physicians ex-
press a hope of saving the unfortunate man’s life.

Sharp Detective Work.

A special from Chicago, October 15, says: Ah Gung,
a self-entrapped Chinese murderer, was in the cage at
the United States Marshal's office here this afternoon
from Rock Island. United States District Attorney Ew-
ing was notified by the Department of Justice that a
Chinese murderer was on his way West, probably via
Rock Island. The police there were notified just in
time and laid hands upon Ah Gung in the depot. Ade-
tective was put in the cell with him, and in an off-hand
way boasted of several murders, when the Chinaman,
who was only under suspicion, told vauntingly how he
too, had gone too the house of a white woman with
whom he consorted and asked her for money, When
she refused he picked up a heavy miner's candle and
stabbed her several times with the prong, inflicting
fatal wounds. The crime was committed in Alta less
than a’week ago.

An Insane Woman's Fury.

A special from St. Joseph, Mo., Oct. 15, says: There
was brought before the County Court to-day a woman
about 40 years of age, who has already served two
terms in an asylum and who yesterday attempted to
drown herself, and, failing in this, tried to kill her
13-year-old son. The woman’s name is Celia Benson,
and sho resides in Maryville, Nodaway county. She
has four children living in this city, the oldest of whom
is a boy about 15 years of age. The children live on the
banks of the river near the railroad bridge.

Yesterday Mrs. Benson came from Maryville, and,
going directly to the hut, threw herself into the river.
She was rescued by some men and taken to the hut
and locked inaroom. An hour or two later she called
her son William, one of a pair of twins 13 years old,
to her, and knocking outa pane of glass from the win-
dow, told him to shake hands. The boy consented,
and, grabbing him tightly around the wrist. she
wrenched his arm, trying to pull him into the window,
and declaring she would kill him. The boy’s cries for
help brought the other children to his assistance, and
he was liberated. The woman was sent back to Mary-
ville to-day. She has only been out of the asylum a
few months.

THE LUCK OF SOME MEN AND HOW THEY:
ACCEPT IT. :

In the grand monthly drawing of the Louisiana State
Lottery October 11, two-tenths of the capital prize of
one hundred and fifty thousand dollars were sold in
this city, the remaining fractions in New York and
Chicago.

Mr. Laurent Faget, a well-known broker doing busi-
ness at 181 Common street, was the first comer at the
lottery office Wednesday morning, and, on behalf of a
friend, presented for redemption one-tenth of ticket
13,646, entitled to fifteen thousand dollars.

Having received a bank check for that amount Mr.

_Faget bowed his acknowledgment, signed a certificate

and departed.

Scarcely had he withdrawn when in stepped two
gentlemen, Mr. Victor Tujague and afriend. Tujague
had drawn a prize and he desired to claim it in person.
His ticket, 58.490, represented two-tenths of the third
capital prize of twenty thousand dollars, and was en-
titled to four thousand dollars.

Mr. Tujague isa handsome young fellow, native of
New Orleans, apparently twenty-one years of age, and
with his faiher keeps a saloon at 213 Decatur street. He
bought his ticket from a peddler in his neighborhood,
and is thoroughly convinced that fortune is kind in the
distribution of favors. €.

He received a check for four thousand dollars on the
New Orleans National Bank like alittle man, smiled,
and wanted everybody to smile with him, and signed
for the biggest sum of money he ever received for his
individual account, for although his father has usually
joined in his lottery ventures, on this particular occa-
sion the old gentleman ‘“‘guessed he wouldn’t go in,”
for which unrighteous guess the o. g. is doubtless in-
vestigating his horoscope with a view of obliterating
from the firmament his zodiacal sign.

Victor expects to add ‘‘& Son” to the sign which
swings over the door of the house of spiritual refresh-
ments, 213 Decatur street, and to invest in such choice
properties as he may consider bargains. He will not

/ loan money at usurious or even doubtful interest.

The other one-tenth of the one hundred and fifty
thousand dollar prize was drawn yesterday by the Union
| National Bank for acconnt of a depositor.—New Orleans
Picayune, Oct. 15.

“Clara King,” the Girl Burglar.

We present this week another chapter of the history
of Charles Kelly, alias George Harris, the burglar ar-
rested with a ganz of men at Princeton. Ind., who
turned out to bea woman. That published two weeks
ago was given by a woman, who then said her name

was Clara King. and that her home was nowhere,
proves to be a string of falsehoods, which she after-
ward claimed was related for the purpose of shielding
her relatives. Had she given her true name her sisters,
who are respectable and well-to-do, would have heard
of her whereabouts, and this she wanted to avoid until
she was taken to the reform school. Notwithstanding
this precaution, her relations discovered the plight she
was in, and one of her sisters wrote to Sheriff McGary,
informing him who the so-calied Clara King was. It
transpires that her true name is Anna Azbel, and the
sister who wrote to the sheriff was Mrs. Kitchell, of
Vincennes. Another sister and a brother also live in
that city. In Washington she also has a sister. When
Anna first donned the male attire she was living with
her sister and brother-in-law at Washington. One day
when the folks were all away from home she appro-
priated a su't of her brother-in-law’s clothing and
starved out on the turf. When she was arrested she
was dressed in men's clothes, and she was put in jail
along with the other four of the gang, the fact that she
wasafemale not being suspected. Shortly after her
incarceration she told the sheriff she was afraid of some
of the fellows. She claimed she was not of age, and
said she wanted to go to the reform school instead of
the State Prison, and for this the others threatened her
until she became afraid to be with them.

BENT TO KILL.

A Thousand Citizens Form a Band of Vigilantes
in West Virginia.

[SUBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION. |]

A special from Charleston, W. Va., Oct. 18 says: Since
the murder of the Rev. Thomas P. Ryan near Spencer,
Roane county, on last Thursday, it has been learned
that an organized band of regulators of over 1,000
citizens, farmers and others of Jackson, Roane, Kan-
awha, Clay and Gilmer counties, has existed for over
six months. The organization was formed tor the
purpose of self-protection against the bands of rob-
bers and murderers who have run riot in certain
localities of Jackson, Roane and Kanawha counties,
in which stores have been robbed and inoffensive
people made to suffer.

It was about eleven 0 relock ¢ on Thursday night when
the door of the Rev. Mr. Ryan’s mountain home was
crushed in after a shot had been fired through the
front door. Ryan immediately sprang from his bed,
grabbed his shot gun, cocking both barrels, exclaimed:
“What is wanted?” The reply was from an inner door:
“Old man, we want your money and mean to have it.”
Asecond shot was fired, and Kyan exclaimed: ‘‘Mother,”

‘speaking to his wife, ‘I am killed. .I am shot through
the bowels.” Thereupon one. barrel of his shot gun

was discharged, taking effect in the side of the room.
The discharge is supposed to have been caused by his
fall. This causei a halt, and the wife and son took
Ryan to an up stairs room, after which the murderers,

‘five in number, ransacked the lower part of the house,

getting nothing, and overlooking some money near at
hand.

Strong circumstantional evidence pointed to Charles
Coon, George Duff, Jr., Robert M. Duff, and Perry
Drake, for whom warrants were issued. Drake was
quietly arrested at his home. Constable Gibbons and
@ posse of about sixty went to the residence of George
Duff, Sr.. in Kaintuck. where George Duff, Jr., and
Coon were quartered. They had prepared for an as-
sault as they were expecting t-ouble. Coon saw the
posse moving upon the house and coolly uotified two
‘women present to leave as there was going to be ashow.

Upon the approach of the officers Coon warned them
away, and immediately opened fire with a pistol.

The fire was returned by the officers, and for a few
minutes bullets flew thick and fast from each party.
The outlaws took refuge in an up-stairs room, where
Duff was brought downby a shot from arifie. The
officers then surrounded the house and were’ about to
set it on fire when old man Duff, a respectable farmer,
prevailed upon Coon to surrender, which he did. as his
ammunition was about exhausted. Robert M. Duff was
arrested the same day at his house near that of his
father, being surprised by the officers.

On Saturday ncon the prisoners were taken to the
scene of their crime, Ryan’s residence, and a justice
set yesterday for their preliminary trial. Meanwhile
George Duff, jr., died at home on Sunday night. The
restof the prisoners were kept under guard until Sun-
day night, when about 330 masked men took Coon from
the officers and with a rope around his neck hurried
him to a convenient tree. On his way he prayed and
made a confession, which is to be received with doubt.
The substance is, that he-was guilty of participating
in the murder; that Bob and George Duff, jr., were

along, and. that:George Duff fired the fatal shot from

Coon’s revolver. Some say he implicated Drake.
Others say he did not speak of him. Whatever the con-
feasion was he was immediately hanged, dying zame.

_. After the hanging of Coon the regulators went after
Bob Dnff, and hurriedly took him toward the scene of
Coon’s execution. Itis both alleged and denied that
he confessed. Shots: were fired at the mob either by
gnards or friends of Duff. The mob scattcred instant-
ly. In the early morning on Thursday the body of
Bob Duff was found in the public road with his throat
cut ‘entirely across and ° frightful stabs in his chest
almost in ‘sight of the body ef Coon which was still
hanging to:the tree. Neither was touched until late on
Sunday evehing, when a coroner’s jury assembled and
adjourned without discovering anything. Coon, who
had no friends near, was buried by afarmer. Rela-
tions of Duff took charge of his remains and buried
them near his home yesterdy.

Drake was spared, and yesterday he was taken to the
Ryan residence for examination. A large crowd of
armed men were present determined upon lynching
him. He waived examination, and was ordered to the
jail in Charleston forsafekeeping. After much trouble
and danger he reached here to-night under the guard
of Capt. Burnett, of the Eureka Detective Agency, and
a strong posse. No warrants have been issued for Dan
Cunningham, who, it is alleged, was one of the gang of
murderers. As the investigation of the affair pro-
gresses interesting results are certain. Officers are
after others who are said tobe members of the out-
law’s band. Coon came from Tyler, Texas, and called
himself Jesse James.

When Bob Duff was shot ond of the vigilants went to
his body and cut his throat, saying: ‘‘This is in remem-
brance of the young lady school teacher you killed for
her money.” A lady school teacher was killed for her
money in the upper part of Roane county some months
ago, and a warrant was out for Bob Duff, charging him
with the crime. - “ oe

bore marks of several bruises. While the post mortem
examination was pending the police learned that the
team which Harlan had used in his trips to Compton
on the night he was last seen was returned at four
o’clock the following morning to the livery: stable at
which it had been hired. :

There the police ascertained that: Hattie Woolsteen
and her sister. Minnie. had been out riding with’two
unknown. men on the night that Harlan is alleged to
have been murdered, and that they came home about
three o’clock in the morning.

Hattie Woolsteen was arrested, charged with being
an accomplice to the murder of Dr. Harlan, although
she denied all knowledge of the circumstances con-
nected with it. She had been in custody but a few days,
however, when she took a large dose of chloroform
with suicidal intent after having made a confession to
the Chief-of Police.

In this confession Miss Woolsteen says that she and
Harlan had a serious quarrel upon the day preceding
the murdcr, because he then told her he was married,
and therefore he could do nothing to right the wrong
he had done her. She declared that she drew from a
concealed pocket in her dress a small revolver, and,
pointing it to where he was — in the buggy, pulled
the trigger.

‘As she was almost overcome by her angry passion,
however, she did not notice where the bullet struck.
She then drove to a barn in a deserted spot near Comp-
ton, and -dragging the body of Harlan to a heap of
straw and hay, she ignited the barn in the hope of ob-
literating the evidences of hercrime. The girl is said
to have been in custody for four days before this
alleged confession was obtained from her, and no one
was permitted to see her.

Awritof habeas corpus was sued out by reporters
who wanted to interview her, and the foregoing alleged
confession is not accepted as true by many people.
The Chief of Police, in answer to numerous questions,
says that Miss Woolsteen has made contradictory con-
fessions.

She asserts that when Harlan told her that he was
married she cried out in horror and that he was so
overcome by her grief that he drew a revolver from
his pocket, put it to his head and fired, killing himself
instantly. She then buried the body as related in her
other confession.

There is considerable sympathy shown for Miss
Woolsteen 1n Los Anveles, as it is thought that she at-
tempted suicide because of the shameful disclosures
which will be made of her relations with Harlan.

DANCING TU. TURKEYS. ,

Device of a Cruel but Ingenious Barkeeper to Attract
Attention.

|SUBJECT OF ILLUSTRATION.)

In a saloon on Frankfort avenue, below Norris street,
Philadelphia, the other day, a reporter saw two turkeys
dancing to the strains of an orguinette. It was a strange
sight to see the ungainly birds bobDing up and down,
first on one foot. then on the other, then up with both
feet, circling and wheeling around each other, chasse-
ing and chanzing sides, keeping perfect time with an
orguinette turned by the hand of the barkeeper.

All the onlookers were mystified, while the barkeeper
grinned and raked in the nickels which were paid over
the bar by the amused crowd. The reporter, aftér the
crowd werit out, investigated the dancing turkeys and
discovered the method by which they were taught—or
rather compelled—to move. He found that the plan
was ingenious, though crucl. They were made to
dance by nieans of fire. Underneath the sheet iron
cage floor there was a shelf set, leaving a space of
about three inches, into which was fitted an iron slide.
When the man wanted the turkeys to dance he would
quietly get a shovel of live coals from the kitchen stove,
distribute them over the iron slide and slip it into
place under the sheet iron cage floor, and in five min-
utes the turkey fandango would be in full blast. First
one foot would be raised, then the other, and soon, the
pace quickening as the heat increased, until the birds
would be going as fast as they could lift their feet, and
they would keep it up until the floor’ would cool off
again.

“They know what’s coming now as soon as I begin to
fool with the slide,” said the barkeeper, ‘and they be-
gin to dance without waiting forthe floor to be heated.
It’s a good.card for the place while it lasts, but I guess
the' novelty will soon wear off.
myself already.”

J. A. Stewart.

J. A. Stewart is the drug clerk of Wichita. Kan., who
pleaded guilty to selling 208 glasses of Deer, and was
sentenced by the District Court of Sedgwick county to
pay $20,800 and go to jail for seventeen years and four
months. The court simply obeyed the mandates of the
Murray law, in delivering sentence, The plea of
guilty was made with a view on the part of Stewart's
attorney, to show the absurdity of the law, being con-
fident that a pardon could be procured for the defend-
ant. Young Stewart woke up after the sentence and
found himself famous.

Charles Havermyer.

One of the most daring and accomplished forgers in
the country, Charles Landers, escaped from the Still-
water (Minn.) prison last week, where he was serving a
24-year’ sentence.

Landers had almost as many names as there are let-
ters in the alphabet, but his real oneis believed to be
Charles Havermyer. The particular “lay” he was en-
gayed upon was in victimizing jewelry firms, and he
had succeeded in securing many thousands of dollars
before he was finally detected, He is known in tho
Southern country, especially New Orleans, for his
clever crookedness, :

‘James H. Jacobs.

Jacobs has just been found guilty of the killing of
Elmer FE. Quigley at Lancaster, Pa, where the trial
caused a great deal of excitement. The circumstances
of the crime may be recited briefly. On the night of
the llth of December, 1886, Jacobs stabbed Elmer EF,
Quigley in the stontach with a butcher knife. ‘The
affair occurred near Jacobs’ house. Quigley came
along the railroad just outside of the back yard fence *
and remonstrated with Jacobs for abusing his children,
who were crying. After some words Jacobs went into
the house, got the knife, came out and plunged it into
his victim. Quigley died the next day. °

“ Blinkey” Morgan.

Blinkey Morgan’s trial forthe murder of Detective
Hulligan is the sensation of the week at Ravenna, O.,
where the crime occurred. “Blinkey” has one of the
strangest records in the country. He appearsin court
each day attired in a black suit and spotless linen. He
is always cleanly shaven, and has more the appearance
of a college professor than a }urglarand murderer.
He reads human nature ata glance, and was wont to
tell his attorneys to challenge jurors who did not
please him before a question was asked: While in
court the prisoner is guarded by two deputy sheriffs
and a guard of six deputies escort him to and from the
jal. Every precaution is being taken to prevent an at-
tempt at escape.
